systems.name: ZFS / btrfs / APFS snapshots
systems.root_model: Two kinds of root: the live filesystem (implicit, always kept) and named snapshots (dataset@name; snapper numbers; APFS local snapshots). ZFS adds 'holds': named, reference-counted tags on a snapshot, so several parties can each promise to keep it; destroy fails while any hold exists.
systems.delete_model: Deleting a file only removes it from the live root. Blocks are freed when no snapshot references them, so space returns only when the last holding snapshot is destroyed. Snapper and APFS add automatic policy: timeline/number cleanup, and APFS purges local snapshots under space pressure without asking.
systems.user_expectation: 'I deleted 47 GB, so I get 47 GB back.' And: a snapshot is a cheap undo point that is still there until I remove it.
systems.known_failure: The common complaint is the reverse of loss: deletes free nothing because a (often automatic, replication) snapshot still holds the blocks, and a snapshot's reported 'used' is only its unique blocks, so nobody can tell what destroying one will free (TrueNAS forum; vdaluz 'The ZFS snapshot that ate my freed disk space'). Snapper timelines filling the root volume. APFS 'purgeable' space counted as available while writes fail. Actual loss comes from recursive verbs (zfs destroy -r, rollback -r), not from the snapshot model.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Named snapshot = root is the model users learn fastest and it almost never loses data. Its real cost is opacity: c4 must be able to answer 'what holds these bytes' and 'what would dropping this root free'. I ran the second with existing verbs (cat -r | awk | comm): closure(snap1) minus closure(snap2) gave exactly the old a.txt plus the snap1 listing. ZFS holds are the prior art for 'a promise list with several promisers'.

systems.name: Time Machine
systems.root_model: Dated backups presented as folders. Policy is fixed and well known: hourly for 24 h, daily for a month, weekly until the disk is full.
systems.delete_model: Automatic thinning, then oldest-first deletion when the disk fills. No user action, at most a notification.
systems.user_expectation: 'Everything I ever had is in Time Machine.' Many people delete from the Mac to free space and treat the backup as the archive.
systems.known_failure: Depth disappears silently: users report losing the oldest 4-5 months with no notice (MacRumors, Apple Communities). A file deleted from the source long ago vanishes for good when the last backup containing it is thinned. Backblaze Personal is the same shape with a harder edge: an external drive unplugged for 30 days is deleted from the backup; it is a documented policy and a recurring complaint.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Dense-recent / sparse-old thinning is the retention policy ordinary people already accept, and a dated folder per snapshot is the presentation they understand. It is safe only while the store is a second copy. c4's stated worry is the case where the store is the only copy; there, any automatic time-based expiry is destruction the user never chose. Automatic thinning belongs to L2 and must be something the user turned on.

systems.name: git (refs, reflog, gc)
systems.root_model: Named mutable refs (branches, tags), HEAD, index, worktrees, plus the reflog: an automatic per-ref journal of every previous value, and those journal entries are roots too.
systems.delete_model: Nothing is deleted by a user verb. Moving or deleting a ref unroots objects; reflog entries expire (90 days, 30 if unreachable); gc then prunes unreachable loose objects older than gc.pruneExpire (2 weeks). gc --auto runs as a side effect of ordinary commands.
systems.user_expectation: 'If I committed it, it is safe.' This is largely true, and it is why git feels safe despite destructive verbs (reset --hard, branch -D, rebase).
systems.known_failure: (1) Roots outside the store: clone --shared / alternates. The git-clone manual warns that gc in the source repo can corrupt the borrower, because the source cannot see the borrower's refs. (2) The grace period is doing double duty as the concurrency guard for in-flight writers; --prune=now removes it. (3) The opposite failure: you cannot make bytes go away. Force-pushed 'deleted' commits stay fetchable by hash on GitHub (Truffle Security, Neodyme); removal needs a support request. (4) Work never written to the object store (uncommitted edits) is simply gone.
systems.lesson_for_c4: The safest-feeling model in the list is: few named mutable roots + an automatic journal of every past root value + time-based expiry of the journal. v1.1's store journal is a reflog with no refs: I ran it and it is a list of anonymous '<time> <id>' lines, nothing is 'current', nothing is named. Git also shows that 'remove by reachability' and 'destroy these specific bytes' are different problems; git only solved the first.

systems.name: restic
systems.root_model: Snapshot files stored inside the repository (snapshots/), each carrying host, paths, tags, time. The repository itself enumerates its roots.
systems.delete_model: Two steps: 'forget' deletes snapshot files (by ID or by policy --keep-last/-daily/-weekly, grouped by host+paths); 'prune' marks from remaining snapshots and repacks/deletes the rest. Needs an exclusive lock.
systems.user_expectation: 'forget' frees space (it does not); a keep policy applies to 'my backups' (it applies per host+path group).
systems.known_failure: Issue #4612 (restic 0.16.0, rclone backend): listing snapshots failed mid-prune, restic treated the error as 'finding data that is still in use for 0 snapshots' and deleted 128 GiB, the whole repository. Fixed by PR #4618. Also: prune aborting on missing tree blobs (#3213), which is the correct behavior; policy grouping surprises when backup paths change.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Roots in the store, and forget/prune as two separate acts, is right. The one catastrophic bug is the one any reachability rule invites: an empty or unreadable root list is indistinguishable from 'nothing is kept'. The sweep must fail closed on any root-list or closure read error. gc-requirements.md section 5.8 already says this (missing or rehash-failing keep-side object refuses the run); that rule should not be traded away. Note c4 cat -r does NOT fail closed today (see experiments).

systems.name: borg
systems.root_model: Named archives listed in the repository manifest.
systems.delete_model: borg delete / borg prune (keep rules; applies to ALL archives unless restricted by prefix/glob). Since 1.2 space is freed only by 'borg compact'; borg 2 makes prune a soft delete with 'borg undelete' until compact.
systems.user_expectation: Prune rules apply to 'this machine's backups'.
systems.known_failure: Issue #4769: 'borg prune -P--' matched every archive (data loss). Shared repos where one machine's prune thinned another machine's archives because the default scope is everything; docs now say always --dry-run --list first. Append-only mode confusion: prune appears to succeed while nothing is actually removed.
systems.lesson_for_c4: A retention policy scoped by a name pattern is where the loss happens, not in the sweep. The fix borg converged on is a recoverable condemned state between 'dropped' and 'freed' (undelete until compact). c4's gc design has this (trash, --empty-trash); prior art says keep that and it is the part users will rely on.

systems.name: Nix store
systems.root_model: Symlinks under /nix/var/nix/gcroots, profile generations, plus 'indirect roots': a symlink in the user's own directory (./result) registered in gcroots/auto. Running processes are runtime roots.
systems.delete_model: nix-collect-garbage / nix-store --gc deletes everything unreachable from roots. -d also deletes old profile generations. Removing your ./result symlink silently unroots the build.
systems.user_expectation: 'I built it, so it is there.' 'My dev shell is installed.'
systems.known_failure: nix-shell / nix develop environments are not rooted, so a GC forces re-download or rebuild of the whole toolchain (nix-direnv exists to add roots). Stale result symlinks scattered over the disk pin gigabytes nobody can find. nix-collect-garbage -d removes the rollback generations people assumed were their safety net. Loss is tolerable only because everything is rebuildable.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Roots registered as a side effect of the act that produces the thing (nix-build writes the root) work; roots the user must remember to add do not. Indirect roots are the closest prior art to 'a c4m file sitting in a project directory is the promise': it works and dangles gracefully, but then the root set is spread across the filesystem and cannot be listed or trusted. Nix can be loose because content is derivable; c4 originals are not.

systems.name: OSTree
systems.root_model: Refs (branch names) and deployments. Each ref points at a commit; commits chain to parents.
systems.delete_model: ostree prune --refs-only, with --depth=N (how many parent commits per ref to keep) and --keep-younger-than=DATE. Pruned commits leave tombstone markers. Docs add --keep-unreferenced-younger-than to avoid racing with builds that are still writing.
systems.user_expectation: A repo is a build artifact cache with history; old commits can go.
systems.known_failure: Truncated history breaks static deltas and clients upgrading from a pruned commit; flatpak repair struggles with missing objects (flatpak #4618). The author's own documented position: 'you should not use OSTree as a primary content store.'
systems.lesson_for_c4: --depth is the lead's 'one dial' already shipped: depth 0 is ordinary filesystem, depth -1 is full history, per named ref. It works there. Two things came with it: tombstones (so 'deliberately removed' is distinguishable from 'damaged') and a time-based exemption for unreferenced young objects. And its author disclaims primary-storage use, which is exactly the use c4 needs.

systems.name: IPFS (kubo pinning)
systems.root_model: Pins (recursive/direct) and the MFS root, per node. Nothing network-wide. 'ipfs add' pins locally by default; fetched or gateway-served content is cached unpinned.
systems.delete_model: 'ipfs repo gc' removes every unpinned block on that node. Pinning services unpin when you stop paying.
systems.user_expectation: 'It is on IPFS' means the network keeps it. A CID feels like possession.
systems.known_failure: The expectation gap is the whole story: content uploaded through a gateway or service without a pin disappears (600 files gone after weeks, discuss.ipfs.tech; NFT/vault metadata collected within a day). Also real bugs where GC removed content that was rooted: kubo #7008 (MFS content deleted by GC, files still listed but unreadable).
systems.lesson_for_c4: Holding an ID is not a promise by anyone. c4 makes this worse by design: descriptions are meant to travel apart from data, so many people will hold c4m files that no store has promised to honor. The rule has to be stated in one sentence users can repeat: only a store's own promise list keeps bytes; a c4m elsewhere is a description, not a claim. A store with an empty promise list is a cache, and should say so.

systems.name: Venti / Fossil (Plan 9)
systems.root_model: Venti has no roots and no delete: the protocol is read/write by score. Fossil holds one root score and presents three trees under it: /active, /snapshot/<date> (ephemeral), /archive/<date> (permanent, written to Venti).
systems.delete_model: Venti: never ('trades the ability to delete for reliability'; filled arenas are immutable). Fossil: ephemeral snapshots expire by age (snaptime -t minutes); archival snapshots never.
systems.user_expectation: Yesterday's tree is a directory you cd into. Archive is forever.
systems.known_failure: The data was safe and still lost in practice when the root score was lost: 9fans threads on recovering fossil from the last archive score, and scripts that scan arenas for candidate roots. And no reclamation at all: full arenas mean buying disk.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Closest ancestor to the hypothesis. Three things it shows: (1) write-once with zero delete is the smallest possible store contract and is what made Venti trustworthy, but it fails 'not everything forever'; (2) the two-tier split (ephemeral, time-expired working tier; permanent archive tier) is what made it livable; (3) retention presented as one root directory with dated subtrees is intuitive, and the root pointer must live in the store, durably, because bytes without their root are unfindable. I ran the c4 equivalent: a hand-written c4m with entries proj@1/ and proj@2/ pointing at two snapshot IDs already works as a single browsable root (see experiments).

systems.name: Perkeep / Camlistore
systems.root_model: Signed permanodes (mutable objects) and signed claims that set attributes; 'keep' claims; anything reachable from a signed root is kept, in principle.
systems.delete_model: A delete is another claim. Garbage collection was designed and never operationalized: issue #792 notes gc.Collect() exists with no callers outside tests.
systems.known_failure: 'It's just marked as deleted, nothing is really gone' (issue #792, 2016); the reporter's company dropped it as a backup system 'because we could not wipe the old data'.
systems.lesson_for_c4: A claims-and-verdicts layer over an append-only store tends to end at never-delete, because the claim model grows faster than the sweep can be made safe. c4's gc-requirements.md is on this path: 1,166 lines, a separate retain file, four verdicts (keep/trash/scrub/drop), aggregate claims, folds, warrants, adoption, substrate sets. That is Perkeep's vocabulary. Treat it as a warning about concept count, not as evidence the semantics are wrong.

systems.name: S3 versioning + lifecycle
systems.root_model: None. Flat keys; each key has a stack of versions. Nothing references anything.
systems.delete_model: DELETE adds a delete marker (soft). Permanent removal is delete-by-version-ID, or lifecycle rules run by the vendor: expire current after N days, expire noncurrent after N days / keep N newer noncurrent versions, scoped by prefix or tag. Object Lock sets a retain-until date that blocks deletion.
systems.user_expectation: Delete frees space and money. Versioning means 'I can get it back'.
systems.known_failure: Both directions. Silent cost: noncurrent versions and delete markers accumulate invisibly because the expiration rule people write only touches current versions (AWS re:Post threads). Silent loss: a lifecycle rule with too wide a prefix expires data asynchronously, and expired noncurrent versions 'cannot be recovered by any means'.
systems.lesson_for_c4: This is what storage vendors already implement and guarantee: keep until told, delete by ID, optional retain-until, optional age/count rules. No vendor API walks a customer's reference graph. If c4 wants vendor adoption, the store contract should ask for nothing S3 lacks; reachability must be computable by the client and executed as delete-by-ID. 'Keep N previous versions for D days per name' is the dial normal users can state.

systems.name: Docker / OCI registries
systems.root_model: Tags (mutable names) point to manifests; manifest lists/indexes point to manifests; manifests point to layer blobs. The spec makes delete-by-digest optional and leaves GC to the implementation.
systems.delete_model: Untag or delete a manifest, then run an offline mark-and-sweep (registry garbage-collect, optionally --delete-untagged). The registry must be read-only during GC.
systems.user_expectation: Deleting a tag deletes 'that image' and frees space; an image referenced by digest in a deployment stays pullable.
systems.known_failure: The worst postmortems in this survey. distribution #3178: --delete-untagged removed the per-architecture manifests of tagged multi-arch images, because children of an index are untagged. #4461: garbage-collect -m took a registry from 445 GB to 4 GB with manifests left in place. Harbor #19308: GC deleted 73,605 blobs / 13,880 manifests of live images (cause not identified in the issue). Deleting by digest removes every tag sharing that digest. Upload during GC loses layers. Re-pushing 'latest' silently orphans the previous image that a cluster still references by digest. Docker Hub's 2020 six-month inactivity deletion policy drew enough backlash to be postponed.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Tag-rooted reachability is the same shape as the hypothesis and shows its three hazards concretely: (1) nested descriptions - closure through an intermediate description is where marking goes wrong, and c4 snapshots are nested one-level listings; (2) mutable names orphan the previous value with no trace unless the old value is journaled; (3) references held outside the store (digests in someone's YAML; a c4m in someone's email) are invisible. Also: the server-side graph walk is the part every implementation got wrong at least once; do not put it in the standard.

systems.name: Bazel remote cache (REAPI CAS)
systems.root_model: None. The CAS API is FindMissingBlobs / read / write; there is no delete and no reference concept. The action cache maps action digest to output digests but pins nothing.
systems.user_expectation: It is a cache; but tooling quietly assumes 'I saw it there, so it is there'.
systems.known_failure: With Build without the Bytes, Bazel remembers that outputs exist remotely; after eviction the build fails with 'Missing digest' / CacheNotFoundException (bazel #18696, #22220, #26657; cockroach #130203). Fixes were retries, rewinding, and client-declared TTL assumptions.
systems.lesson_for_c4: Rootless eviction is legitimate only when every consumer treats absence as normal and can regenerate. The failures came from a remembered presence, i.e. assertion instead of verification. For c4: a record that says 'store X has ID Y' is a hint with an age; has(ID) must be asked at use. Also a second precedent, with Venti, for a widely implemented CAS contract that contains no delete at all.

systems.name: casync / desync
systems.root_model: Index files (.caibx/.caidx) kept outside the chunk store. The store knows nothing about them.
systems.delete_model: casync gc / desync prune -s <store> index1 index2 ...: delete every chunk not referenced by the indexes named on the command line.
systems.known_failure: Forget to pass one index and its chunks are gone; desync's own README warns prune 'can lead to data loss' and asks for confirmation. Multiple users of one store cannot prune safely without a complete list of everyone's indexes.
systems.lesson_for_c4: This is exactly c4's withdrawn 'c4 gc <file.c4m>...' (store-gc.md, withdrawn 2026-07-09 for this reason). Confirms the withdrawal. I also confirmed on the installed 1.0.18 that a store written by 'c4 id -s' contains only objects and no root record, so every existing 1.0.x store is in the casync position: its roots exist only as c4m files elsewhere. Any retention rule needs a one-time adoption step for those stores.

systems.name: git-annex (added: the many-stores precedent)
systems.root_model: Branch tips and tags define which content is 'used'; a per-key location log records which repositories are believed to hold each key; numcopies sets the required number of copies.
systems.delete_model: 'git annex drop' removes local content only after contacting other repositories and verifying, at that moment, that numcopies will still be satisfied; the location log is not trusted for this. 'unused' + 'dropunused' removes content no branch tip or tag references. --force overrides.
systems.user_expectation: I can free space on this machine and the file still exists somewhere.
systems.known_failure: 'unused' counts only current branch tips and tags, so old versions of files are 'unused' and dropunused removes them; --unused bypasses numcopies settings from .gitattributes; forum threads on move not respecting numcopies.
systems.lesson_for_c4: The only system surveyed that uses the existence of other stores to make deletion safe, and it does it by verification rather than by record: a drop is licensed by another store proving possession now. This is something c4 can do that ZFS, S3 and restic structurally cannot, and it gives 'explicit destruction by ID' a safe default: refuse unless another store answers has(ID), or the user says destroy.

prior.synthesis:
VERDICT ON THE HYPOTHESIS: prior art supports its core and attacks three of its edges. Supported: 'retention = reachability from descriptions the store itself holds' is what every system users trust converged on (ZFS, restic, borg, OSTree, git). Attacked: (1) it needs a grace state between 'dropped' and 'freed'; (2) the as-built journal is not the named promise list the hypothesis describes; (3) 'destruction by ID leaves partial knowledge' is not how the v1.1 binary behaves today.

WHAT RECURS

1. Roots must live in the store and be enumerable by the store. Every system with roots outside it has a documented loss mode: casync/desync index files, git alternates, registry digests referenced from deployment YAML, Nix result symlinks, and c4's own withdrawn gc (store-gc.md). restic, borg, ZFS and OSTree keep roots inside and do not have this failure.

2. The catastrophic bug is always the same one: an unreadable or empty root list is read as 'nothing is kept'. restic #4612 deleted a whole 128 GiB repository when snapshot listing failed; distribution #4461 took a registry from 445 GB to 4 GB; distribution #3178 deleted children of tagged multi-arch indexes; Harbor #19308 deleted live images. The sweep must fail closed on any root or closure read error. gc-requirements.md section 5.8 already requires this; keep it.

3. Nobody ships exactly one dial. Each system ends with a named kept set plus a time-windowed safety net: git refs + reflog (90/30 days) + prune grace (2 weeks); borg 2 prune + undelete until compact; S3 current version + noncurrent-for-N-days; ZFS snapshots + holds; macOS Trash. The 'ordinary filesystem' baseline people now expect is 'current state plus roughly 30 days of undo', not 'exactly one description'.

4. People choose what to keep by name and by time, never by ID. Policies users can state are 'keep 7 daily, 4 weekly for this machine' (restic, borg, snapper, Time Machine) or 'keep 3 old versions for 30 days' (S3). Systems with anonymous roots (git dangling commits, untagged manifests) fall back on time expiry because nobody can pick among hashes. This answers 'how would we choose?': by name group and age.

5. Standards that got adopted specify no garbage collector. Venti (read/write, no delete), REAPI CAS (find-missing/read/write, no delete), OCI distribution (delete-by-digest optional, GC implementation-private), S3 (delete by key+version; lifecycle keyed on age and prefix, never on a graph). The only server-side graph walkers are registries, and they produced the worst postmortems. For vendor cost, the store contract should be put/get/has, optionally list and delete-by-ID, plus one sentence: a store never removes bytes on its own initiative. Reachability is then a pure client computation (closure of a c4m, set difference) executed as delete-by-ID. That also collapses the hypothesis's two destruction paths into one L0 act.

6. Something must protect in-flight writers: a lock (restic, borg), read-only mode (registry), or an age exemption (git 2 weeks, OSTree --keep-unreferenced-younger-than). c4's gc design uses 'strays are reported, never touched', which needs no clock and is stricter than all of these. That part survived attack and should not be changed.

7. Stores have roles. Fossil+Venti (ephemeral tier with expiry + permanent archive), Bazel (cache is safe because something else is authoritative), git-annex (drop only when another store proves possession). The dial has a zero position: a store that promises nothing is a cache, and that is legitimate if it says so. IPFS's expectation gap is users not knowing which role the node they used was playing.

WHAT USERS FOUND INTUITIVE
- A named snapshot that holds space until you remove it (ZFS, btrfs, borg archives).
- History shown as dated folders you can browse; dropping one is deleting a folder (Time Machine, Fossil /archive and /snapshot, .zfs/snapshot).
- Dense-recent, sparse-old thinning, when it is a second copy.
- A trash state: condemned, recoverable, then emptied (borg 2, S3 delete markers, desktop Trash).
- Git's 'committed means safe for a long time', which rests on the automatic reflog, not on refs.

WHAT CAUSED LOSS
- Roots outside the store (casync, alternates, registry digests).
- Root-list read failure treated as an empty list (restic, registries).
- Closure through nested descriptions (multi-arch indexes).
- Policy scoped by a name pattern or prefix that matched too much (borg -P--, S3 lifecycle prefix, restic grouping).
- Automatic time or space expiry when the store was the only copy (Time Machine, Backblaze 30-day rule, APFS purge, Docker Hub inactivity policy).
- Believing an ID or a remembered presence is possession (IPFS unpinned content, Bazel 'Missing digest').
- The mirror failure, inability to delete (Perkeep, Venti, GitHub dangling commits), which makes systems unusable for backup and for secrets.

EXPERIMENTS (all under /tmp/retention-study/prior-art/, C4_STORE and HOME isolated; v1.1 binary built from master d1d1b0a as /tmp/retention-study/prior-art/c4-master, which reports itself as 1.0.16; installed c4 is 1.0.18)

E1. v1.1 root catalog: 'c4 id -s' writes <store>/journal with header '@c4 journal 1' and lines '<time> <id>'. Entries are anonymous; there is no name and no notion of 'current'. (gc-requirements.md calls this file log.c4m; the binary writes 'journal'.) It is not a c4m. So the hypothesis's 'promise list is an ordinary named c4m' is not what exists.

E2. 1.0.18: a store written by 'c4 id -s' holds 6 objects and no root record of any kind. Existing stores are in the casync position.

E3. Neither binary has any deletion verb (gc, retain, rm, forget, prune, drop all print usage).

E4. One leaf object removed from a store copy: 'c4 restore' (dry run and --force) prints 'Missing content for 1 entries; nothing restored', exit 1, and restores 0 of 3 files. So today a description with one destroyed leaf is not treated as partial knowledge by restore; it is all-or-nothing. The hypothesis's last clause needs this changed, or it is untrue in practice.

E5. One directory-listing object removed: 'c4 cat -r <snapshot>' prints the tree with sub/ childless and exits 0, with no warning; 'c4 restore' correctly refuses ('target incomplete: no stored record for directory sub/'). A marker built on the cat -r recursion would under-mark silently, which is the restic #4612 class. The gc design's refuse rule covers the sweep, but cat -r itself reports a truncated closure as success.

E6. 'What would dropping root 1 free' is computable now: IDs of cat -r snap1 minus IDs of cat -r snap2 = the old a.txt and the snap1 listing object. No new primitive needed for the question ZFS users cannot answer.

E7. A promise list as an ordinary c4m already works for reading. I wrote roots.c4m with two directory entries, 'proj@1/' and 'proj@2/', whose IDs are the two snapshot IDs (size null). 'c4 cat -r roots.c4m' walked the full closure; 'c4 id -s -q roots.c4m' stored it and returned one root R; 'c4 cat R/proj@1/a.txt' printed 'alpha' and 'c4 cat R/proj@2/a.txt' printed 'alpha v2'; 'c4 diff R/proj@1 R/proj@2' worked. This is the Fossil /archive and .zfs/snapshot model built from existing parts, and a c4m entry line already carries what retention policies key on (name, time, size). What is missing: storing it only appended a third anonymous journal line; the first two roots remain, so 'dropping an entry' has no effect as built, and nothing marks R as the current list.

OPEN CONFLICTS THE LEAD SHOULD DECIDE
- Current-pointer. Every edit of a promise-list c4m yields a new ID, so something mutable must say which is current. Git's answer is one mutable pointer plus a journal of its past values with time expiry. The existing journal could be read that way (last line = current root, earlier lines = grace window), but that is a design choice, not something the binary does.
- Deliberate destruction under a kept description. The gc design refuses any sweep when a keep-side object is missing (correct per restic), so 'destroy by ID, description stays' needs a way to tell 'deliberately destroyed' from 'damaged'. OSTree uses tombstones and S3 uses delete markers; the gc design has drop lines. Nulling the ID in the description is not available because it changes the description's ID and every ancestor's (the git history-rewrite problem).
- Concept count. gc-requirements.md is 1,166 lines with a retain file, four verdicts, aggregates, folds, warrants and adoption. Perkeep took the claims route and never shipped deletion. Prior art suggests the durable minimum is three things: an in-store named root list, a recoverable trash state, and fail-closed marking.

NOT VERIFIED / CAVEATS
- Harbor #19308 and distribution #4461: the issues do not identify a root cause; I report the observed loss only.
- A search result attributing 'missing object makes subtree unreachable during prune' to OSTree was actually about an unrelated project; I did not use it.
- restic fix release (I believe 0.16.3), the Docker Hub policy's final fate, git-annex details, Venti/Fossil root-score recovery, and Nix behaviors come from documentation, search summaries and prior knowledge, not from running those tools.
- c4 experiments used a three-file tree; they show behavior, not scale.

Root list as c4m. v6/v7 decided the journal is "an ordinary c4m patch chain" and used that property to reject putting verdicts in it and to reject a writable master c4m. v9 then declared the journal "masqueraded as c4m" and replaced it with a non-c4m two-field file. The rejection of Joshua's master-c4m idea rests partly on a premise the record later abolished.
2. gc-requirements versus the built journal. gc-requirements (committed 06:30 on 2026-07-13) takes root kind and aggregate identity from journal names and origins; v9 (13:37 the same day) deleted both. The doc was never updated. Run-confirmed: a tree claim and a stdin-blob claim are indistinguishable journal lines. The accepted gc is unimplementable as written.
3. "Nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable" (v7 pin, still in master's c4-log help, to be frozen at v1.1.0) versus the accepted trash/empty design (v8 Amendment 3b scoped it in design text only).
4. Names. "Named refs rejected" and "handles are IDs, never refs" versus substrate-map's bindings (mutable name → ID) versus gc-A1's reserved journal names `adopted`/`condemned` carrying collector semantics, which is the same "name-field-as-schema" charge used to reject the master c4m.
5. Where retention authority lives. "Naming/refs/GC policy stay outside the store ... not a VCS" (v6 candidate) versus "the store names its own roots" (v6 merge onward) versus a retention record inside the store. Never framed as a layering choice.
6. Who may write a store. "c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers" and "a store is a local directory" versus vendor adoption, imgbin, the 1.0.x fleet, and S3/multi-store. Run-confirmed: with two stores in C4_STORE, master prints claims and undo handles that are never journaled (journalClaim returns silently).
7. Partial knowledge. The philosophy says degrade gracefully; restore is all-or-nothing on one missing object (run-confirmed), gc refuses on a missing keep-side description, and condemning an interior object is refused. The hypothesis's "destroy by ID, description stays as partial knowledge" has no support in the designed gc.
8. Split. v7 calls split both "the deliberate-forget boundary" and "never what the store retains"; v8 moved forgetting to the drop verdict; v9 removed split from journals entirely.
9. No-expiry is listed as a competitive differentiator while gc is "required in the next major"; the default was never decided.
10. Joshua's "deletion is deliberate, via trash folders in a master c4m" was kept in spirit and inverted in mechanism (the master c4m became a read-only derived view of two other files).

WHAT THE RECORD SAYS ABOUT THE HYPOTHESIS:
- Supported: reachability from kept descriptions is the only retention rule the project has ever written (store-gc.md, 2025 retention manifests, Joshua's master c4m). Per-root dropping matches v8 3(a). One dial from "one description" to "all" is consistent with the fold's default (no verdict = live).
- Contradicted or unanswered: (i) a writable c4m promise list is a recorded rejection needing named new context, which exists (items 1, 2 and the 'wrong fundamentals' statement); (ii) it must be populated automatically or it is the withdrawn gc; (iii) it needs a third class, unaccounted bytes that are reported and never removed, or it is the rejected negative sweep, and today that class includes 1.0.x writes, imgbin writes and all multi-store claims; (iv) names in the list collide with "named refs rejected" and with v9's nameless roots; (v) destroy-by-ID needs a durable 'deliberately absent' mark distinct from damage; (vi) in-place reclamation drags a writer/collector lock into the store contract.
- Strongest untested lead in the record: the "interim mitigation" (copy what kept descriptions reach into a fresh store, discard the old one) is retention with zero new concepts, uses many stores, and needs no lock, tombstone or deletion verb. It was never evaluated as the primary rule.

RUNS (all under /tmp/retention-study/history/, C4_STORE set, artifacts left in place; master built to /tmp/retention-study/history/c4-master, reports itself as 1.0.16): journal is `@c4 journal 1` plus `<time> <ID>` lines; no gc or retain verb on 1.0.18 or master; 1.0.18 writes into a master store without journaling; removed object leaves the description readable, per-file cat fails, restore fails closed, a second store cures it; multi-store config prints unjournaled claims; single-store restore pre-images and repeat claims are journaled.

use_cases.name: Ash failover sync (Mac <-> cloud VM mirror)
use_cases.must_never_lose: (1) Any Mac file outside the mirror set: "absent from the remote's root c4m" means not in the set, never deleted. (2) The last agreed root, which is the base of the three-way merge. (3) Pre-images of every replaced or deleted file until both sides' root IDs agree by full rehash; a prewritten restore must run after a reboot mid-transaction, before any service starts. (4) Attic contents (cloud-side deletions, the losing side's whole git repo, X.conflict files) until Joshua has audited them.
use_cases.should_be_reclaimable: Superseded file versions as soon as both roots agree ("The store exists only during a sync. No long-lived history store."). Staged copies. The attic after audit. Measured on the real mirror store: 0.79 GiB (6.5%) superseded after three pushes in about 80 minutes, with nothing reclaiming it.
use_cases.who_decides: The sync tool, mechanically, on evidence (root IDs equal on both hosts). Joshua for failover switches, any Mac-side deletion in v1, deletions over a threshold, and the attic flush.
use_cases.notes: Sources: ~/ws/active/ash/ashnarrate/docs/23-failover-sync.md, handoffs/c4-sync.md, ~/.ash/c4-init.noindex/push.sh. Surprising points: (a) Rule 3 says "Not kept must never look like deleted... Pruning for space is a storage choice, not a change to the description": the cloud's description carries entries for files it does not hold. (b) The reclaim condition is a fact about another store, which one store cannot evaluate alone. (c) The minimum is not one description: it is base + new + attic during a transaction. (d) The root c4m lives beside the store, not in it. (e) Cleanup today is a hand-written rm script; the doc says the c4 way "is not fully implemented yet". (f) No sub-file dedup: a 10 MB transcript that grows a line is a whole new object, so the c4 session advised against storing every generation. (g) Steady state has other sources of truth (both working trees); the store is the sole copy only for pre-images and the attic.

use_cases.name: c4snap (background description of a 12.46 TB / 10.4M-entry volume)
use_cases.must_never_lose: The newest committed block and every block it reaches through first-line base IDs, until a consolidated base replaces them. The journal: its last claim is the only handle to the current root, and it records the true scan start each block needs for the reuse rule. None of the volume's bytes are in the store.
use_cases.should_be_reclaimable: Blocks superseded by a consolidation (about 1,000 blocks per full pass; a full restatement layer is about 1.5 GB of text at 10.4M entries). Earlier passes, if only the current description is wanted.
use_cases.who_decides: The service, by policy; the consolidation trigger is an open question in its requirements. The operator decides how many past snapshots to keep. Deletion and gc are listed as non-goals.
use_cases.notes: Sources: oss/c4snap/design/requirements.md, block.go, oss/c4/design/chain-resolution.md. Surprising points: (a) The store holds descriptions only; content ingestion is a non-goal ("12.46 TB will not fit in a 667 GB store"), so every leaf ID is absent by design. (b) Descriptions depend on descriptions: a block that looks superseded may be the base of the current head, so "hold one description" really means hold its chain closure. (c) Losing the description costs about 86 hours of rehashing, so it is expensive derived data even though the volume is the source of truth for bytes. (d) Blocks are stored verbatim with store.Put; `c4 id -s` cannot be used because it canonicalizes. (e) For paths that have vanished from the volume, the chain is the only record.

use_cases.name: imgbin (Swift app writing the store directly)

(d) A c4m stored as a root is indistinguishable from a c4m that was merely content in a scanned tree (the store holds c4 test fixtures). uses.summary:
One thing to know first: an experiment of mine wrote two 300,000-byte test objects into ~/.c4/store, against the read-only rule. I ran git in a c4git-configured temp repo without C4_STORE set, and c4git 1.0.18 prefers the global store over the repo-local one. Nothing else changed, I did not delete them, and the paths are in store_measurements. The store numbers were taken before this.

**What the evidence says about the hypothesis**
- **Supported:** reachability from descriptions is what every real consumer already uses to decide (c4git gc, the Ash mirror, c4snap chains).
- **Contradicted: "the promise list is a c4m in the store."** For five of the eight cases the roots live outside the store: git history, the imgbin session folder, root.c4m beside the Ash store, loose c4m files, production tracking. The default store's log names one 6-byte object out of 194,127.
- **Contradicted: "dropping an entry is the only way space is reclaimed."** A store with no entries (every 1.0.x store) would be either all garbage or kept forever. A third state is needed: unclaimed, kept, and reported.
- **Understated: "holding one description is ordinary filesystem behavior."** Ash needs base + new + attic during a transaction, and c4snap needs the chain closure of its head.

**Requirement classes any retention rule must satisfy**
1. **Descriptions outlive bytes.** A description pointing at absent bytes stays valid and never reads as "deleted" (Ash rule 3, the receipts degradation rule, c4snap by design; 107,945 absent IDs measured in the default store).
2. **Roots are mostly external.** The rule must work when the store holds no record of who needs an object.
3. **Unreferenced is not garbage.** Run on 1.0.18: `c4git gc --force` deleted another tool's snapshot in a shared store. The earlier `c4 gc` was withdrawn for the same reason.
4. **Legacy and dumb writers.** imgbin, rsync and a future vendor only put bytes under an ID. 1.0.18 writes no root record. Objects with no claim must be safe by default.
5. **Three kinds of reclaim trigger, with different deciders.**
   - Evidence that another location verifiably holds the bytes (Ash root agreement, DIT card reuse, imgbin while the folder holds the files). This is the c4-only one, and it spans stores.
   - Supersession (mirror, c4snap consolidation).
   - Age or count policy (agent undo).
6. **A holding state with human approval.** Ash's attic is audited before flush and large deletions stop for approval; c4git defaults to a dry run.
7. **Destruction by ID, independent of reachability.** Whole-tree snapshots capture .env.
8. **Description-to-description links count.** Base IDs and directory listing objects must be followed.
9. **A transactional window.** Pre-images must survive a crash until both roots agree.
10. **Space sits in few objects.** The largest 1% hold 77% of bytes in the default store and 74% in the Ash mirror; 88% of objects hold 8%. With no sub-file dedup, a few hot large files drive the cost of history.

**Use cases with no source of truth other than the store**
- Agent undo snapshots and patch/restore pre-images, once the tree is damaged.
- c4git: every version of a managed file that is not currently checked out.
- Ash: only pre-images and the attic during a transaction.
- c4snap: the chain is the only record of vanished paths, and costs about 86 hours to recompute.

**Not sole copy:** imgbin (folder holds all 9,910 files), Ash steady state, and DIT/media/ML (no store used). For the default store as found it cannot be determined, which is itself the strongest requirement.

Not verified: imgbin's APFS clone sharing (from the source comment only), and anything on the VM side of the Ash sync.

proposal.name: Holdings: a store is a filesystem whose root directory is one c4m listing
proposal.one_sentence: A store has one mutable thing, a one-level c4m listing at <store>/holdings.c4m; bytes leave the store only when that listing is replaced (exactly reach(old) minus reach(new), moved to a trash store) or when someone destroys an ID outright, and bytes that no holdings ever reached are reported and never removed.
proposal.model:
STORE = objects named by ID + at most one file `holdings.c4m` in the store root (+ transient `holdings.c4m.lock`, + optional `trash/`).

1. HOLDINGS FILE. `<store>/holdings.c4m` is a canonical ONE-LEVEL c4m listing: existing entry grammar, no indentation, no inline children. Each line is an ordinary entry: a directory entry (name ends "/", ID = ID of a one-level listing object in the store) or a file entry (ID = bytes). Kind comes from the entry, so a tree snapshot and a stdin blob are distinguishable (they are not in the built journal). Names mean nothing to the store. Default name written by `c4 id -s` is the scan-start UTC time (ID prefix appended on collision), i.e. the same information as today's journal line `<time> <ID>`, written as a c4m entry. Products pick their own names and nest through listing objects (`undo/<day>/<time>/`, `ash/base/`). The holdings is itself a directory: its ID is `c4 id` of the file and is recomputable (run: `c4 cat -r H | c4 id -q -` reproduced H). File absent = the store holds nothing (cache or legacy store). File empty or unparseable = error, never "nothing held" (master already refuses to parse an empty c4m).

2. REACH. reach(L) = every ID on an entry of L, plus reach(listing(ID)) for every directory entry. File and symlink entries are leaves. No byte sniffing, no chain/base-ID following.

3. THE RULE (the whole standard): a store removes an object only (a) because holdings O was replaced by N, and then only objects in reach(O) - reach(N), or (b) by destroy(ID). Three classes follow: held (in reach(holdings)), released (dropped by a replace), unaccounted (in no holdings this store has had: kept, reported, never removed). The rule limits removal, not presence: a holdings may name bytes the store never had (c4snap, mirror stores); possession is always answered by has(ID).

4. REPLACE is the only mutation, and it is compare-and-swap. hold(N, expect=ID(O)):
 a. Create `holdings.c4m.lock` exclusively (O_EXCL; on object storage, conditional create). Refuse if ID(current holdings) != expect. Write N into the lock, fsync.
 b. Keep-side walk of N: every listing object must be present and rehash to its name, else refuse and delete the lock (fail closed). Anything N reaches that is absent from the store but present in trash is moved back.
 c. released = reach(O) - reach(N). A missing listing on the O side skips its subtree (can only under-release).
 d. Move released objects to the trash store `<store>/trash/` (same object layout), each listing after the objects it names.
 e. Rename lock -> holdings.c4m, fsync the directory.
 An empty N (release everything) is refused without a long-form flag.

5. WRITERS. `c4 id -s` puts objects with no lock. Then: take the lock; check that every object the new entry reaches is present (move back from trash if it is there, else re-put or fail without printing); write O + one entry; rename. The ID is printed only after the rename (print barrier = bytes durable AND entry durable). Tools that only put bytes under an ID (imgbin, 1.0.x, a vendor's dumb client) need no change: their objects are unaccounted.

6. CRASH. Before step e the holdings is still O and the lock holds N. Re-running the same hold resumes (ordering in d keeps every not-yet-moved released object reachable from a listing that is still present). Rolling back is hold(O): it pulls everything back from trash. A crashed writer leaves unaccounted objects and a stale lock; a stale lock is resolved by rollback. Trash cannot be emptied while a lock exists.

7. HISTORY OF THE HOLDINGS. Not kept by the store. The dial applies to itself: to keep yesterday's holdings, hold it as an entry (`previous/ <ID(O)>` keeps everything O kept). The v1.1 journal has no retention role in this design.

8. THE DIAL. No file = cache. One entry replaced on every save = conventional filesystem (the old version is released, as when a file is overwritten). Many dated entries = history. Same rule at every position.

9. ANSWERS TO THE THREE RECORDED DEFECTS OF THE REJECTED MASTER C4M. Atomic update: lockfile + rename with CAS (git's ref protocol). Bare ID with no name: the name is its time. Name-field-as-schema: the collector reads no names; a `trash/` or `previous/` folder is just held content, and release happens only when an entry leaves the listing.
new_concepts: `<store>/holdings.c4m`: one well-known filename; grammar is the existing one-level c4m listing, so zero new parsers. Per implementation: locate, read, write canonical listing (assumed present in all five; I did not verify the four non-Go implementations).
reach(L): the closure definition, pure c4m grammar, about 50 lines per language plus vectors (nested listing, file leaf, symlink no edge, missing listing).

hold(N, expect): compare-and-swap replace with `holdings.c4m.lock` (transient file, O_EXCL create, rename). One L1 verb `c4 hold`, dry run by default. About 100 lines per language. Replaces gc + retain.
Three states: held, released (sitting in trash), unaccounted. No verdict vocabulary.
`<store>/trash/`: a second store in the same layout; reclamation moves, never unlinks. One directory name; readable today with C4_STORE=store,store/trash.
destroy(ID): L0 remove-by-ID already exists in the Go Store interface (store/store.go Remove); one L1 verb `c4 destroy`, long-form explicit.
Changed behavior of `c4 id -s`: adds a holdings entry under the lock and verifies presence before printing.
`c4 cat -r` must fail on a missing listing (today exits 0 with a truncated tree), and one way to emit a closure as bare IDs (one flag) so scripts do not scrape entry text.
Vendor contract: put/get/has/list/remove + one small mutable object with conditional create and conditional replace. No server-side graph walk.

Conformance vectors: about 10-12 (reach cases, keep-side refuse, release-side skip, CAS refuse, empty-N refuse, resume after crash, rescue from trash, unaccounted untouched) against 38 in gc-requirements.md.
removed_concepts: `<store>/retain` record file and its line grammar and fold semantics (gc-requirements.md, store-records-architecture.md).
Verdict vocabulary keep/trash/scrub/drop and the three reserved actors.
Aggregate claims, folds, residual lists, substrate objects and `adopt` as retention machinery (adoption becomes: hold a listing of the strays, then drop it).
Deletion warrant as a recorded artifact; it is the computed difference of two listings.
Staging directory and the shared/exclusive sweep lock held by every claim path; replaced by one short exclusive lock around the holdings swap.

The store journal (`@c4 journal 1`) as root catalog, and `c4 log` defaulting to it; holdings entries carry time + ID and also say what is current. If the journal is kept as an audit log it has no retention meaning.
Root kind taken from a `.c4m` name suffix (gc-requirements section 3.1), which the built journal cannot supply anyway.
The help sentence `nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable`, which must not be frozen at v1.1.0.
Roots kept beside the store: Ash's root.c4m next to its store and c4git's private gc root set both become holdings entries.
`c4 gc <file.c4m>...` (already withdrawn) stays withdrawn; nothing asks the caller to enumerate what to keep.
proposal.how_a_person_chooses: By name and date in a listing, the way they delete folders. `cat <store>/holdings.c4m` shows what the store keeps, one line per kept thing with time, size and name. To let something go they remove its line (or a product verb removes it by name or by policy such as keep 7 daily). `c4 hold` without --force prints two things: the entry diff (on master `c4 diff H H2` already prints exactly the dropped entry line) and the released objects with their total bytes, computed as reach(old) - reach(new), so the answer to `what will this free` is exact before anything moves. Nobody chooses by ID except in one case: adopting a store that predates holdings, where the strays have no names; there the tool lists them largest first (in the 33 GB store the largest 1% of objects hold 77% of bytes, about 1,900 lines to review).
proposal.how_expectations_are_met:
- Nothing leaves the store except through an edit to a listing the person can read. Storing something and forgetting about it never loses it: unlisted bytes are unaccounted and are not removed.
- `Saved means safe`: `c4 id -s` prints the ID only after the bytes and the holdings entry are both durable.
- `I deleted it, I get the space back`: the dry run states the exact bytes; bytes shared with another kept entry stay and are not counted.
- A delete is recoverable: released bytes sit in trash until the person deletes that directory. Undo is holding the old listing again (run: 4 objects came back from trash and the dropped snapshot restored).
- Failures refuse instead of deleting: empty or unparseable holdings, a missing listing on the keep side, holdings changed since the plan was made (CAS).
- Filesystem position of the dial behaves like a filesystem: overwrite replaces, old bytes are released.
Where it does not meet expectations: space does not return until trash is emptied (the ZFS complaint in a milder form), and a legacy store returns no space at all until its strays are adopted and dropped.
proposal.destruction_vs_reclamation:
RECLAMATION (space back) is a side effect of replacing holdings: reach(old) - reach(new) moves to the trash store; it is reversible until trash is emptied; it never touches a held or unaccounted object; emptying trash is deleting a directory, which c4 does not need a verb for.

DESTRUCTION (must be gone) is `destroy <ID>`: the object is removed from this store and its trash now, whether or not holdings reach it. It promises only that this store no longer serves the bytes (the scrub ruling: no physical-erasure claim; vacate the name first so presence at a hash name always means good bytes). Holdings is not edited, because nulling an ID would change every ancestor ID. The description stays and has(ID) answers false.
Limits found by running: (1) `c4 restore` on both binaries refuses the whole tree when one leaf is absent, so `description stays as partial knowledge` is true for cat and diff and false for restore until restore can materialize the rest. (2) Destroying a leaf never blocks later replaces, because leaves are not opened; destroying a listing object does block them (keep-side refuse), so removing secret names means replacing the entry with a re-made snapshot, then destroying. (3) L0 records no tombstone, so a deliberate hole and damage look the same; a product can hold a plain list of destroyed IDs as an ordinary file entry and subtract it in its integrity check.
proposal.layer_placement:
L0 standard: the store contract (put, get, has, list, remove by ID); the holdings object (one c4m listing per store, conditional create and conditional replace); reach() as c4m grammar; the removal rule in section 3 of the model; `a store never removes on its own initiative`.

L1 toolbox: `c4 id -s` adds an entry under the lock; `c4 hold` (CAS replace, dry run default, release to trash, rescue from trash); `c4 destroy`; `c4 cat -r` failing closed plus bare-ID closure output; the directory-store binding (`holdings.c4m`, `.lock`, `trash/`). Everything else is composition: what-holds-this, what-would-this-free, and cross-store evidence (`is every released ID present in store B`) are set operations over `cat -r` output.

L2 product: names and nesting; drop-by-name; thinning policies (keep N, dense-recent); undo windows; sync transactions as entries (base, new, attic) with release licensed by evidence from the other store; adoption helper for legacy stores; when trash is emptied; a record of deliberate holes; the default position of the dial.

proposal.cost:
Per language implementation (five): no new format. Needed: read/write a one-level listing (existing), reach() walk with fail-closed keep side (about 50 lines), CAS replace with lockfile, ordered move and rescue (about 100 lines), entry append in the store-writing path, destroy by ID. About 10-12 conformance vectors. An implementation that only reads and writes objects (imgbin today) stays conforming with zero work; it just never holds.

Vendor: put/get/has/list/remove plus one small mutable object with conditional create (the lock) and conditional replace. S3-class APIs document both; I did not run against one. No graph walk, no lifecycle engine, no journal. One obligation: never remove on its own initiative, which rules out age-based lifecycle on a c4 bucket.

Against the design of record (gc-requirements.md, 1,166 lines): it removes a record file with its own grammar, four verdicts, three reserved actors, aggregates, a staging directory, a two-mode lock and 38 vectors, and replaces two verbs + one flag with two verbs + one flag.

Runtime: adding an entry rewrites holdings.c4m (1.37 MB at 10,000 flat entries) and stats every object the new entry reaches while holding the lock. A replace walks reach(old) and reach(new): cost is proportional to what is kept, not to what changed. Disk: released bytes stay in trash until emptied.

Migration: existing stores need nothing and lose nothing; they reclaim nothing until someone holds what they want and adopts-then-drops the rest. v1.1 must change before its contract freezes: `id -s` writes an entry instead of a journal line, and the RETENTION help text changes.
weaknesses_admitted: It reopens two recorded decisions and reverses one ratified refinement: the rejected independently-writable master c4m (store-records-architecture.md), `handles are IDs, never refs` (holdings names are mutable names that resolve through ID/path), and the v9 nameless non-c4m journal that v11-surface-review.md lists under do-not-churn. My new context is the three items the history agent found plus the runs above; Joshua has to accept that as sufficient.

Dedupe coincidence: an unaccounted object (imgbin, 1.0.x, c4git, a vendor's dumb client) whose ID also appears in a released set moves to trash with it. The writer that relied on it never said so and the store cannot know. Trash makes this recoverable, not safe.

It is not lock-free. An exclusive lock is held across the release move and across a writer's presence check. Stale-lock recovery is a rule people must follow. O_EXCL and rename on NFS/SMB and conditional writes on object storage are assumed from documentation; I tested local APFS only.

Filesystem equivalence holds for semantics, not for cost. A filesystem frees in time proportional to the change; a holdings replace must test each released candidate against all of reach(new). On the 10.4M-entry volume, replace-on-every-save would mean a full membership pass each time. Without a reference index (a new concept I did not add) the one-entry position of the dial is expensive on large trees.

One dial is not the whole design. It needed a trash state, a separate destroy act, a CAS rule and a nesting convention before it survived my own experiments, and the real cases need more than one entry (Ash: base + new + attic). It is one rule plus three supports, not one concept.

Unaccounted bytes are never reclaimed without a person. The 33 GB default store stays 33 GB, and the Ash mirror's 0.79 GiB of superseded objects stay, until someone adopts and drops them. For roughly 950 objects with no description anywhere, choosing by ID and size is all the design offers.

c4snap conflict: reach() does not follow first-line base IDs, so a chained description is kept only if the producer holds every block as its own entry. Holding only the head leaves the bases unaccounted (safe, never removed, never reclaimed). Following bases would add chain grammar to L0; and master's chain resolver currently drops external bases silently (chain-resolution.md defect A).

c4git conflict: its roots are git refs and reflog. It must write and maintain a holdings entry listing its blob IDs, which puts a holdings rewrite near the clean filter's hot path, or its objects stay unaccounted. Its existing `gc --force` breaks the rule and would have to go through hold.

Destruction is under-specified at L0: no tombstone, so a deliberate hole and damage are indistinguishable without an L2 list; destroying a listing object wedges later replaces until the entry is re-made; and restore is all-or-nothing today, so the hypothesis's last clause is not yet true for restore.

Default names are times because that preserves the v9 ruling against invented names and origins, but people choose by meaningful names. Good names are pushed to L2, and if L2 nests by hand it meets the stale-parent-ID hazard from E3.

Many stores: each store has its own holdings and a replace on store A looks only at A. With C4_STORE=a,b the entry goes to the first store. I did not test multi-store writes; the history agent reports master journals nothing in that configuration, so this path is unverified end to end.

The default position of the dial is not decided here. `Nothing expires` for agent undo and `gc is required` both remain true statements on the record; this design makes either cheap to implement and does not choose.

My protocol evidence is a shell composition on three-file trees in flat-layout temp stores. It shows the ordering and the CAS requirement are right in the cases I forced; it does not show correctness under real crashes (power loss, partial fsync), sharded layouts, names with spaces, or scale.

attack.proposal: Holdings: a store is a filesystem whose root directory is one c4m listing (<store>/holdings.c4m, CAS replace under holdings.c4m.lock, release = reach(old) - reach(new) moved to <store>/trash, destroy(ID) separate, unaccounted bytes reported and never removed).

fatal.scenario: Shared store, one holdings-aware writer and one unregistered writer (run, x3, real c4git 1.0.18). c4git commits hero.mov v1; its clean filter puts the 300,000-byte object in the store with no holdings entry. A holdings-aware undo snapshot of the working files (undoA) reaches the same ID. v2 is committed, undoB taken. The undo policy drops undoA: released = {undoA listing, the v1 object}; both move to trash. Holdings fsck reports 0 missing. `git checkout HEAD~1` exits 0 and writes a 90-byte ID in place of the file ('content not found ... passing ID through'); `c4git verify`: '0 ok, 1 not restored'. Emptying trash (a plain directory delete with no verb and no check) makes it permanent. Git held only the 90 bytes, so the store was the sole copy.
fatal.why: The three-class guarantee is keyed by ID, not by who relied on the bytes. 'Unaccounted: never removed' is void the moment any holdings entry reaches the same ID, and the store cannot know another tool depended on it. The proposal calls this a 'dedupe coincidence'; it is systematic: whole-tree undo snapshots reach every c4git-managed and imgbin file that was ever in the working tree, so thinning undo history releases exactly the old versions c4git alone was keeping. The claim 'tools that only put bytes need no change' is false for any store shared with a holdings-aware tool; the only repairs are one store per tool (gives up the shared store the c4git README advertises) or every writer registering (c4git, imgbin, 1.0.x and vendor clients all change).

fatal.scenario: Live lock treated as stale (run, x1). Holdings has snap1..3. Process A runs hold(N = snap3 only) and is slow (1 s per move, standing in for a large release or object storage). Process B sees the lock, applies the proposal's rule 'a stale lock is resolved by rollback', rescues 3 objects from trash and removes the lock. A keeps moving, puts 12 objects in trash, then its rename fails because the lock is gone. Final state: holdings lists snap1, snap2, snap3; no lock exists; 9 objects that holdings reach are in trash. The proposal's own fsck (built on cat -r) reports only 2 missing because cat -r truncates at the missing listings. With no lock present, trash may be emptied.
fatal.why: The design has no definition of stale: no owner, lease, heartbeat or fencing token in the lock, and the final rename is not conditional on still owning it. On object storage a dead client's lock object and a slow client's are indistinguishable, and release time grows with the released set (copy+delete per object), so the window is minutes. An unattended agent harness must either never break a lock (see serious item on wedged saves) or break it by guess, which produces this state. Fixing it adds a lease protocol to the L0 store contract for every implementation and vendor.

serious.scenario: Crash mid-hold, then the git habit (run, x2). hold crashes after 3 moves; holdings is still O, lock present. A writer (`snap`) blocks on the lock indefinitely (still blocked at 3 s; the loop would wait 60 s then fail). The user deletes holdings.c4m.lock as they would .git/index.lock. The next writer succeeds, holdings lists snap1..4, no lock, and 3 file objects that snap1/snap2 reach sit in trash: `c4 cat snap1/b.txt` -> 'content not found'. Same end state arises from `rsync --exclude '*.lock'` of a store mid-hold.
serious.why: The save path and the delete path share one lock and one file. A crashed release blocks every `c4 id -s` and every `restore --force` pre-image, so undo is unavailable exactly after a failed thinning run. The recovery step people already know (remove the lock) converts a recoverable state into held-but-trashed bytes with nothing flagging it. This is the Review Method's 'separate the subtraction from the addition' violated in the protocol itself.

serious.scenario: Trash configured as a second store, as the proposal recommends for reading (run, x5/x5b). Object F exists only in <store>/trash. With C4_STORE=store,store/trash both master and 1.0.18 run `c4 id -s` on a tree containing F, skip the put because has(F) is true via trash, and print the claim with exit 0. F is not in the store proper. Emptying trash destroys a just-printed snapshot's content. Related run (x4): with C4_STORE=a,b master skips putting an object into a when b has it, so an entry in a's holdings reaches bytes governed only by b's holdings.
serious.why: Cross-store dedupe already exists in the shipped binaries. A per-store holdings plus a per-store lock cannot protect an entry whose bytes live in another store, and the writer's 'verify present under the lock' is undefined: present in the first store (then cross-store dedupe must be switched off) or present anywhere (then store b can release it). 'Many stores' is one of the properties the rule was supposed to use; here it is the hole.

serious.scenario: The old holdings is not kept anywhere (run, R1 on x3). After hold drops undoA, `grep -r undoA <store>` finds nothing; trash holds two objects named only by ID. 'Undo is holding the old listing again' works only if the user saved the old text outside the store. Likewise holdings.c4m removed or overwritten (run, x8): the next writer creates a one-entry holdings; the three earlier snapshots stay in the store with no name and no root record.
serious.why: The removal rule is safe here (nothing is released), but the catalog is one mutable file with no history, so its durability is weaker than the bytes it names. This is the Fossil lesson: bytes whose root is lost are lost in practice. Recovery means sniffing objects for listing-shaped text, which the project has ruled out on the deletion path and which found 114 ambiguous root candidates in Joshua's real store. The append-only journal the proposal removes did not have this failure. The proposal's fix ('hold previous/ as an entry') is opt-in and recursive.

serious.scenario: Trash has no release time (run, x9). A snapshot whose objects were ingested 60 days ago is released now; `find trash -mtime +30` matches 6 of 6 objects, because rename preserves mtime. The obvious cron for a '30-day trash' deletes thinned history seconds after release.
serious.why: The recoverable window that every surveyed system has (borg undelete, S3 noncurrent days, git prune grace) is not actually provided; it needs either touch-on-move (a rule five implementations and vendors must share) or a release record. The only irreversible step in the design is a bare `rm -r` outside c4: no dry run, no lock check ('trash cannot be emptied while a lock exists' is unenforceable), no fail-closed. That inverts 'destructive by long-form-explicit'.

serious.scenario: A user reads `hold` as additive (run, x7). `hold proj.c4m` where proj.c4m is a one-level c4m of a project directory: accepted (N is non-empty), 18 objects of three snapshots go to trash, holdings becomes the single line 'readme.txt'.
serious.why: ZFS 'hold' and the plural 'holdings' both suggest adding. The empty-N guard does not cover it and CAS does not help if the CLI fills expect from the current file. Dry run by default protects an attentive human, not a script or agent that passes --force. A replace-the-whole-set verb is the highest-blast-radius shape available for the one mutation.

serious.scenario: A holdings entry names a directory whose listing this store does not have (run, x11): a line 'studio-delivery/ <ID>' is added. Writers keep succeeding and adding entries; every hold that keeps that line refuses ('REFUSE: listing absent'); `c4 cat -r` on the same holdings exits 0 with empty stderr. Same wedge after destroy(ID) of a listing.
serious.why: Section 3 says a holdings may name bytes the store never had; section 4b refuses any replace when a kept listing is absent; section 5 says a writer must find every reached object present or fail. These contradict each other for c4snap (all leaves absent by design), mirror stores, and received descriptions. In practice there must be two kinds of entry (bytes promised / description only) and the entry cannot say which. A hole then has three indistinguishable causes: never had, damaged, destroyed. No integrity check over holdings can be meaningful in a mixed store (Joshua's store already has 107,945 referenced-but-absent IDs).

serious.scenario: Scale (run, s2). `c4 cat -r` over a holdings with 2,000 entries pointing at a 1,260-entry tree: 32.9 s, 2,522,000 lines, 349 MB of text (200 entries: 3.2 s). The walk is snapshots x tree, about 77k entries/s, with no sharing. Extrapolated, not measured: 30 days of agent undo at 1,000 snapshots/day over a 50k-entry repo is 1.5e9 lines per closure; a single 10.4M-entry description is about 135 s per walk, two walks per hold, under the exclusive lock that blocks all writers.
serious.why: The proposal's L1 claim that what-holds-this, what-would-this-free and release are 'set operations over cat -r output' does not hold past toy size. A memoizing reach primitive is required (a real new verb or mode, with vectors), and even then each replace costs O(everything kept), so the 'conventional filesystem' dial position (replace on every save) costs O(tree) per save where a filesystem costs O(change). Also computed, not run: with nested undo/<day>/<time>/ every snapshot orphans the previous day listing (about 137 B x 1..1000 entries, roughly 68 MB/day into trash), and a flat holdings at 30k entries is a 4 MB rewrite+fsync per snapshot.

serious.scenario: Default names are scan-start times. A DIT's one-off `c4 id -s /Volumes/card` and an agent hook's per-prompt snapshot produce the same kind of line: time + ID. An L2 policy 'keep 7 daily' over default-named entries cannot tell them apart and thins the card snapshot. Entries created on a machine with a wrong clock sort as oldest and are thinned first.
serious.why: This is the borg/restic policy-scope failure made the default. 'How would we choose?' is answered 'by name and date', but the store supplies only the date, which is what the anonymous journal already had. Meaningful names are pushed to L2, and stable names that are replaced on save are a ref namespace, which the record rejected ('handles are IDs, never refs').

serious.scenario: Existing stores. Joshua's 33 GB store (194,127 objects, no roots) is entirely unaccounted. The only reclaim path is: hold what you want, list every other object as a stray entry, hold that, drop it. Any object a 1.0.x `c4 id -s`, imgbin, or c4git wrote moments before the stray listing was made is in that list.
serious.why: Adopt-then-drop is the rejected negative sweep ('unmarked implies garbage') done in two steps with a person approving a list of IDs and sizes. It keeps the letter of 'strays are never touched' and loses its protection for in-flight unregistered writers. Finding 'what you want' in a legacy store still needs byte sniffing or the c4m files outside the store. The design gives this store nothing it does not have today.

philosophy_violations: Fewest concepts: billed as one dial; the actual count is holdings file, lock file, trash directory, reach(), hold verb, destroy verb, CAS expect, rescue-from-trash, move ordering/resume rule, stale-lock rollback rule, empty-N flag, default-name and collision rule, nesting convention, bare-ID closure output, cat -r behavior change, and (after this attack) a lock lease and a trash timestamp. It is smaller than gc-requirements.md but it is not one concept.
Separate the subtraction from the addition: `c4 id -s` (addition) now takes the same lock and rewrites the same file as release (subtraction). Run: a crashed release blocks every save.

Safe by default, destructive by long-form-explicit: the one irreversible act (emptying trash) is outside c4, has no dry run and no guard, and is licensed by the absence of a lock file that users and rsync excludes routinely remove.

Verification over assertion: holdings.c4m reads as 'what this store keeps' but asserts nothing about possession; classes 'released' (is in trash) and 'unaccounted' (in no holdings this store has ever had) are defined by history the store does not keep, so neither can be recomputed from the store. Run: after a lost holdings, formerly held snapshots are indistinguishable from strays.

Ask what question an artifact answers: a holdings entry does not carry whether it promised bytes (snapshot) or only a description (c4snap, mirror, hand-added line), so presence checks compare it against the wrong thing.

Partial knowledge is a valid state: a directory ID without its listing is valid c4m and poisons holdings (every later release refuses); restore is still all-or-nothing; three causes of a hole are indistinguishable.

Capabilities from the outside: mutable state, a lock and a trash area are placed inside the store, which until now was a bag of immutable objects (v9: 'roots are purely virtual'). The store contract a vendor must meet grows from put/get/has to put/get/has/list/remove + conditional create + conditional replace + a move-to-trash convention + lock recovery semantics.

Beside, not instead: a mutable root directory, a lock and a trash folder is what ZFS/APFS/borg already do. The one reclaim rule only c4 can offer (release licensed by another store proving possession now) is not in L0 or L1; it is left as an L2 composition.

Composition over configuration: the claimed compositions over `cat -r` are O(snapshots x tree) (349 MB of text for 2,000 small snapshots), so the working form is a new memoizing primitive, not a recipe.
Determinism: entry names come from wall clocks; trash age comes from preserved mtimes; the outcome of a lock dispute depends on a human or harness guessing liveness.

Cost every new concept in implementations: 'a putter-only implementation conforms with zero work' is true only in a store no holdings-aware tool shares. c4git and imgbin must change or get private stores; all five implementations must agree on the holdings ID (run: on master `c4 id -q` of the file is the canonical listing ID and equals the ID with sizes null or 0 and with lines reordered; raw-bytes ID differs; an empty file gets a raw ID from `id` with exit 0 but fails to parse in `cat -r`).

The dry run that states exactly which objects and how many bytes a drop releases. In x3 it did list the c4git object; the information was there, the user just had no way to know it mattered.
