proposal.name: Pure bag: drop-warrant + attic (roots are c4m files outside the store)
proposal.one_sentence: The store is a bag (put/get/has/list/remove-by-ID) that knows nothing about roots, names or history; bytes leave it only when a description the owner explicitly drops names them and no description the owner keeps, or that sits in the bag itself, names them, and they leave by moving to a second bag (the attic) that is emptied later after the same check is re-run.
proposal.model:
BAG (L0). Operations: put(bytes)->ID, get(ID)->verified bytes, has(ID), list()->IDs with sizes, remove(ID). Two rules: (B1) a bag removes an object only when its owner calls remove for that ID; no expiry, no eviction, no graph walk. (B2) presence under an ID means the bytes hash to it. No journal, retain file, types, or roots in the contract. Anything that writes bytes under their ID is a conforming writer (1.0.x, imgbin, rsync, a vendor).

CLOSURE (L1, pure). closure(D) = every non-null ID in an entry of D; for a directory entry whose children are not inline, fetch the listing and recurse; for a folded-sequence entry, fetch the ID list and add every line; for a chain, union over all sections and base IDs. Kind comes only from the parent entry (name ends '/'), never from sniffing bytes. A listing that must be fetched and is absent or fails rehash is an ERROR (no output accepted). An absent leaf is not an error. A file-kind entry never descends, so a description can be named as bytes without naming what it describes.

ROOTS. Ordinary c4m files outside the bag, supplied by the caller at reclaim time. Convention (L2): two folders beside the bag, keep/ and drop/. A root file is either a one-line pointer ('- - - projA/ <snapshot ID>', verified working) or the full 1.0 artifact (c4 id dir > x.c4m), whose closure needs no store reads.

RECLAIM RULE. implicit = every object in the bag, outside closure(drop), that parses in full as a listing. keepset = closure(keep files + implicit). warrant = closure(drop) - keepset. unaccounted = list(bag) - keepset - closure(drop): reported, never touched. Any closure error refuses the whole run. So forgetting to name a c4m costs space, not data, and a description stored in the bag protects its bytes whether or not anyone listed it.

ACT. reclaim (dry run by default) moves warrant objects from the bag to the attic, which is just another bag directory. empty-attic (long-form flag) recomputes keepset now, moves back any attic object it contains, and calls remove on the rest. The recheck replaces the writer/collector lock.

CACHE ROLE (optional, no descriptions needed). An object may be removed from bag A when bag B returns verified bytes for the same ID at that moment (git-annex rule). Size/age/LRU eviction without that evidence is allowed only on a bag the owner has declared a cache, and is not in the standard.

DESTRUCTION. remove(ID) on every bag the owner controls, attic included, immediately. Descriptions are not edited.

My honest reading after the runs: this is the right L0 store contract and an incomplete L2. Where hooks create roots and the store is the only copy (agent undo), the product still needs an automatically written root list; the pure bag only says that list is not the vendor's problem.
new_concepts: L0: list() and remove(ID) named in the store contract, plus the sentence 'a bag removes an object only when its owner asks for that ID'. Go already has TreeStore.Walk and Remove; four other implementations add two small functions each; a vendor needs nothing S3 lacks.

L1: a fail-closed closure that emits bare IDs (one flag on cat -r, or one verb). Today cat -r exits 0 on a truncated closure and the only way to get IDs is awk on entry text, which the machine contract forbids. Cost: 5 implementations, about 6 conformance vectors (flat, nested, folded sequence, chain, missing listing = error, missing leaf = ok).
L1: predicate 'this object parses in full as a listing' used for implicit keep roots. No new code beyond each implementation's existing c4m parser; it is a sniff, used only in the keep direction.
L2: reclaim porcelain with dry-run default and a long-form --empty-attic. Go CLI only; documented as a composition of closure + sort/comm + move, so other languages need not implement it.
L2: the attic, a second bag directory. One new object state (in attic). No format.

L2: keep/ and drop/ folder convention for root files. No format; they are c4m files. A policy (keep 7 daily, 30 days of undo) is a program that moves files from keep/ to drop/, off unless the user turns it on.
L2 optional: evict-by-evidence for cache-role bags (remove from A what B verifies). Composition of existing verified cat plus remove.
Total: 0 new file formats, 0 new store-root files, 1 new state, 1 L1 flag or verb, 1 L2 verb with 1 flag.
removed_concepts: <store>/retain and its line grammar and fold semantics
The four verdicts keep/trash/scrub/drop and the three reserved actors
Aggregate claims, folds, substrate sets, residual lists (the 550k-line archive workload becomes one drop c4m)
adopt and the gc-A1 journal amendment (reserved names 'adopted'/'condemned')
Warrants as stored records; the trash staging directory (replaced by an attic that is itself a bag)
The shared/exclusive sweep lock in the store contract (replaced by move-then-recheck)
'Strays' as a concept: everything unaccounted is simply untouched
The journal as a retention authority and as part of the store contract. It may remain as an L2 undo log and as one source of keep roots; reclaim does not depend on it.
'c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers' and 'mixed fleets are out of gc's contract'
The help sentence 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable' (must go before the v1.1.0 freeze under any retention rule)
c4git's private sweeper: c4git only emits its keep and drop ID sets
38 gc conformance vectors, replaced by about 6 closure vectors
proposal.how_a_person_chooses:
By name and date, never by ID. Roots are files in a folder (for example 'projA 2026-10-03.c4m'). To let a version go, move its file from keep/ to drop/ (a product can present this as deleting a dated snapshot). The dry run then states what would leave: total bytes, the largest objects with the names the dropped description gives them, and what stays because another description still needs it. Space returns when the attic is emptied, like a desktop Trash.

Bytes that no description names cannot be chosen by this rule at all. To reclaim them a person must first describe them (a drop c4m listing those IDs). In the 33 GB default store the largest 1% of objects hold 77% of bytes (grounding figure, not re-measured), so that review is about 1,900 objects, not 194,000.

Automatic choice exists only as an L2 policy the user turned on, and it acts by moving root files to drop/, so it passes through the same warrant, the same dry run and the same attic.
proposal.how_expectations_are_met:
Default is that nothing ever leaves: a bag with an empty drop/ folder is keep-everything. The dial is which root files sit in keep/.

Why an ordinary user is not surprised by a loss:
- Nothing unnamed is touched. Forgetting to list a c4m (the July hazard) leaves its bytes in place; the cost is space.
- A description stored in the bag protects its own bytes even if nobody listed it. Run: an unlisted snapshot sharing a 300,000-byte file with a dropped snapshot kept that file; a nested shared subtree was kept in full; a root written by 1.0.18 with no journal line was found by the scan.
- Dropped bytes go to the attic and still read with the attic on the read path (run: C4_STORE=bag,attic).
- The dry run answers 'what will this free' exactly, which ZFS users cannot get.
- The only irreversible step is emptying the attic, a long-form explicit act that re-checks first.

Where a surprise is still possible: bytes shared between a description you dropped and a description held only outside the bag that you did not put in keep/ (a c4m in email, git history, an imgbin session file). They go to the attic and are lost when it is emptied. The attic delays this; it does not prevent it. Also 'I dropped 47 GB and got nothing back' until the attic is emptied.
proposal.destruction_vs_reclamation:
Reclamation (space back): warrant = closure(drop) minus closure(keep + in-bag descriptions); move to attic; later empty attic with recheck. Reversible until emptied, licensed only by descriptions, dry run by default.

Destruction (must be gone): remove(ID) on the bag and the attic, immediately, by ID, no attic, no reachability test. It promises only 'no longer servable from this bag', not physical erasure (the scrub ruling). Descriptions are untouched and keep naming the ID; because an absent leaf is never a closure error, one destroyed leaf does not wedge later reclaims (run: cat -r of the description exit 0, sibling file still reads).

Limits: the bag keeps no tombstone, so 'destroyed' and 'damaged' look the same unless the owner keeps a plain ID list outside it. Destroying a listing object makes closure fail closed for every pointer-style root through it; the owner must hold that root in full form or drop it. Run-confirmed: c4 restore refuses the whole tree when one leaf is gone ('Missing content for 1 entries; nothing restored'), so 'description stays as partial knowledge' is true for reading and false for restore today.
proposal.layer_placement:
L0 standard: C4 ID, c4m grammar, the bag contract (put, get, has, list, remove) and the one sentence B1. No roots, no journal, no retention vocabulary. This is all a vendor implements.

L1 toolbox: closure (fail-closed, bare IDs), set algebra on ID lists (sort/comm or intersect), verified membership (c4 cat ID >/dev/null), the listing-parse predicate. All pure; none writes.

L2 product: keep/ and drop/ folders, reclaim and --empty-attic, the attic, retention policies by name and age, evict-by-evidence for cache bags, and whatever writes a root file (or journal line) automatically at snapshot time. Snapshot, undo, history and sync live here and own their root lists.

proposal.cost:
Per implementation (x5): list and remove on the store (Go has both), one fail-closed closure with bare-ID output, about 6 vectors. The listing-parse predicate reuses the existing c4m parser.

Go CLI only: reclaim with --empty-attic, as documented porcelain over the L1 pieces.

Vendor: put/get/has/list/delete-by-ID and one sentence. No graph walk, no lock, no journal, nothing S3 lacks.

Compared with the design of record (gc-requirements.md, figures from the grounding): 2 verbs, 1 flag, 1 record file with its own grammar, a staging directory, a journal amendment, 3 reserved actors, a shared/exclusive lock, 38 vectors, all multiplied by five.

Runtime cost: each reclaim opens every object outside closure(drop) far enough to reject it as a non-listing, and fully parses the ones that are listings (grounding: 13,851 listing-like objects of 194,127 in the default store). Not measured at that scale by me.

Not costed: fixing restore to degrade on a missing leaf, and the directory-bag layout. The store uses an adaptive trie that splits at 4,096 files per directory (store/treestore.go), so my shell moves on a flat layout are a demonstration only; a real reclaim must go through list/remove.
weaknesses_admitted: Roots outside the store is the casync/git-alternates position. Bytes shared between a dropped description and a description held only outside the bag (email, git history, an imgbin session file) and not placed in keep/ are lost when the attic is emptied. The attic and the in-bag scan narrow the July hazard; they do not close it.

It reopens Joshua's 2026-07-09 ruling (no deletion verb until the journal is a complete root catalog) by arguing a positive drop warrant plus in-bag scan makes the catalog unnecessary. That is his call, not mine. It also conflicts with 'the store names its own roots' and with the v9 journal listed under 'do not churn'.

The implicit-root scan is a sniff on the deletion path, which the record rejected. I use it only to keep more, but it also means a description stored in the bag pins bytes against reclaim, against the letter of 'links never pin'. A peer able to put descriptions in your bag can block reclaim (space, not loss). False positives (c4m fixtures stored as content) pin space.

The composition is unsafe on today's binary: cat -r exits 0 on a truncated closure and under-marked the keep side (E2b), and extracting IDs with awk is scraping entry text. Needs a fail-closed bare-ID closure before anything ships.
An attic in C4_STORE creates new dependencies on itself because writers deduplicate against it (E3a). Safety rests on the empty-time recheck, which sees only descriptions in the bag or in keep/.

Agent undo fits worst. Hooks create roots and the user never sees one, so L2 must write a root file or journal line per snapshot with its own durability ordering. For that use case this is the lead's hypothesis with the list moved one directory over, outside the print barrier, and less safe.

Default behaviour is still keep everything forever. Bytes nobody describes are never reclaimable until someone writes a description of them (grounding: 6.53 GiB in the default store are named by no in-store description, about 2.5 GiB by none anywhere). The disk-growth complaint is not solved by default.
No tombstone: the bag cannot tell destroyed from damaged. A destroyed listing object makes reclaim refuse for every pointer root through it.
Two-step reclaim reproduces the ZFS complaint in another form: dropping frees nothing until the attic is emptied.

The bag adds no durability. When it is the sole copy (undo pre-images, c4git non-checked-out versions) reliability is whatever the filesystem gives; 'the source of truth is elsewhere' is false for those cases.

c4snap: the closure must follow chain base IDs, which I did not test, and every stored block is an implicit keep root, so the service must explicitly drop about 1,000 superseded blocks per pass (as file-kind entries in one drop c4m). Workable but subtle.
restore remains all-or-nothing on one missing leaf (E3c); this proposal does not fix it, and 'partial knowledge' is not true for restore until it is.

Evidence: all runs used trees of 3 to 6 files on a flat store layout with the master build; nothing was run against the real 33 GB store, the Ash mirror, folded sequences, chains, or the adaptive trie layout. Store-scale figures are quoted from the grounding, not re-measured.

attack.proposal: Pure bag: drop-warrant + attic (roots are c4m files outside the store). Store contract = put/get/has/list/remove-by-ID; reclaim = closure(drop files) minus closure(keep files + every in-bag object that parses as a listing and is outside closure(drop)); warrant moves to an attic bag, emptied later after a recheck; optional evict-by-evidence for cache bags; destruction = remove(ID).

fatal.scenario: Back up, then delete (run a2). Nightly snapshots of proj/ are registered in keep/. The user runs `c4 id -s -q proj/assets_old` by hand before deleting that folder; the claim prints and is journaled. A typeless bag cannot tell 'a root someone holds' from 'an interior listing of a dropped root'. Including such listings as roots would make every drop free nothing, so the hole cannot be closed without a root record written at snapshot time, which is the thing the proposal removes. positions.stance: Journal + verdicts (steelman of the v1.1 design)

proposal.name: Journal with releases (the v1.1 journal-plus-verdicts design, reduced to one file and two added line kinds)
proposal.one_sentence: A store keeps everything reachable from a claim it journaled and has not released; bytes may go only when they are reachable solely from released claims (or are destroyed by ID), and bytes no claim reaches are reported and never touched.
proposal.model:
STEELMAN, THEN THE CUT. The case for anonymous append-only roots plus verdicts rests on three things, and all three held up when run:
(1) Roots are a side effect of the act that prints the ID, so nobody has to remember to name anything (Joshua's 2026-07-09 ruling).
(2) Deletion needs a positive line naming a root. An empty or lost journal therefore yields an empty warrant; under any promise-list rule it yields a full one (run: header-only journal gives 0 reclaimable, a negative sweep with an empty root list would take 17 of 17 objects).
(3) There is no mutable authority: no current pointer, no compare-and-swap, no ref namespace. Names stay advisory, so losing them costs convenience and never data.

What does not survive is the second record file. gc-requirements.md is written against a journal with names and origins that v9 deleted seven hours later. And two files have no order between them: a tree re-snapshotted unchanged after `retain trash` prints the same ID as a durable claim and is still swept (shown on a simulated fold; no gc is built). So I keep the journal and move verdicts into it.

THE MODEL (implementable from this):
1. Record. `<store>/journal`, first line `@c4 journal 2`. Append-only, each line fsynced before its ID prints, an unterminated final line is ignored. Three line shapes, the ID always last:
   - `<time> <ID>` is a claim (unchanged from v1.1).
   - `<time> released <ID>` withdraws the promise for that root.
   - `<time> destroyed <ID>` is a tombstone for one object.
   Any other non-tail line makes every retention reader refuse, exit 1.
2. Fold. Scan in line order; a claim sets the ID live, a release sets it released, the latest line per ID wins. A release of an ID never claimed is inert and reported. Order is line position, never the timestamp (run: timestamps in a real journal are not monotonic).
3. Reach. A pure function of c4m grammar over rehash-verified bytes.
   - A root is a listing if its bytes parse wholly under the strict c4m grammar, otherwise a leaf.
   - Below the root, kind comes only from the parent entry: a directory or sequence entry, a first-line base ID or a boundary ID is a listing; a file entry is a leaf and is never opened; a symlink gives no edge.
4. Sets.
   - K = reach of live roots. An absent or rehash-failing listing in K refuses the run.
   - R = reach of released roots, tolerant of absence.
   - Warrant = (R minus K) intersected with present objects.
   - Strays = present objects in neither K nor R: counted, sized, reported, never touched.
5. Acts.
   - `c4 release <ID>...` appends release lines; nothing physical changes.
   - `c4 gc` is a dry run: warrant IDs on stdout, the bill and stray count on stderr.
   - `c4 gc --empty-trash` takes the exclusive lock, recomputes, and unlinks leaves first, listings last.
   - Rescue is a new claim, which existing verbs already make: `c4 cat -r <ID> | c4 id -s -q -` (run: it appends a fresh claim line for the same ID).
   - A stray is brought into account the same way: `c4 cat <ID> | c4 -s` (run).
6. Destruction. `c4 gc --destroy <ID>...` takes the exclusive lock, refuses an ID that any live root walks as a listing, appends the `destroyed` line durably, then vacates the name, overwrites best-effort and unlinks. It promises only "no longer servable from this store". Descriptions that name the ID stay valid; readers report "destroyed <date>" instead of "missing".
7. Exclusion. Every claim path holds the shared lock from first store write through its print; sweep and destroy hold it exclusive (v8 Amendment 3c, unchanged).
new_concepts: Journal line `<time> released <ID>`: one more line shape in the journal parser of each of five implementations. Only Go has a journal today (c4m/journal.go, 231 lines); a grep for the magic string finds nothing in c4py, c4ts, c4m-swift or libc4, so the journal itself is still owed four times.
Journal line `<time> destroyed <ID>`: one more line shape, plus a lookup in cat and restore so the error says destroyed rather than missing. Five implementations.

Journal format version 2: the v1.1 reader refuses three-field lines (run: `c4 log` fails with 'want 2 fields, got 3'). Free if it lands before v1.1.0 freezes the machine contract, a version bump after.
The fold (latest line per ID wins): about 30 lines per implementation, around 4 conformance vectors (my estimate).

The reach function with root kind decided by bytes: the real cost, a strict c4m classifier and walker in five languages with shared vectors. It is the same cost as gc-requirements section 5, minus the ID-list shape and the aggregate rules.
Three object states: kept, released (reclaimable), stray (reported, never touched). A concept, with no code beyond the set arithmetic.
Verb `c4 release`: one verb in the CLI; the other languages need only the library append.
Verb `c4 gc` with long-form flags `--empty-trash` and `--destroy`: one verb, two flags, CLI only.
Shared/exclusive store lock: already designed (v8 Amendment 3c). Per implementation and per medium, and unproven on NFS, SMB and S3.
removed_concepts: `<store>/retain` file and its four-field grammar (`<id> <verdict> <actor> <time>`)
Verdict words keep, trash, scrub and drop: one word, released, replaces them. Keep becomes a claim, drop becomes derivable (released and absent), scrub becomes destroy by ID.
`c4 retain` verb with its five modes and the fold view (`c4 log` shows the lines)
`c4 retain adopt`, the initialization marker, and gc refusing an uninitialized store (strays are safe without adoption; a stray is claimed with existing verbs)
Aggregate claims, residual lists, the substrate set, single-level distribution, and journal amendment gc-A1 (reserved names `adopted` and `condemned`)
Reserved actors c4:adopt, c4:gc, c4:split and the actor field
Retained split archives as record-layer catalog members
`<store>/scrub/` staging as a per-root obligation recomputed from record history (destroy is immediate and by object)
`c4 explain retain` topic
The refusal to act on interior objects (destroy takes any non-listing ID)
The help sentence 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable', and the documented head/tail journal shortening, which becomes unsafe once releases exist
proposal.how_a_person_chooses:
What the user sees today (run on master, `/tmp/retention-study/propose-journal/e1`): `c4 log` prints `index time ID`, for example `3 2026-10-03T22:12:46Z c43N7diX...` with a 90-character ID. Nothing else: no name, no path, no size, no kind. A single-file claim and a tree claim look identical.

To find the snapshot holding a stray `.env` I had to loop `c4 cat -r` over every root and grep for the object's ID. That is O(roots) closure walks and no ordinary user will do it.

So the answer has three parts:
- **By time, as a pipe.** `c4 log | awk '$2 < "2026-09-01" {print $NF}' | xargs c4 release`, then `c4 gc` to read the bill, then `c4 gc --empty-trash`.
- **By content, with existing verbs.** Which roots reach this ID (the loop above), and what dropping root X frees (closure difference). Both work today.
- **By name, only at L2.** The product that made the roots (undo plugin, sync tool, c4git) keeps its own list of what it claimed and issues releases by ID. Since the journal has no scope, the practical rule is one store per purpose, and a time policy is then per store.

For an agent-undo user the choice is a setting made once (keep D days or N snapshots) that the plugin turns into release lines. The user never handles an ID.
proposal.how_expectations_are_met:
- **Nothing is removed without two deliberate acts.** A release line names a root, then the long-form `--empty-trash`. Between them `c4 gc` prints exactly which objects would go.
- **The default is keep.** No clock, no space pressure, no automatic expiry. The Time Machine and Backblaze class of loss needs an L2 policy the user turned on.
- **Release is undoable until the empty.** A re-claim is one pipeline of existing verbs, and a later snapshot of an unchanged tree revives the root on its own because the latest line wins (run).
- **Failures degrade toward keeping.**
  - Lost or header-only journal: warrant empty.
  - Garbled line: refuse.
  - Unreadable listing under a kept root: refuse.
  - Lost claim lines: their objects become strays, not garbage. The exception is partial loss while a release line survives; that can expose shared objects, so the journal must never be shortened by hand.
- **Bytes written by tools that do not journal are never swept as unreferenced.** Run: three objects written by installed 1.0.18 were reported as strays and left alone. This covers 1.0.x, imgbin, rsync and a vendor's own writer.
- **Where it does not match filesystem expectations:** deleting a file from the working tree frees nothing, and neither does releasing one root while another still reaches the bytes. That is the ZFS complaint. The dry-run bill is the mitigation, not a cure.
proposal.destruction_vs_reclamation:
**Reclamation (space back)** is per root and two-step: `c4 release`, then `c4 gc --empty-trash`. It frees only what no live claim reaches, so it never leaves a hole under a kept description. It may free less than expected.

**Destruction (must be gone)** is per object, immediate and irreversible: `c4 gc --destroy <ID>`. It ignores reachability, so a 15-byte `.env` captured in 200 snapshots goes without giving up 200 undo points. The as-designed gc cannot do this: it refuses interior objects and makes you condemn every root.

After a destroy, every description naming the ID stays valid and keeps its own ID. The hole is recorded by the `destroyed` line, so it reads as deliberate rather than damage. gc is not wedged, because the keep walk never opens leaves.

Three limits:
- It promises only "not servable from this store", never physical erasure (Joshua's scrub ruling).
- It refuses a listing that a live root walks through, so a secret filename cannot be removed without releasing its roots.
- Restore is all-or-nothing on one missing leaf today (the grounding run), so a destroyed leaf blocks restore of every snapshot naming it until restore learns to materialize the rest.

proposal.cost:
**Against the design of record.** gc-requirements.md costs 2 verbs, 1 flag, 1 new file with its own grammar, 4 verdict words, 3 reserved actors, a staging directory, a journal name amendment, the aggregate and substrate machinery, a lock, and about 38 conformance vectors.

**This proposal.** 2 verbs (`release`, `gc`), 2 long flags, 0 new files, 2 new journal line shapes, 1 format-version bump, the same lock, and roughly 15 vectors (my estimate: about 4 fold, 8 walk, 3 sweep order and crash).

**Per implementation.**
- Journal parse and append with the three shapes. Go has it; the other four have none.
- A fold of about 30 lines.
- The strict reach walker. This is the bulk and the only part where a bug destroys kept data.
- The sweep and destroy sequences.
- The lock.
An implementation that only needs to write safely needs just the append.

**For a storage vendor.** Nothing, if the vendor is a bag (put, get, has, list, delete-by-ID) and the c4 client holds the journal and does the walk. To own the promise the vendor would need an ordered append log and a writer/collector exclusion, which this design does not make cheap.

**Runtime.**
- A claim line is 112 bytes and a release line 121. 550k releases come to about 66 MB with no aggregate machinery.
- 1000 snapshots a day is about 40 MB of journal a year.
- Every sweep re-reads every listing under every live root. For the 10.4M-entry snapshot service that is about 1.5 GB of text per layer.
- A dry run followed by an empty pays the walk twice.

**Not costed.** Fixing restore so one destroyed leaf does not block the other files.
weaknesses_admitted: The choice problem is not solved, only moved. Anonymous roots mean `c4 log` gives a person nothing to choose by except time, and the grounding says people choose by name and time. Naming, scoping and policy all land on L2 or on a one-store-per-purpose convention.

It is not an L0 rule. The promise lives in a file only the Go CLI writes, inside a local directory, guarded by a local lock. It does not meet 'as fundamental as ID + c4m', and it gives a vendor nothing to implement beyond a bag.
The default is still 'keep every version forever'. A store nobody runs a policy on grows without bound: 33 GB on Joshua's machine, 2.9 GB a day measured for the undo loop.
Strays are never reclaimed by gc. Every existing 1.0.x store is 100% strays, so the 33 GB store gets nothing back until someone claims descriptions and releases them, or destroys large objects by ID.

Shared-object hazard: an object written by c4git or imgbin that happens to equal content in a released root is swept, because their roots are outside the journal. Tools sharing a store must journal their claims; c4git and imgbin would both need changes.

Root kind by bytes reverses a recorded rejection ('no heuristic sniff on the deletion path'), for roots only. Releasing a stored text file that parses as c4m also releases what it names. The walk is exact and rehash-verified, but it is still classification by content.

It contradicts Joshua's record in three places: it changes the journal grammar ratified 2026-07-13 and listed under 'do not churn'; it deletes the retain file from the architecture he accepted 2026-07-10; and it breaks the snapshot service's `c4 log | tail -1` handle when the last line is a release.
The journal can never be shortened by hand once releases exist: losing an old claim line while a release survives exposes shared objects. No compaction is designed, so the file grows forever.

Destroy is weak in practice. The next hook snapshot re-ingests a secret still in the tree, it cannot remove a listing under a kept root, and it blocks restore of every snapshot naming the leaf until restore handles holes.
In-place deletion needs the writer/collector lock, which is unproven on NFS, SMB and object stores. A copy-to-fresh-store rule avoids it; this design cannot.

Evidence is thin: the mechanism was run as a shell simulation over 17 objects. The lock, crash ordering, the destroy sequence and scale were not tested, and the claim that the other four implementations lack a journal rests on one grep for the magic string.
Two build defects must be fixed before any of this is safe: claims are not journaled when two stores are configured, and `c4 cat -r` reports a truncated closure as success.

attack.proposal: Journal with releases (attack-journal): one append-only <store>/journal with claim, `released` and `destroyed` lines; latest line per ID wins; warrant = (reach of released roots minus reach of live roots) intersected with present objects; strays reported and never touched; `c4 release`, `c4 gc [--empty-trash | --destroy]`.

The journal holds S1 on lines 1, 4 and 5 (restore reproduces mtimes, so the ID is identical). Then the proposal's pipe `c4 log | awk '$2 < cutoff {print $NF}' | xargs c4 release`, with the cutoff at line 3's time, selects S1 and S2 from the old lines. philosophy_violations: Ask what question an artifact answers: a release line carries an ID but not which claim it withdraws or who made it, so it is applied to claims it was never meant for (X1). This is the 'silent false match' class.

Plain text, line-local under merge: the fold depends on line order across the whole file; journals cannot be merged, sorted, concatenated or shortened without changing what is kept (X10). The master help text documents head/tail shortening today.

Verification over assertion: a claim line asserts retention but nothing checks that leaves exist (X2); a `destroyed` line is an assertion that goes stale when the same bytes are put again; 'released' cannot be recomputed from store contents.
Determinism: the kept set depends on the interleaving of a release append and a concurrent claim append of the same ID; the same acts in a different order keep different bytes.

Partial knowledge is a valid state: the keep walk refuses the whole run on one absent listing or boundary ID under a live root (X4), and restore stays all-or-nothing on one destroyed leaf (admitted, uncosted).

Safe by default, destructive by long-form-explicit: `c4 release` is a short common word with no dry run that is destructive in effect once a policy automates the empty; `--destroy` is immediate with no dry run and hangs off a verb whose bare form is a dry run.
No heuristic on the deletion path (recorded rejection): root kind is decided by sniffing bytes, and the decision flips on CRLF or a comment line (X5).

Fewest concepts, fully load-bearing: three line shapes, a fold, three object states, two verbs, two flags and a lock, none of which is an existing primitive. The journal becomes a second positional grammar with verbs in it, where c4m and the existing algebra (diff, patch, set difference of closures) are unused.

Cost every concept in implementations: the journal exists only in Go; four implementations owe the journal, the fold, the strict classifier and the lock, and the lock is per medium and undefined on NFS, SMB and object stores.

Capabilities from the outside / vendor adoption: retention authority is a file inside the store directory that only one client writes. A vendor store has no append log or flock to hold it, so the standard gains nothing a vendor can implement or guarantee.
Composition over configuration: 'one store per purpose' is offered as the scoping rule, which gives up cross-purpose dedup and contradicts the shared default store.

Roots registered as a side effect of the act that prints the ID. Nothing in my attack touched this; every loss I produced came from how promises are withdrawn, not how they are made.
Withdrawal (logical) separate from removal (physical), with a dry-run bill between them.

Destruction by ID as a separate act from reclamation, allowed on interior leaves, promising only 'not servable from this store'. The need is real (.env in 200 snapshots); the tombstone mechanics are what need work.

One ordered record instead of journal plus retain file. The proposer's E3c point stands: two files have no order between a verdict and a later identical claim. The single file fixes that case; it does not fix the claim-identity problem in X1.

positions.stance: Store classes (retention is the store's contract)

proposal.name: Store classes: retention is one declared word per store, and reclamation is demotion down the store list
proposal.one_sentence: Each store states one word answering "who may make has(ID) go from true to false" (archive: nobody; mirror: only a root replacement, and only for bytes the old root reached and the new one does not; cache: anyone, any time), an undeclared store is an archive, and space is reclaimed by moving superseded bytes to the next store in C4_STORE rather than by a collector.
proposal.model:
STORE CONTRACT (L0). Operations: put(bytes)->ID, get(ID), has(ID). Optional: remove(ID), list(). This is already the Go Store interface plus TreeStore.Walk (store/store.go, treestore.go; S3Store has Remove but no list - code read).

CLASS. A store states exactly one class. It is a promise about what has(ID)=true means tomorrow:
- archive: still true. No tool removes by inference; nothing leaves except explicit destruction by ID.
- mirror: still true while the store's root reaches the ID. The store carries one root ID. Bytes may leave only at a root replacement, and only the positive set closure(old root) - closure(new root). The store itself never removes anything.
- cache: no promise. The store or anyone may drop anything; has() must be asked at use.
An undeclared store is an archive. So every 1.0.x store, every imgbin write and the 33 GB default store keep today's behavior: no c4 verb removes a byte from them.

STATEMENT. One line of text at `<store>/class`: `archive`, `cache`, or `mirror <ID>`. Object-store/vendor form: the same line under the key `class`, or an API call returning it. The mirror line is the only mutable cell (substrate-map's "one mutable binding kind"): replaced by temp+rename locally, conditional PUT on an object store. The root is an ID, not a name; to hold several descriptions the root is a listing whose entries are dated directory entries pointing at snapshot IDs (ran this, E5). Entry names are inert labels with no lookup semantics. The existing journal is unchanged; each root replacement can append the old root as an ordinary `<time> <ID>` line.

CLOSURE (grammar rule, L0). closure(ID) = the ID, plus every ID in an entry of a listing; descend only where the parent entry says directory (name ends "/") or chain base. Never sniff bytes. A missing listing makes the closure UNKNOWN below it; a missing leaf is simply absent. Three answers: held, missing these IDs, unknown below this listing.

THREE SETS IN A MIRROR. Reached by the root (kept). Reached by the replaced root only (superseded: moves out). Reached by neither (unaccounted: reported, never touched by any verb). There is no negative sweep.

VERBS (L1).
- `c4 has <ID|file.c4m>`: walk the closure, print missing IDs on stdout. Exit 0 all held, 1 some missing, 2 unknown (a listing is absent). Which stores are asked is C4_STORE. Vendor optional batch form: ID list in, missing ID list out.
- `c4 keep <new-root>`: first store must be class mirror. Computes closure(old) - closure(new). Refuses if any listing under the NEW root is unreadable (that is the over-delete direction); an unreadable listing under the OLD root only shrinks the set and is reported. Dry run by default: warrant IDs on stdout, byte total on stderr. `--force`: copy the warrant to the second store in C4_STORE, verify has() there, swap the root line, then remove from the mirror. With no second store it refuses.
- `c4 destroy <ID>...`: remove(ID) on every store in the list, any class, then verify has() is false on each and report any store that refused.
Cache eviction is not a verb: a cache permits removal of anything by anyone, so emptying it is deleting or age-thinning its directory (a recipe), or the vendor's lifecycle rule.

COMPOSITION (C4_STORE list, as built: writes to the first, reads fall through). 
- `archive`: v1.1 as built.
- `mirror,cache`: a folder plus Trash. 
- `mirror,archive`: bounded working store, full history in a second (vendor) store.
- `cache,archive`: local accelerator in front of an authoritative store.
keep acts on store 1 and demotes to store 2; destroy acts on all; put goes to store 1.

USE CASES.
- Ash mirror: each side is a mirror whose root is the agreed root; the sync tool calls keep only after both root IDs agree by rehash; the demoted pre-images land in a cache that is the attic, emptied after audit. During a transaction the root is a listing with base/ and new/. The remote's description may name bytes it does not hold: `c4 has` exit 1 is a valid state, not deletion. The existing 0.79 GiB of superseded objects has no recorded prior root, so it is unaccounted and leaves only by copy-out.
- c4snap: mirror, root = head block, closure follows base IDs; consolidation is one keep. Leaf IDs absent by design is legal.
- imgbin: put-only writer; legal in any class. In the shared undeclared store its objects are kept forever (today's behavior). Its correct class is cache, which needs its own store path.
- Agent undo: `mirror,cache`; the hook puts the snapshot then keeps old-listing-plus-one-dated-entry; an age/count policy drops dated entries (L2, opt-in). Or declare archive for "nothing expires". Which is the default is Joshua's decision.
- 33 GB default store: stays an archive. To reclaim: make a new store, write `cache` into the old one and put it second in the list, re-snapshot or copy the closures still wanted, check with `c4 has`, then delete the old directory.
- c4git: its store is a mirror whose root is a listing c4git generates from refs+reflog+index; `c4git gc` becomes keep. The warrant is positive, so another tool's snapshot in the same store is unaccounted and untouched, which removes the measured loss. In an undeclared store gc refuses.
new_concepts: Store class: three words (archive, mirror, cache) with one sentence each. Cost: a 1-line parser in 5 languages; about 4 conformance vectors.

`<store>/class` file (one line; `mirror <ID>` carries the root). One new store-root file, but no new grammar beyond word + optional ID. Cost: read in 5 languages; atomic replace (temp+rename, or conditional PUT) wherever keep is implemented.
Default rule: undeclared store = archive. No code; one sentence in the standard.

Closure rule with a three-valued answer (held / missing / unknown below an absent listing). Go has the walk inside restore and cat -r; the other four implementations need a store-resolving walk. About 4 vectors (nested dirs, absent leaf, absent listing, chain base).
Verb `c4 has` (missing IDs on stdout, exit 0/1/2). 5 implementations; optional vendor batch endpoint (ID list in, ID list out).

Verb `c4 keep <root>` (dry run default, --force). Set difference, copy to next store, root swap, remove. 5 implementations if every language ships the reference store; otherwise Go only. About 3 vectors (positive diff, stray untouched, refuse on unreadable new closure).
Verb `c4 destroy <ID>` (remove on every store in the list, verify absent). Thin over the existing Store.Remove; 1 vector.
State 'unaccounted' (in a mirror, reached by neither old nor new root): reported, never removed. A report, not a format.

Vendor minimum: archive or cache = put/get/has plus stating one word (nothing S3 lacks: Object Lock bucket, lifecycle bucket). Mirror = that plus remove(ID) and one conditionally-writable cell. No vendor walks a graph.
removed_concepts: `<store>/retain` record file and its line grammar (gc-requirements)
Verdict vocabulary keep/trash/scrub/drop and the fold over verdict lines
Warrants as stored records (the warrant becomes the difference of two closures, computed and discarded)
Aggregate claims, ID-list claims minted for verdicts, residual lists, substrate sets, reserved journal names adopted/condemned (amendment gc-A1)
Adopt verb and the three reserved actors
Trash/staging directory inside the store and --empty-trash (trash is a second store of class cache)
Shared/exclusive sweep lock in the store contract (replaced by one compare-and-swap on the root line plus demotion instead of unlink)
The planned `c4 gc` and `c4 retain` verbs
The journal as the retention root catalog: it stays as built (`@c4 journal 1`, time + ID) and stays a history, not an authority
The rule 'c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers': a put-only writer is legal in every class
The unscoped help sentence 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable': it becomes true for class archive and is scoped to it
proposal.how_a_person_chooses:
Nobody picks objects, and nobody picks by ID except for destruction.
1. Per store, once: write one word. Leaving it blank means archive, so the default choice is "nothing goes".
2. In a mirror: edit the root listing, whose entries are dated folders with names, times and sizes. Deleting a line drops that snapshot. `c4 diff old new` shows the dropped line (ran it, E5); `c4 keep new` as a dry run prints exactly which IDs would move and how many bytes.
3. `c4 keep --force` moves those bytes to the cache store (the Trash). Space comes back when the person empties or age-thins that cache directory.
4. Policies such as "keep 30 days" or "keep 7 daily" are L2: a product rewrites the listing and calls keep. They are opt-in per product, never a store default.
5. For a legacy store with no root: the person never chooses what to delete, only what to copy out; the rest goes when they delete the old directory themselves.
proposal.how_expectations_are_met:
- No store loses bytes unless its owner wrote `mirror` or `cache` into it. Existing stores are archives.
- A mirror behaves like a folder: what the listing shows is what is kept; what you remove from the listing goes to a trash that is still readable (E1: with the cache second in the list, the dropped snapshot restored in full).
- Bytes nobody described are never touched, so another tool's writes, a 1.0.x write or an in-flight ingest cannot be collected (E1: the stray blob was in neither closure and stayed readable).
- A cache is declared losable in advance, like a browser cache; the user was told by the class word.
- The opposite complaint (ZFS: "what will this free?") is answered before acting: the dry run prints the warrant.
- keep fails closed if the new root's closure cannot be read in full (the restic #4612 class).
Where a surprise remains: a store declared cache that has silently become the only copy (imgbin after the source folder is deleted). The class word makes that the owner's stated risk; nothing detects it.
proposal.destruction_vs_reclamation:
Reclamation (space back) is never an unlink by inference. It is (a) demotion: `c4 keep` moves the positive warrant from a mirror to the next store; (b) eviction: a cache drops things under its own policy; (c) retirement: the owner deletes a whole store directory after copying out what is still wanted (E3: the re-ingested root ID was identical, 7 objects instead of 12). Archives are never reclaimed in place.

Destruction (must be gone) is `c4 destroy <ID>`: an explicit act naming IDs, independent of class and reachability, applied to every store in the list and verified by has() returning false. It promises only "these stores no longer serve these bytes", not physical erasure (consistent with the shred -> scrub ruling). A WORM vendor archive may refuse; the verb reports which store refused.

After destroying a leaf, every description that names it stays valid: the closure walk never opens leaves, so keep still works and `c4 has` reports the ID as missing. Destroying a listing that the current root reaches is refused, because it would make the closure unknown and block every later keep; the path is to write a description without it, keep that, then destroy.

Not solved: nothing records that an absence was deliberate rather than damage, and a later snapshot of the same bytes puts them back.
proposal.layer_placement:
L0 (standard): put/get/has, optional remove and list; the three class words and where the line lives; "undeclared = archive"; the closure rule; the sentence "a store never removes bytes except as its class states".
L1 (toolbox): `c4 has`, `c4 keep`, `c4 destroy`; the C4_STORE list semantics (write first, read through, demote to second, destroy on all).
L2 (product): who builds the root listing (snapshot/undo adding dated entries), age and count policies, when the cache is thinned, Ash's agreement evidence and attic audit, c4git generating its root from git history, migration of legacy stores.
Honest caveat on placement: `mirror` needs a mutable root cell and remove(ID), so for a vendor it is an optional tier above the two classes every vendor already ships. It could be argued mirror is L1 behavior over a store that merely permits owner removal.

proposal.cost:
Per language implementation: a one-line class parser; a store-resolving closure walk with the three-valued result (Go has it inside restore; the other four need it); `has`; `destroy` (thin). `keep` (set difference, copy to next store, root swap, remove) only where the reference store ships. Roughly 12 conformance vectors against the 38 in gc-requirements, and three verbs plus one one-line file against two verbs, a flag, a record grammar, a staging directory, a journal amendment, three actors and a lock.

Storage vendor: archive or cache needs put/get/has and stating one word, which is what S3 with Object Lock or with a lifecycle rule already is. Mirror adds remove(ID) and one conditionally-writable key. No graph walk, no lock, no collector on the server.

Costs that move rather than disappear:
- Users now set up more than one store (a mirror and a cache) and a C4_STORE list. The complexity leaves the store format and lands in configuration.
- Demotion copies bytes when the two stores are on different devices; on the same device it is a rename and frees nothing until the cache is emptied.
- Copy-out of a legacy store needs free space for the kept set while both exist.
- c4git and the Ash sync script must be changed to generate a root and call keep; c4snap must set its root on each commit.
- Master does not write the journal when C4_STORE is a list (found by the history agent; consistent with my E1). List mode is what this design leans on and it is the least exercised path today.
weaknesses_admitted: A class is a declaration, not enforcement. E4: 1.0.18 ignores the file. An old `c4git gc --force`, a hand-run rm, or any tool that does not read the class will still delete from an archive.

The 'ask' does not exist today and the nearest existing checks lie. E2: `cat -r` exits 0 on a truncated closure and the documented recompute check passes on incomplete stores. The whole design rests on a closure walk that five implementations must get exactly right; under-enumerating the new root in keep is the catastrophic direction.

Dropping a root drops its description objects too (E1). Listings are small in most stores (0.07 GiB of 33) but they are the entire payload for c4snap, so they cannot simply be exempted. As specified, a dropped snapshot's description survives only while the cache holds it.

Unaccounted bytes are never reclaimed in place. The 33 GB default store, the Ash mirror's 0.79 GiB and every imgbin object are unaccounted, so the only path is copy-out and retiring the store. For a 500 GB media store that means a second copy's worth of free space (APFS clones might avoid it; not verified).
Two steps to get space back (keep, then empty the cache). This is the restic forget/prune confusion and the ZFS 'I deleted it and got nothing back' complaint, chosen deliberately for safety.

The grace period is a clock in the cache tier. The accepted gc design's 'strays are never touched' needed no clock. A concurrent ingest that deduplicates against an object being demoted ends up with a root that reaches bytes now only in the cache; it is recoverable only until the cache evicts, and keep must re-verify and copy back. I have not specified or tested that.

One class and one root per store. The shared ~/.c4/store used by c4, c4git and imgbin cannot be a mirror for all three without all of them cooperating on one root listing; in practice this forces a store per purpose, and concurrent writers (two agents' undo hooks) contend on the root swap.

No record distinguishes deliberate destruction from damage, and destroyed bytes return if the same content is snapshotted again. Destroying a listing under the live root is refused, so removing a secret file NAME requires rewriting the description and its ancestors first.

Mirror may not belong in L0. A vendor that offers only put/get/has can be an archive or a cache; mirror needs a mutable cell with compare-and-swap, which is weak on NFS/SMB and only recently available on S3. If mirror is really L1, the standard has two classes and this proposal is thinner than it claims.

It conflicts with recorded rulings and needs them reopened: 'no deletion verb until the journal provides a complete root catalog' (I replace the catalog with a positive warrant between two roots plus the store's declared consent); the rejected 'second mutable authority' (the class line is one); 'c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers' (I allow put-only writers). It keeps: links never pin, handles are IDs not refs, positive warrant only, fail closed, the v9 journal unchanged, scrub not shred.
It does not decide the default for agent undo (archive for 'nothing expires' versus mirror,cache with an age policy). It only makes the choice one word; the decision still goes back to Joshua.

It does not use c4's strongest many-stores property as a rule. 'Drop only when another store proves possession now' (git-annex, DIT card reuse, Ash root agreement) is possible with `c4 has` against another store, but I specified no class that requires it; a cache may evict without asking. Derivation-based elision ('having A and computing A are fungible') is not covered at all.

Experiments used a 5-file tree and hand-moved files. They show the mechanism is expressible, not that it is correct at 194,127 objects, across devices, under crash, or with concurrent writers. E3(c) also showed that copying objects by ID through the CLI turns every object into a journal line, so the copy step inside keep needs a store-level path that does not exist as a verb.

attack.proposal: Store classes: each store declares one word (archive / mirror <root-ID> / cache) answering "who may make has(ID) go from true to false"; undeclared = archive; space is reclaimed by `c4 keep <new-root>` demoting closure(old root) - closure(new root) from the first store in C4_STORE to the second, plus `c4 has` and `c4 destroy`.

fatal.scenario: mirror,cache ('a folder plus Trash'), run on the master build (A1). Snapshot R1, change files, snapshot R2, demote closure(R1)-closure(R2) to cache T. User reverts the files (an undo) and the hook snapshots again with C4_STORE=M,T. The claim prints, exit 0, but the reverted 300 KB file and a.txt are NOT written to the mirror: big.v1 is in M 0 times, in T once. Remove T from the list (trash emptied): `c4 restore` of the new, kept snapshot fails with 'Missing content for 2 entries; nothing restored'; `c4 cat -r` on it still exits 0.
fatal.why: Ingest skips any object for which MultiStore.Has is true in ANY store of the list (cmd/c4/id.go:550 and :611; store/multi.go Has), and Put goes only to store 1. So a kept root can reach bytes that exist only in the store whose class says 'anyone may drop anything'. The mirror's promise is about has() going true->false in that store; it never held the bytes, so the contract is satisfied while the data is gone. `c4 has` run with the configured list would report 'all held'. keep's guard checks only listings, read through the same list, so it does not refuse. Restoring from trash and re-snapshotting is the most ordinary thing a Trash is used for.

fatal.scenario: Unaccounted description hollowed, run (A2). One store. Mirror root lists snap-1 (R1) and snap-2 (R2). Another writer (1.0.18, c4git's clean filter, imgbin plus its c4m, a hook whose keep failed or lost the root race) stored description D of a tree that contains the same hero.mov bytes as R1. Drop snap-1: warrant = 3 IDs, including that file. After demotion `c4 restore D` goes from exit 0 to 'Missing content for 1 entries; nothing restored'; `c4 cat -r D` still exits 0.
fatal.why: The proposal's guarantee 'reached by neither root: reported, never touched by any verb' holds only for objects unique to the stray. The warrant is computed from two roots only, so any object shared between a dropped root and a description the root does not list is classed 'superseded' and moved. Shared content is the likely case, not the corner: c4git and an undo snapshot look at the same working tree, so the proposal's claim that this 'removes the measured c4git loss' is false for exactly the large files c4git manages. This is the reason for Joshua's 2026-07-09 ruling (no deletion verb until there is a complete root catalog); a positive warrant between two roots does not replace the catalog. The proposer's E1 tested a stray blob with unique bytes, which cannot show this.

fatal.scenario: Folded sequence under-marked, run (A4). Five frames + slate. R1 = `c4 id -s` (unfolded), R2 = `c4 id -s -S` (folded: one entry `frame.[0001-0005].exr` whose ID names an ID-list object). Warrant for dropping R1 while keeping R2, computed the proposer's way (cat -r closures, set difference) = 6 IDs: all five frame objects plus R1's listing.
fatal.why: The proposal's L0 closure rule says 'descend only where the parent entry says directory (name ends "/") or chain base'. A folded entry is neither, and `c4 cat -r` does not expand it. So the kept snapshot's frames are in closure(old) and not in closure(new) and are demoted. This is under-enumeration of the NEW root, the direction the proposal itself calls catastrophic, and it hits the media users with the strictest loss expectations. Fixable by adding a third descend case, but that makes sequence-pattern name parsing (escaped `\[` vs fold, A11) part of the closure rule in five languages, and it shows the 'about 4 vectors' closure rule was not checked against the grammar that exists.

fatal.scenario: cache,archive ('local accelerator in front of an authoritative store'), run (A12). `class` files written as proposed, C4_STORE=K,A. `c4 id -s -q work/` prints a claim, exit 0. Objects in cache K: 2. Objects in archive A: 0. Journal lines anywhere: 0 (`c4 log`: 'the configured store has no local journal').
fatal.why: As built and as the proposal specifies ('put goes to store 1'), every new snapshot under this listed composition has its only copy in the store that promises nothing, and no journal line records the root. The print barrier ('printed only after durable') is met in a store where durable means nothing tomorrow. A user who chose this composition from the proposal's table loses new work at the first cache eviction.

serious.scenario: Root cell lost update, run (A5). 40 concurrent hooks each read the root listing, append one dated entry, and replace it by temp+rename (the proposal's stated local mechanism). Entries surviving: 6 of 40, in three rounds.
serious.why: rename is atomic replace, not compare-and-swap. A local filesystem needs a lock to get CAS, so the 'shared/exclusive lock removed from the store contract' line in removed_concepts is not true; the lock returns under another name, with the same NFS/SMB weakness the proposal cites. The 34 lost snapshots are not deleted, but they vanish from the only list a person can see, become unaccounted, are never journaled in list mode, and are then exposed to the A2 hollowing. This is the 'second mutable authority creating a divergence/lost-update class' recorded as the reason the writable master c4m was rejected.

serious.scenario: Concurrent thinner and hook. A policy job computes warrant W against root L and starts copying (minutes to hours for large warrants). A hook ingests a new snapshot that dedups against an object in W (same skip as A1), then keeps L+new. Whichever root swap wins, W is removed afterwards; the new root's keep does not refuse because only listings are checked.
serious.why: This is the defect the record already reopened ('append-time-only lock let a sweep run between staging and append... printed=>durable falsified with no crash'). The proposal admits it and specifies no fix. In mirror,cache it is recoverable only until the cache evicts, and the cache has no promised grace.

serious.scenario: Grace period keyed on the wrong event, run (A6). An object ingested in March is demoted by rename into the cache today. `find T -mtime +30` matches it immediately (1 of 1).
serious.why: The proposal says same-device demotion is a rename and that emptying the cache is 'deleting or age-thinning its directory (a recipe)'. Store objects carry ingest time as mtime (measured: 100% of the default store's bytes are older than 30 days). The obvious recipe gives a grace period of zero. A correct grace needs a demotion timestamp, which is a new record the proposal says it does not have.

serious.scenario: A valid but wrong new root. An L2 generator emits a short listing: c4git run in a second clone sharing the store, a hook run in the wrong cwd, a policy glob that matches too much. `c4 keep --force` demotes everything the other party's root reached. Also run (A8): the empty listing and the empty file share one ID; once any tree with an empty file is stored, `c4 cat -r <empty-ID>` exits 0, so an empty new root is 'readable' and the warrant is the whole old closure.
serious.why: The fail-closed rule covers unreadable listings, not wrong ones. One root per store means the last writer's view is the authority; two generators on one store each drop the other's content with a positive warrant (borg shared-repo, borg -P--). The dry run protects a person; an unattended harness runs --force.

serious.scenario: `c4 destroy <ID of an empty .env>`, run (A10). After removing that one object, restore of a snapshot containing pkg/__init__.py fails: 'Missing content for 1 entries; nothing restored'.
serious.why: IDs name bytes, not files. Destroying one secret's ID removes every file with those bytes from every description in every store on the list, including archives ('nobody' is not nobody), and restore is all-or-nothing, so each affected snapshot becomes unrestorable as a whole. The same ID is also the empty-directory listing. No dry run is specified for destroy, and nothing records that the absence was deliberate, so a later damage check cannot tell it from loss and the next hook snapshot puts the secret back.

serious.scenario: Scale, measured (A7). 50,000-file tree: `c4 cat -r` walks 50,400 entries in 0.46 s (about 108k entries/s, 139 bytes/entry). A root listing with 50 dated entries pointing at that tree: 2,520,050 lines, 19.6 s (no memoization). Dated root entry = 147 bytes.
serious.why: Extrapolated, not run: 10.4M entries is about 96 s and 1.45 GB of text per closure, twice per keep, plus a 10.4M-ID set difference; c4snap commits about 1,000 blocks per pass. The exact warrant cannot be a tree diff, because a dropped object may be reached at another path in the new root, so every keep enumerates the whole new closure unless a persistent index is added (a new concept). For agent undo at 1,000 snapshots/day a flat root listing of 30 days is 30,000 x 147 B = 4.4 MB rewritten per prompt, about 4.4 GB/day of superseded root listings, more than the measured 2.9 GB/day the snapshots themselves cost. Nesting by date fixes the size and turns entry names into a schema policies parse, which is the recorded 'name-field-as-schema' objection.

serious.scenario: A mirror that is not bounded. Any put without a keep (1.0.18, imgbin, a crashed hook between put and keep, a keep that lost the root race, a crash after the root swap and before removal) leaves unaccounted bytes that no verb may ever remove in place.
serious.why: The mirror converges on an archive with a root cell on top. The measured Ash mirror already has 0.79 GiB of this after 80 minutes. The only remedy is copy-out and deleting the directory, which for the 33 GB default store means the user names what to copy and the roughly 950 objects (about 2.5 GiB) with no description anywhere are destroyed by omission: the withdrawn explicit-roots model, performed by hand.

serious.scenario: Class line travels with the directory, run (A9). `rsync -a mirror/ archive/` (consolidating two stores) leaves the former undeclared archive declared `mirror <ID>`. E4 (proposer) already showed 1.0.18 ignores the file entirely.
serious.why: The protection 'undeclared = archive' is one file copy away from being changed, without any c4 verb being run, and the installed fleet neither reads nor preserves it. A corrupted or truncated class line also loses the root ID, which is the only handle to the list of snapshots, and list mode writes no journal to recover it from.

serious.scenario: The word 'mirror'. A studio engineer reads it as RAID mirror or site mirror: a safe second copy. A user reads 'cache' for imgbin's store as harmless, then deletes the source folder.
serious.why: Declaring `mirror` is the act that opts a store into removal, and the common meaning of the word is the opposite. The proposal's own imgbin recommendation ('its correct class is cache') creates the sole-copy-in-a-cache case it admits nothing detects.

serious.scenario: Vendor claim 'nothing S3 lacks'.
serious.why: Not run; from S3's documented checksum set (CRC32/CRC32C/CRC64NVME/SHA-1/SHA-256). put(bytes)->ID needs SHA-512 on the server or trust in the client's key name, and a class word from a vendor is an assertion nobody can recompute. Mirror additionally needs remove and a conditional write, which the proposal concedes may make it L1. If so, L0 has two classes (never delete; no promise), and that is the original tension restated as two words.

philosophy_violations: Verification over assertion: a class word is a promise about tomorrow that cannot be falsified in one command; has() reports presence, not good bytes; demotion 'verified by has()' in the next store verifies a name.

Composition over configuration: semantics live in the ORDER of an environment variable (which store receives writes, which is demoted into, which may evict). The same directories in a different order give different loss behavior (A1, A12).

Fewest concepts, fully load-bearing: three classes, a class file, a root cell, three verbs, a three-valued closure, an 'unaccounted' state, and four compositions, of which two lose data as built. The root listing with dated entries and the journal are two records of the same thing (time + root ID); 'delete duplicate implementations on sight'.

Safe by default, destructive by long-form-explicit: `c4 destroy` has no dry run and acts on every store in the list including archives; the documented cache-thinning recipe has zero grace after a rename demotion (A6).

Determinism: the warrant depends on which listings happen to be present ('an unreadable listing under the OLD root only shrinks the set'), so the same keep on two replicas of a store removes different sets; ingest results depend on what other stores in the list hold (A1).

Partial knowledge is a valid state: keep refuses when any listing under the new root is absent, so a mirror cannot hold a root that describes a subtree it never received; restore remains all-or-nothing on one absent leaf (A1, A2, A10), which the 'destroy leaves descriptions valid' clause depends on.

Check the premise before proposing the fix: the closure rule was stated without the fold entry kind that the built grammar already has (A4), and 'unaccounted is never touched' was tested only with a stray that shared nothing (A2).

Ask what question an artifact answers: a class answers 'who may remove from this store' but the user's question is 'are the bytes my kept description names still somewhere I control'; A1 satisfies the first and fails the second.

Design before code / recorded rulings: reopens 'no deletion verb until a complete root catalog' and the rejected 'second mutable authority' without new evidence; A2 and A5 reproduce the two failure classes those rulings named.

Cost every new concept in implementations: a store-resolving, memoized, fold-aware, chain-aware closure walk with three outcomes is required in five languages before any verb is safe; the estimate of about 12 vectors omits folds, escaped names, list-mode dedup, root-cell contention and crash points.
survives: Undeclared store = archive, and no c4 verb removes bytes by inference. Existing 1.0.x stores, imgbin writes and the default store keep today's behavior. This is the one default that cannot surprise anyone and should be the L0 sentence.

Positive warrant only (difference of two readable closures), never a negative sweep, with dry run as default and refusal on an unreadable listing under the new root. Correct direction; it needs a complete root set to be sufficient, not replacement.

`c4 has` as a real missing primitive with a three-valued answer (held / missing these IDs / unknown below an absent listing). Re-confirmed here: `c4 cat -r` exited 0 on every hollowed snapshot in A1 and A2. This is worth shipping independently of any retention rule, and it must be askable per store, not only through the list.
Vendor contract without a graph walk: put/get/has, optional remove-by-ID, client computes reachability. Matches every adopted CAS standard in the prior-art survey.
Reclamation and destruction as separate acts, with destruction promising only 'these stores no longer serve these bytes'.

Moving bytes to another store instead of unlinking as the recoverable state (proposer E1: dropped snapshot restored in full with the second store in the list). Sound as a mechanism once the dedup-through-list (A1) and grace-clock (A6) problems are fixed.

Copy-out to a fresh store as a reclamation path with no lock, no tombstone and no deletion verb (proposer E3a: identical root ID, 7 objects instead of 12). Its failure mode is a missing copy caught by restore's pre-flight.
The v9 journal left as built, and a cache as a legitimate declared role for a store that is not authoritative.

Does not resolve Joshua's tension: the default remains keep-everything, filesystem-like behavior needs two stores, class files and an ordered list, and 'how would we choose' is deferred to an L2 edit of a listing. What it does contribute is the framing that the store's promise, not a collector, is the fundamental object.
