proposal.name: Described and witnessed (redundancy accounting)
proposal.one_sentence: A store lets go of bytes only when a description still names them and it has just re-read and rehashed the same ID from another configured store; anything else leaves only by explicit destruction by ID, and in both cases the description is unchanged.
proposal.model:
TERMS
- Store: objects named by ID. Operations: put, get, has; optional list and delete(ID).
- Configured set: the ordered list in C4_STORE / ~/.c4/config. The first store is "home" (written). The rest are "witnesses" (read only).
- Leaf: an ID in a file entry. Listing: an ID in a directory entry, or a root ID. Kind comes from the parent entry (name ends "/"), never from sniffing bytes.
- Witnessed(ID, n): at least n stores other than home each returned bytes that were read in full and rehashed to ID during this run. This is the existing check `C4_STORE=<witness> c4 cat <ID> >/dev/null` (exit 0 = present and byte-verified). has() alone is never a witness (E2).

L0 STORE CONTRACT (three sentences, no new format)
S1. A store never removes an object on its own initiative.
S2. Bytes served under an ID hash to that ID; readers rehash, and a mismatch means "no".
S3. has(ID)=false is an ordinary answer. A description naming an ID that a store lacks is still valid; absence never edits a description.

THE RULE
Bytes may leave home only if (1) a description presented to the verb names them, and (2) they are witnessed. Everything else stays. The licence is positive on both sides, so every failure (unreadable listing, truncated walk, unmounted witness, corrupt witness) shrinks the set that may leave. There is no sweep, no root set, and no "unreferenced" class: strays and pre-journal objects are simply never named, so never touched.

VERB: c4 shed [--force] [-n N] [--into <store>] [--witness <dir>] <id | file.c4m | ID...>
1. Resolve the target in home alone. An ID target whose root listing is not in home is refused (exit 1): the knowledge must stay where the bytes leave. A file.c4m target is kept by the caller.
2. Walk the listings that home holds. For each file entry with a non-null ID present in home:
   a. Check witnessed(ID, N), default N=1. If not: keep, count as "sole".
   b. Vacate: rename the object to <home>/shed/<ID> (no longer servable).
   c. Check witnessed(ID, N) again. If not: rename back.
   d. Unlink.
   Vacate-before-verify is the whole concurrency protocol (E6). A crash leaves the object in shed/; the next run resumes from step c.
3. Listing objects are never shed. Home keeps the full description.
4. --into <store>: first put the object into that store and verify it there, then proceed. This is a move. It is the only form allowed for bare IDs and for bytes with no witness. A store used this way is the trash, attic, or archive; no separate trash state exists.
5. --witness <dir>: accept a file at <dir>/<entry path> that rehashes to the entry ID. A directory makes no promise (E7), so this is opt-in and meant for cache-role stores.
6. Dry run is the default. stdout: c4m entries that would leave. stderr: four counts with bytes: held+witnessed (sheddable), held only here (sole), absent here but witnessed, absent everywhere. Exit 2 if anything was kept for lack of a witness.

VERB: c4 fill <id | file.c4m>
Inverse of shed. Copy into home, from witnesses, every object the description names that home lacks, rehashing each, and journal the root once.

VERB: c4 destroy <ID>...
By ID only. Delete from every configured store (the library's MultiStore.Remove already does this). Descriptions are untouched. No tombstone: with no sweep, nothing needs to distinguish deliberate absence from loss in order to proceed.

WHEN THE OTHER COPY LATER VANISHES
Home still holds the description. `c4 restore` refuses and lists exactly the missing IDs, touching nothing (E3c). Any source of the bytes heals it: the original path, another store, a re-download (E3d, E3e). Shed spends redundancy: with N=1, one copy remains, and losing that witness loses the bytes.

SINGLE MACHINE, SINGLE STORE
- Default: nothing is ever removed, as today.
- `c4 id` without -s stays the way to describe bytes that have a living source.
- To get space back: attach any second store (external disk directory, NAS path, S3 URL) and shed. Or, on one disk, create a second store directory, fill it with the descriptions to keep (hard links cost no space), and shed the old store against it. What remains in the old store is exactly the bytes no kept description holds (E5). Deleting that directory is the only destructive act, and it is an ordinary filesystem act.
new_concepts: L0: three store-contract sentences (never removes on its own initiative; served bytes hash to their ID; absence is a valid answer). No format. Cost: documentation only, plus rehash-on-read, which every implementation already needs.

L1 verb `c4 shed` with --force, -n N, --into <store>. Cost: 5 implementations of a loop over a description using get/has/delete, rehash, and rename. Reuses the leaf-vs-listing walk that cat -r and restore already need. Roughly 8-10 conformance vectors (witness present, absent, corrupt, vanishes between checks, missing listing, null ID, duplicate ID, N=2, --into).

L1 verb `c4 fill` (inverse of shed). Cost: 5 implementations, about 4 vectors. Needed because the existing-verb recipe writes one journal line per object (E1) and because 1.0.18 (sharded) and master (flat) store layouts differ, so cp/rsync is not a portable fill.
L1 verb `c4 destroy <ID>...`. Cost: 5 thin wrappers over delete-by-ID across the configured set, about 2 vectors.

Flag `--witness <dir>` on shed (a directory as a weak witness). Cost: 5 implementations of path-join plus rehash, 2 vectors. This is the most droppable concept; without it the imgbin case is not covered.
Transient vacated location `<store>/shed/` in a directory store. An ordering detail, not a persistent state. A vendor store that is only ever a witness does not need it.
Four status words in the shed dry-run narration: sheddable, sole, absent-here, absent-everywhere. stderr only; stdout stays c4m.
Changed wording, not a new concept: 'durable' and 'restorable' are properties of the configured set, not of home alone. The master binary already behaves this way (E3b).
Required fixes this design leans on: journal the claim in home when several stores are configured; restore should materialize what is held and declare the rest (exit 2) instead of all-or-nothing.
removed_concepts: The `<store>/retain` file and its line grammar (gc-requirements.md).
The verdict vocabulary keep/trash/scrub/drop and the fold that derives state from verdict lines.
Aggregate claims, ID-list claims minted for gc, and the reserved journal names `adopted` / `condemned` (amendment gc-A1, which cannot be built against the v9 two-field journal anyway).
Warrants as a record, adoption, substrate sets, and three reserved actors.
The shared/exclusive sweep lock held by every claim path. There is no sweep, and writers only ever write to home.
The mark-and-sweep closure walk and its refuse-on-missing rule (section 5.8). Nothing is removed by unreachability, so an unreadable root list cannot delete anything.
Strays as a managed class. Objects no presented description names are never touched; no report-or-adopt machinery.
The planned `c4 gc` and `c4 retain` verbs and `--empty-trash`. Trash is a store; emptying it is deleting a directory.
The dependency of retention on a complete journal. 1.0.x stores, imgbin writes, vendor stores and unjournaled multi-store claims need no adoption step for shed.

From the lead's hypothesis: the promise list as the authority for reclamation, and with it the current-pointer and named-ref questions. It is not removed for choosing which sole copies to discard (see weaknesses).
Tombstones or drop lines to tell deliberate absence from damage.
proposal.how_a_person_chooses:
For reclamation a person does not choose what goes. They choose how many copies must exist and where: "this store keeps only what is not verifiably held in <other store>, N copies." `c4 shed <snapshot>` then needs no judgment, and its dry run says what would leave and what would be left as the only copy.

For bytes that exist nowhere else, the person chooses by description, in two steps:
1. Move: `c4 shed --into <trash-store>` for a snapshot, or for the unique closure of old snapshots. That closure is computable today (E5: closure(S1) minus closure(S2) printed the old big.bin and mid.bin by name and size). With the trash store still configured, everything still restores.
2. Delete the trash store directory with ordinary tools, after the dry-run report has listed which snapshots get holes, by name and size.

Size is the practical handle. In the real default store, objects under 64 KB are 88.2% of objects and 8.4% of bytes (2.75 GiB of 32.90 GiB), the top 1,000 objects hold 23.19 GiB, and description-like objects total about 0.03 GiB (recomputed from the use-case agent's listing). Keeping every description and every small object forever costs under 9%. The choice that matters is a short list of large named files.

This design gives no criterion for which sole copies to discard (age, count, name). It makes the consequence exact and the act reversible until a directory is deleted. The criterion has to come from an L2 policy.
proposal.how_expectations_are_met:
- No c4 verb removes the last known copy of anything except `c4 destroy <ID>`, which names its victims one by one. Shed requires a rehashed witness at the moment of removal. A corrupted copy under the right name does not count: E2 shows presence-by-name passes and the verified read fails.
- Every failure keeps bytes. Unmounted witness, truncated description, unreadable listing: the shed set shrinks. E7(1): `c4 cat -r` on a description with a missing listing object exits 0 and enumerates 2 leaves instead of 4. In a mark-and-sweep that is the restic #4612 class. Here it means two files are not shed.
- A store with no roots (every 1.0.x store) is neither all garbage nor frozen. It is all "sole" until something witnesses it.
- Shed behaves like moving files to another disk, which people already understand: afterwards the bytes are on the other disk. The dry run says "N entries will exist only on <store>".
- Loss is enumerable. After the witness is gone, home lists exactly what is missing, by name, size and ID, and accepts the bytes back from anywhere (E3). An ordinary filesystem cannot say what it lost.
- "Not kept" never looks like "deleted": the description is byte-identical before and after. E1: after shedding all four files, `c4 cat -r S1 | c4 id -q -` still returned S1.
- Where a surprise remains: shed with N=1 goes from two copies to one. A user who thinks "my snapshots are in my store" and then loses the external drive has lost them. The tool states this; it cannot prevent it.
proposal.destruction_vs_reclamation:
RECLAMATION (space back, nothing lost): `c4 shed`. Scope is home only. Precondition: the description stays and the bytes are witnessed. Safe to automate and needs no human choice. Variant `--into <store>` moves bytes that have no witness; space returns only when that store is deleted or sits on another device.

DESTRUCTION (must be gone): `c4 destroy <ID>...`. Scope is every configured store. By ID only, never by description, so there is no recursive form (the zfs destroy -r lesson). It promises only "no longer servable from these stores", not physical erasure (the shred-to-scrub ruling). Descriptions stay as partial knowledge; restore then reports the ID as missing content.

The two differ in scope (home vs every store), precondition (witness vs none), and who may run them (policy vs a person).

Known limits of destruction:
- The ID stays in every description, so a short secret can be confirmed by guessing. Removing the knowledge too means writing a new description with the ID nulled and destroying the old listing objects, which changes every ancestor ID.
- Stores that are not configured (another machine, a vendor) are not reached. The kept ID is what lets you ask them has(ID) and repeat the act there.
- A destroyed object and a lost object look the same afterwards.
proposal.layer_placement:
L0 (standard)
- ID, c4m grammar, and a store contract of put/get/has plus sentences S1-S3.
- delete(ID) is optional and only needed on a store that is shed from.
- No graph walk, no lock, no journal, no retention record in the standard. A vendor witness store is S3 as it exists.

L1 (toolbox, pure verbs over a description and the configured set)
- shed, fill, destroy.
- The witness check is the existing verified read (`c4 cat ID`).
- The leaf-vs-listing rule taken from the parent entry.
- The vacate, verify, unlink ordering.
- The four-way redundancy report in the shed dry run.

L2 (product)
- Which descriptions to shed and when: "home keeps the newest k snapshots, the archive store holds the rest", size-first thinning, age rules. Anything automatic must be turned on by the user.
- Trash, attic and archive as store roles by convention.
- Evidence L1 cannot check. Root agreement reported by another host (Ash) and git refs/reflog (c4git) are testimony. Those products decide on their own authority and call destroy by ID with a positive list.
- The journal stays what v9 made it (time + ID). L2 reads it to enumerate snapshots; shed does not depend on it.

proposal.cost:
PER LANGUAGE (five implementations)
- Three verbs (shed, fill, destroy), each a loop over a description using put/get/has/delete, rehash and rename. About 15 conformance vectors in total.
- No new file format, no record grammar, no fold, no lock, no reserved names, no journal change.
- The design of record costs 2 verbs, 1 flag, a record file with its own grammar, a staging directory, a journal amendment, 3 reserved actors, a shared/exclusive lock and 38 vectors.
- Optional `--witness <dir>` adds one flag and 2 vectors.

VENDOR
- A witness store: put/get/has and the three sentences. This is what S3 already offers.
- A store that is shed from: delete-by-ID as well.
- No reference graph, no GC, no lock, no journal.

RUNTIME
- Shed reads and SHA-512s every byte it removes, from the witness, twice as specified (before and after vacate). The second read could be reduced to an existence check if the witness is known never to shed.
- On an object store this is egress for everything shed.
- Fill is a full copy unless both stores are on one filesystem (hard link or clone).

FIXES TO EXISTING CODE (found by running, not new concepts)
- Journal claims in home when several stores are configured (E3b).
- Restore pre-flight checks only existence, so a corrupt object is written before it is detected (E2).
- A dry run creates a missing store directory (E3a).
- Restore is all-or-nothing on holes (E4).
- The help text 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable' and 'every journaled ID stays restorable for as long as the store directory exists' must be scoped to the configured set before v1.1.0 freezes.

FIT AGAINST THE USE CASES
- Ash mirror: best fit for the attic (a store, audited, then its directory deleted), for 'pruning is not deletion', and for not triplicating the mirror set. Poor fit for the actual reclaim trigger, which is root agreement reported by another host: testimony L1 will not accept. Superseded versions (0.79 GiB measured) are sole copies and need the sync tool's own destroy.
- c4snap: no benefit. Its leaves are already 'described, not stored'; its problem is superseded description blocks, which shed never touches.
- imgbin: covered only with --witness <dir> (6.23 GiB, all 9,910 files still in the folder per the use-case agent; not re-verified by me).
- Agent undo: no reclamation without a second store. Destroy by ID handles a captured .env.
- 33 GB default store: shed works with no adoption step, but almost nothing there has a witness today. The realistic path is the E5 generation switch.
- c4git: its gc becomes a positive list (shed against the remote's store, destroy what the repo itself used to reference). That removes the measured defect of deleting another tool's snapshot in a shared store. I did not run c4git.

CONFLICTS WITH RECORDED RULINGS
- 2026-07-09 (no deletion verb without a complete root catalog): shed is outside its rationale, since it cannot remove a last copy and its list is positive. Destroy by ID, and deleting the residue store in E5, are inside it. The residue step still discards anything referenced only by an unnamed c4m, softened only by being a whole-directory act with a report.
- v7/v9 pins ('nothing a journal line reaches is collectable'; 'the journal travels with the location-independent store'): after a shed, home alone cannot serve its own journal roots.
- 'c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers' and 'a store is a local directory': this design drops that dependency for retention, in the direction vendor adoption needs.
- gc-requirements 2.1 (verdicts only on journaled roots; interior objects refused): shed and destroy act on any description and any ID.
- Lead's hypothesis: rejects 'dropping an entry is the only way space is reclaimed'; agrees that destruction by ID is separate and leaves descriptions as partial knowledge.

CONSISTENT WITH
- Positive deletion warrant; links never pin; no named refs; nameless journal; vacate-before-overwrite; 'having A and computing A are fungible' (a witness is the identity route); no automatic GC (2025 plan); the Ash rule 'not kept must never look like deleted'; Joshua's 2026-07-10 idea of deletion as moving items to a trash folder (here the folder is a store).
weaknesses_admitted: It does not resolve the tension for one disk and one store. Sole copies are never sheddable, so that user gets 'move to a trash store, then delete the directory', and the choice of which old snapshots go (age, count, name) is not supplied by this design. It needs a policy from one of the other proposals.
Shed spends redundancy. With N=1, two copies become one. If the witness later dies or is deleted, the bytes are gone; home can list what was lost but cannot recover it.
Nothing records where shed bytes went. I keep no location log because it would be an assertion that goes stale. If the config changes, the user has to remember which store was the witness.

The witness check costs a full read and SHA-512 of every shed byte. On S3 or a vendor store that is egress for the whole set. Accepting a vendor's has() instead is assertion, not verification, and E2 shows why that matters.

No network protocol means only co-configured stores can be witnesses. Ash's real evidence (root IDs agree on two hosts) is testimony from another machine, and L1 refuses it. Cross-host reclamation stays an L2 decision executed as destroy by ID.

A directory is a weak witness. E7 lost the old big.bin after an edit, and the next snapshot refilled what was shed. --witness <dir> is only safe for cache-role stores, yet the largest verified-redundant block in the real store (imgbin) needs it.

Concurrency is argued and simulated, not proven. Vacate-then-verify survived three hand-run interleavings on a local filesystem. It is untested on NFS, SMB and S3, and it fails if two processes use different store lists.

A destroyed object and a lost object look the same afterwards. The ID also stays in every description, so a short secret can be confirmed by guessing; removing that means rewriting descriptions and changing every ancestor ID.

It leans on behavior the binary does not have: restore is all-or-nothing on a hole (exit 1), the nulled-ID path exits 3 instead of 2, multi-store claims are unjournaled, and restore pre-flight trusts existence. Making several stores the normal configuration makes those bugs central.
'Descriptions are kept forever' is cheap in the default store (about 0.03 GiB of 32.9) but not for c4snap, where one restatement layer is about 1.5 GB of text. This design gives c4snap nothing.

A second store on the same disk, or hard-linked, is reclaim safety and not durability: same device, same inode. The tool cannot tell a real second copy from a link unless it compares device and inode, and that only works for directory stores.
It still adds three verbs, and 'shed' has no familiar analogue except git-annex drop, whose documented confusions about copy counts would apply here too.

The E5 generation switch reintroduces the withdrawn-gc defect one step removed: whatever the user did not fill into the new store sits in the residue, and deleting the residue deletes anything referenced only by a c4m they forgot.

Experiments used a four-file tree. They show behavior, not scale. I did not run c4git or anything against ~/.c4 or ~/.ash; the imgbin, Ash and c4git statements rest on the use-case agent's measurements.

attack.proposal: Described and witnessed (redundancy accounting): bytes leave home only when a presented description names them and another configured store has just re-read and rehashed them; otherwise only by `c4 destroy <ID>`. Verbs shed / fill / destroy; trash and archive are stores; no retain file, no sweep, no root set.

fatal.scenario: A1 (run). Trash-as-store plus dedup. Store A holds snapshots S1 (old) and S2 (current). User follows the proposal's single-store path: `c4 shed --into T S1`, confirms everything still restores with T configured (it does, exit 0), then deletes directory T. Result: `c4 restore S2` from home fails, 'Missing content for 4 entries; nothing restored' — .env, big.bin (4 MiB), mid.bin, sub/b.txt of the CURRENT snapshot are gone. Shed moved 5 leaves; 4 were shared with S2.
fatal.why: Shed acts on what a description names, not on what only that description needs. Under dedup those differ for almost every file. The proposal's remedy ('shed the unique closure', 'dry run lists which snapshots get holes, by name') requires walking every other kept root, which is the complete root catalog the design claims to have removed; journal roots have no names, and unjournaled roots (1.0.x, imgbin, multi-store claims) get holes with no report. A user who reads 'shed a snapshot' as 'remove that snapshot' loses live data at an `rm -r` that no c4 check guards. This is the 2026-07-09 ruling's defect (caller must enumerate what to keep) reached by the documented workflow.

fatal.scenario: A13 (run). A listing object aliased as a file leaf. proj/shots/ was snapshotted (root SH); `c4 cat SH > proj/docs/shots-listing.txt` (file ID equals SH, verified); proj snapshotted as S3. `shed S3` against a full witness B: shed=3, exit 0. Home alone afterwards: `c4 cat -r S3` exits 0 showing shots/ with no children; `c4 cat -r SH` 'content not found'; `c4 restore S3` 'target incomplete: no stored record for directory shots/'.
fatal.why: The design's central invariant is 'listing objects are never shed; home keeps the full description; the description is unchanged'. Kind-from-parent-entry cannot uphold it: the same ID is a listing under one parent and a leaf under another, and shed sees only the presented description. Home silently loses part of a description (cat -r still exits 0), and if the witness later dies the names for those files are gone. Fixing it across descriptions needs a root catalog. It is not contrived: on master, ingest records every *.c4m file in a tree under a file entry carrying the canonical description ID (A12: shots.c4m entry ID == SH), so the alias arises automatically for the 1.0 habit of keeping c4m files beside the data.

fatal.scenario: A2 (run). Witness is a mirror of home. B = `rsync -a A/ B/` (an external-drive backup of the store, the most likely 'second store' an ordinary user has). `shed S2` against B: every check passes, shed=6, exit 0, restore from the pair works. The next scheduled `rsync -a --delete A/ B/` shrinks B from 4644K to 20K. Restore: 'Missing content for 6 entries'. Zero copies. Same shape for Syncthing/Dropbox-synced store directories and Time Machine thinning.
fatal.why: A rehash proves possession at one instant; shed is permanent. Nothing in the design can test that a witness is independent of home or has promised anything, and the design deliberately keeps no location record. S1 ('a store never removes on its own initiative') is an unverifiable sentence a mirror violates without knowing it exists. The loss is deterministic, caused by the shed itself, and discovered only at restore.

fatal.scenario: A11 (run). Single-disk generation switch, the only space-reclaim path offered to a one-store user. Store A holds two journaled snapshots, a snapshot written by installed 1.0.18 (no journal line; its c4m is in the user's files), and an undo pre-image from `c4 restore --force` run with two stores configured (unjournaled; contains draft.txt 'precious uncommitted edit'). User fills B from every journal root and discards A. From B: the photo object is 'content not found'; the undo pre-image is 'not in the store'.
fatal.why: This is the withdrawn `c4 gc <file.c4m>...` with the unlink replaced by a directory delete. The proposal admits it (weakness 13) but it is the design's entire answer to criterion (c) for one disk, and it loses exactly the classes measured in the real store: 3.99 GiB described only by external c4m files, c4git blobs, unjournaled undo handles.

serious.scenario: A4 (run). Ingest is shed-by-has() in reverse. Home A empty, witness B holds the closure with one flipped byte in big.bin. `C4_STORE=A,B c4 id -s -q tree` prints an ID, exit 0, and writes only 2 listing objects to A (cmd/c4/id.go:550 skips any entry some configured store Has). Original deleted; `restore --force` writes a corrupt big.bin and exits 3. No good copy exists anywhere.
serious.why: The proposal says has() is never a witness, then makes multi-store the normal configuration where every snapshot skips writes on has(). The fix is a trilemma it does not address: verify the witness by full read on every snapshot (cost of the whole shed set per snapshot), or always write to home (every snapshot of a live tree refills what was shed, so shed is futile), or trust has() (assertion). The print barrier fails either way today.

serious.scenario: A9 (run). Witness unavailable and its path not creatable (an unplugged /Volumes drive). `C4_STORE=A,<unavailable> c4 id -s -q newtree` prints an ID, exit 0, one stderr warning, and stores nothing: object count 11 -> 11, journal unchanged, `c4 cat <printed ID>` from home 'content not found'. In the same state `c4 cat` and `c4 restore` fail outright ('Error opening store', 'restore requires a configured store') even for content fully in home.
serious.why: The laptop-plus-external-witness setup the design recommends means: with the drive unplugged, an agent hook that ignores stderr collects snapshot IDs that name nothing, and nothing in home can be restored. Existing bug, not in the proposal's fix list, and central once several stores are normal.

serious.scenario: A5 (run). Listings are the growth and shed never touches them. Tree of 10,000 files (50 dirs x 100 plus one 5,000-file frames directory), 20 snapshots with 3 small files changed each: 80 new listing objects = 14.7 MB; 60 new leaf objects = 2.3 KB. 735 KB of listing per snapshot, about 735 MB/day at 1,000 snapshots/day.
serious.why: The claim 'keeping every description forever costs under 9%' comes from a static 1.0.x store. In the snapshot loop (agent undo) and c4snap (1.5 GB per restatement layer), descriptions are more than 99.9% of growth. For those workloads the design is 'keep every version forever' unchanged.

serious.scenario: A10 (run). Witness chain. Workstation sheds A against NAS store B (N=1, exit 0). NAS admin later sheds B against C (N=1, exit 0). C is a trash store to its owner and is emptied. Workstation restore: 'Missing content for 6 entries'.
serious.why: Redundancy accounting is not transitive, and vacate-first only covers concurrent mutual sheds. The workstation's belief 'it is on the NAS' is recorded nowhere and nobody is told when it stops being true. git-annex needs a location log, trust levels and remote content locking for this; the design omits all three by choice.

serious.scenario: A3 (run). `-n 2` with witnesses B and Blink (symlink to B): shed=6, exit 0, one physical copy of big.bin remains. Same for two mount paths of one NAS share, or a hard-linked store (the proposal's own E5 fill).
serious.why: N counts configured paths, not copies. The studio engineer's 'two verified copies' requirement is satisfiable by one disk.

serious.scenario: A6 (run). Destroy does not do what a person means. (i) After removing snapshot root IDs S1 and S2, `c4 cat <.env ID>` still prints SECRET=hunter2: destroying a snapshot ID destroys a 671-byte listing and no content. (iv) After removing the .env object by ID, the next `c4 id -s` of the live tree puts it back.
serious.why: 'By ID only, no recursive form' means the natural request ('destroy this snapshot', 'purge this secret') either leaves the secret servable or is undone by the next per-prompt hook. With no tombstone, `fill` from any witness that destroy did not reach (unmounted, vendor without delete) also resurrects it. The heal-from-anywhere property and durable destruction are the same mechanism pointed in opposite directions. Destroy also writes to witnesses the model calls read-only, and has no dry run.

serious.scenario: Scale (measured rates, computed totals). Verified read: 1 GiB in 1.10 s. Description walk: 10,071 lines in 0.09 s (about 93 s per 10.4M entries). `c4 cat` per-invocation overhead 5.3 ms. Deciding is cheap; licensing costs a full read of every shed byte twice, plus once more for the dry run, because the four counts require verified reads.
serious.why: 33 GiB: about 100 s locally, about 99 GiB of egress on S3 per run including dry run. 12.46 TB: three passes are 9.7 h at the local best case, about 258 h at the volume's measured rehash rate (86 h per pass), and about $3,360 of S3 egress at $0.09/GB. The gc design of record reads descriptions only (minutes). As a shell recipe the per-object overhead is 34 min for 194k objects x 2, so it must be a verb in all five languages.

serious.scenario: Vendor goal. Joshua wants vendors to 'supply durability/performance guarantees'. This rule accepts only a full re-read as evidence; a vendor's guarantee is an assertion and is refused. A vendor store can only ever be a witness (no atomic rename for vacate), so nothing in the rule ever reclaims space on a vendor store; removal there is destroy-by-ID from a client-computed list, which again needs the root catalog. S1 conflicts with S3 lifecycle rules the customer may already have.
serious.why: The design has no slot for the thing vendors are supposed to sell, and gives the vendor-held store no retention rule at all.

serious.scenario: A12 (run), incidental master bug. Fresh store, single store configured: `c4 id -s -q proj` where proj/docs/shots.c4m exists prints an ID, exit 0; `c4 restore <that ID>` fails 'target incomplete: no stored record for directory docs/'. The root listing names docs/ as c43CWtq...; the stored docs listing is c44Z78X..., which records shots.c4m under the description's canonical ID instead of its byte ID (c44FuTUr...). The file's 355 raw bytes are not in the store.
serious.why: Not caused by the proposal, but it shows the built ingest takes kind from the file extension, so 'kind from the parent entry, never from sniffing' is not a property the proposal can inherit. Any tree containing a .c4m file yields an unrestorable printed ID on master today.

philosophy_violations: Verification over assertion: the licence verifies possession now and treats it as a promise about later. S1 is not recomputable. After a shed, 'where are my bytes' has no falsifiable record (A2, A10).

Fewest concepts: 3 verbs, 3 flags (-n, --into, --witness), a reserved in-store directory, 4 status words, and home/witness roles assigned by position in C4_STORE. `shed --into` is fill plus shed; fill is a second cross-store ingest; destroy is MultiStore.Remove. The root catalog was not removed, it was moved to the user's head and to L2 (A1, A11, A13).

Composition over configuration: the same `c4 shed X` is safe or lossy depending on ambient C4_STORE order and what happens to be mounted; safety of a destructive verb lives in an environment variable.

Safe by default, destructive by long-form-explicit: the actual destructive step for sole copies is `rm -r <trash store>`, outside every c4 check and dry run. `c4 destroy` is specified with no dry run and reaches every configured store.

Capabilities from the outside / never decorate the core: `<home>/shed/<ID>` adds a reserved name inside the store. TreeStore.Walk (store/treestore.go:312, read not run) reports any file whose name parses as an ID, so vacated objects would be listed as present by `list` unless all five implementations and every foreign writer learn the name.
Partial knowledge as a valid state: leaned on, but A13 shows shed turning 'bytes elsewhere' into 'description partly gone' with exit 0, and restore remains all-or-nothing on a hole.
Determinism: dry-run stdout depends on which stores are mounted and their momentary contents; identical inputs give different data on different days.
Zero dependencies / cost: 'S3 as it exists' as witness means paid egress as the price of correctness; the cheap alternative (has) is the assertion the design forbids.
Beside, not instead: this is git-annex drop with numcopies, minus the location log, trust levels and remote content lock that git-annex found necessary.
Design of record conflict left standing: help text 'every journaled ID stays restorable for as long as the store directory exists' is false after any shed.
survives: S2 and S3 as store-contract sentences: served bytes rehash to their ID; absence is an ordinary answer and never edits a description. Both installed 1.0.18 and master `c4 cat` fail on a one-byte flip (run).
has() is never evidence. A4 shows the cost of trusting it on the ingest side as well; this should be applied to ingest and restore pre-flight regardless of which retention rule is chosen.

Positive licence: every failure in the shed path itself shrank the removable set. A home path aliased as its own witness was caught by vacate-first (A3b: shed=0, sole=6). No clocks anywhere, so clock skew has no effect. Foreign writers need no registration to be safe from shed proper.
Vacate, verify, unlink ordering for concurrent mutual sheds on a local filesystem (the proposal's E6; I found no interleaving that beats it locally).
Reclamation and destruction as separate acts with different scope and preconditions, and destruction promising only 'no longer servable'.

Witness-licensed drop is the one reclaim rule only c4 can offer, and it fits the 'may I destroy this copy' class (DIT card reuse, Ash root agreement, imgbin). It is worth keeping as one L1 verb with a narrow contract: leaves only, IDs checked against listing use, never --into, never presented as the retention rule.

Deleting the retain-file grammar, verdict vocabulary, aggregates and reserved journal names. The attack found nothing that needs them back; it found that a complete in-store root record is still needed.
The size observation: 1% of objects hold about 77% of bytes, so human review of large named files is practical. It does not hold for the snapshot loop, where listings dominate (A5).

It does not resolve Joshua's tension; it restates it. One store: nothing is ever removed (the keep-everything horn), or the generation switch (the withdrawn gc). Two stores: the question 'which versions go' becomes 'which store holds them', still unanswered, and safety now rests on an unrecorded belief about another store. What it does answer correctly is a different question: when is a redundant copy safe to drop.
