judges.lens: Does it feel fundamental? I judged each position by whether its rule reads as a consequence of ID + c4m (fewest concepts, each load-bearing, no new format, no vocabulary a vendor or a fifth implementation must learn), and whether Joshua would recognize it as c4 1.0's idea extended rather than a product bolted on. I applied the cap: a fatal finding I accept limits the score to 3. I accept at least one fatal finding against every position, so all scores are 3 or below; the ordering inside that band and the 'uncapped' figure in each reason carry the judgment. I ran one experiment set of my own (J1, /tmp/retention-study/judge-fundamental/j1, master build d1d1b0a, HOME and C4_STORE isolated; ~/.c4 and the repo verified untouched afterwards) to test the idea my hybrid rests on.

rankings.reason: Capped at 3; uncapped I would give it 6, the highest. It is the only position where the retention rule is written in c4m itself: what a store keeps is a listing, that listing has an ID, dropping is an edit, the dry run is `c4 diff`. That is recognizably c4. I accept both fatal findings. x3 (shared store, c4git object released because an undo snapshot reached the same ID, fsck reports 0 missing) shows 'unaccounted is never removed' is false under dedup; the proposer's label 'coincidence' is wrong, it is systematic. x1 (live lock treated as stale, 9 held objects left in trash with no lock) shows the replace-under-lock protocol needs a lease, which would put lock semantics into the store contract. I also accept the concept count: the adversary listed 17 items (lock, trash, rescue, resume ordering, stale-lock rule, empty-N flag, collision rule, nesting convention...). That is the 'one rule plus supports' lumpiness Joshua walked away from. What survives is the shape (positive warrant = reach(old) - reach(new), kind from the parent entry, fail-closed keep side, CAS on the list). My J1 run shows the three worst supports (lock, trash directory, lost old holdings) are unnecessary if the list is a patch chain instead of a rewritten file.

Capped; the position splits in two under my lens. Its L0 half (put/get/has/list/remove-by-ID plus 'a bag removes an object only when its owner asks for that ID') is the most fundamental statement in the study, no attack touched it, and I adopt it unchanged as the standard. Its reclaim half is the least c4-like: implicit roots by sniffing whether an object parses as a listing (a recorded rejection, and two sniffers already disagree 13,851 vs 13,830 on the real store), keep/ and drop/ folder names carrying collector meaning, and roots supplied from outside the store, which is the gc Joshua withdrew on 2026-07-09. I accept all four fatals: a2 (a by-hand snapshot that is an interior node of a dropped root is destroyed with 'unaccounted=0'), a6 (recheck does not replace a lock; a printed claim dangles with no crash), a12 (evict-by-evidence plus reclaim on the other bag gives zero copies), a7 (a keep file truncated at a line boundary is valid c4m and widens the warrant from 1 to 5). a7 matters most to me: c4m's appendability, a core virtue, is exactly what makes an external keep-list unverifiable.

Capped; uncapped about 4. The rule statement is the one most derived from what an ID is (a copy counts only if it was just rehashed), and S2/S3 ('served bytes hash to their ID', 'absence is an ordinary answer and never edits a description') belong in L0. But it answers a different question (when may a redundant copy go) and is not a retention rule: on one disk it is either keep-everything or the withdrawn gc done as a directory delete (A11, accepted). I accept A1 (shed acts on what a description names, not what only it needs; the current snapshot lost 4 files), A13 (the same ID is a listing under one parent and a leaf under another, so 'listings are never shed' cannot be upheld from one description) and A2 (a witness that is a mirror of home). It claims to remove the root set and in fact moves it into the user's head. Three verbs, three flags, a reserved in-store directory, and safety that depends on the order of an environment variable is not few concepts.

rankings.proposal: Store classes (retention is the store's contract)
rankings.reason: Capped; uncapped about 3. The framing that survives is right and short: the store's promise is the object of design, and an undeclared store never removes anything. But class words are configuration vocabulary, not a consequence of ID + c4m; a vendor's class word is an assertion nobody can recompute; and the proposer concedes mirror may not be L0, which leaves two classes (never delete / no promise) and restates Joshua's tension as two words. I accept A1 (mirror,cache: ingest skips on has() in any listed store, so a kept root's bytes live only in the cache), A2 (unaccounted description hollowed through shared content), A4 (folded sequence under-marked: all five frames of a kept snapshot in the warrant) and A12 (cache,archive puts every new snapshot only in the cache). Two of its four advertised compositions lose data as built. The root listing with dated entries plus the untouched journal is two records of one fact.

rankings.proposal: Journal + verdicts (steelman of the v1.1 design)
rankings.reason: Capped; lowest under this lens even uncapped (about 2.5). It is an honest and useful reduction (one file instead of two, and E3c correctly shows two files have no order between a verdict and a later identical claim), and its safety property is the one to keep: removal needs a positive line, so a lost record yields an empty warrant. But it makes retention a second positional grammar with verbs in it ('released', 'destroyed'), unused by diff/patch/merge, existing only in Go, not mergeable by any text operation (X10), with root kind decided by sniffing bytes that flips on a carriage return (X5). I accept X1 (a release names an ID, not the claim it withdraws; the proposal's own time pipe released the current tree: live=0, warrant 7 of 7), X3 (1.0.18-written bytes swept when a journaled root with the same content is released) and X2 (documented rescue prints success over missing bytes). X1 is the Review Method's 'artifact that cannot say what it is an answer to'. This is the direction that produced the smell.

judges.best_hybrid:
A BAG AT L0, AND ONE C4M PATCH CHAIN AS THE STORE'S PROMISE. Almost nothing here is new grammar; my J1 run shows the central piece already works on master with existing verbs.

L0, THE STANDARD (all a vendor implements)
- put, get, has; optional list and remove(ID).
- Three sentences: (1) a store removes an object only when asked for that ID, never on its own initiative; (2) bytes served under an ID hash to it; (3) absence is an ordinary answer and never edits a description.
- reach(D), defined by c4m grammar only: every ID on an entry; descend only where the parent entry says directory or folded sequence; leaves are never opened; a missing listing is an error, a missing leaf is just absent.
- No roots, lock, journal, classes or trash in the standard.

L1, THE TOOLBOX
1. `<store>/holdings.c4m` is one ordinary c4m patch chain and replaces `<store>/journal` (which has not shipped in any release). Every `-s` claim and every restore pre-image appends one entry line before its ID prints: time, name, ID, with the name ending in '/' exactly when the claim is a tree. That carries the root kind the two-field journal lost.
2. Drop = append the output of `c4 diff current new` (boundary ID, the restated entry, boundary ID). Nothing physical changes. Undo = append the entry again.
3. Reclaim (dry run by default, long-form flag to act): warrant = reach(entries removed by sections present in the chain) minus reach(current state), intersected with present objects. Refuse on any chain parse error, boundary mismatch, or unreadable keep-side listing. Objects in neither set are reported and untouched.
4. One real new primitive: a fail-closed, memoizing closure that emits bare IDs (the same walk answers 'does this store hold this description': held / missing these / unknown below here).
5. `destroy <ID>`: remove by ID, long-form, refuses a listing under a held entry, promises only 'not servable from this store'.
No retain file, verdicts, actors, aggregates, adopt, classes, trash directory, lease, or second record.

WHAT J1 SHOWED (three-file trees, hand-built chain; the verbs are unbuilt)
- Base listing + appended `c4 diff` section: `c4 log` lists '+0 -1 ~0', `c4 patch` resolves the current state, `c4 patch -n 1` returns the prior state. So the old promise list is never lost (answers attack R1/x8).
- Released = closure(prior) - closure(current) = S1's listing, old a.txt, old big.bin: exactly 3 objects.
- The strict loader (`c4 id`, `c4 cat -r`) already refuses a section whose leading boundary is not the accumulated state ('patch ID does not match prior content'). Compare-and-swap is already in the grammar; no lock file with stale-lock rules is needed, only the short append lock the journal already uses.
- A removal line restates the entry, so it names which claim it withdraws and carries the ID: a positive warrant (answers X1). A lost, empty or truncated chain yields a smaller warrant; an empty file errors.
- A bare appended entry line is accepted as an add. An entry whose name is the ID itself works (`c4 cat H/<ID>/a.txt` printed 'alpha'), and a later re-claim with the same name resolves to one entry with the newest time.
- Against my own hybrid: (a) 'restated-identical means removal' is a toggle; the same entry appended twice across a boundary removed it, so add must be read-then-append under the lock. (b) An unterminated final line makes the whole chain unparseable (exit 1), where the journal ruling ignored a torn tail. (c) `c4 patch` and `c4 log` exit 0 on tampered boundaries while `c4 id` and `cat -r` refuse.

WHAT THE HYBRID DOES NOT SOLVE
- Dedup with unregistered writers (attacks x3, X3, A2, each run independently). No mechanism fixes it. The rule must be said plainly: only a held entry keeps bytes; in a store that has holdings, a put without a hold is a cache write. c4git and imgbin must hold, or have their own stores.
- Writer versus reclaimer. Proposed: the writer verifies after its append that everything its entry reaches is present, re-putting if not, before printing; the reclaimer vacates, re-reads holdings, then unlinks. The two halves were simulated separately by proposers (E4c, E6); the combination has not been run.
- Scale: chain fold is O(sections x entries) (chain-resolution Defect C), so the C1 fix and a compaction step are prerequisites. Destroy is undone by the next snapshot of a tree still containing the bytes.

ORDER OF WORK (subtraction before addition)
A. Fixes that are right under any design: `cat -r` exits 0 on a missing listing; multi-store claims are unjournaled and ingest skips on has() in any listed store; `-S` does not store the fold ID list; .c4m files in a tree yield an unrestorable printed ID; restore is all-or-nothing on one absent leaf; remove the help sentence 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable' before v1.1.0 freezes.
B. Holdings chain written at claim time, plus drop (logical only). This is safe to ship alone: no byte is removed.
C. Reclaim and destroy, after the race protocol is run under crash and on a real store.
Legacy stores: absent holdings means nothing is ever removed; reclaim by copy-out to a fresh store and retiring the old directory (proposer E3a: identical root ID, 7 objects instead of 12).
The c4-only rule (drop only what another store proves it has now) stays an L2 composition over the closure walk, not a class or a verb.
decisions_for_joshua: Reopen two recorded decisions before v1.1.0 freezes the machine contract: the rejected 'independently-writable master c4m' and the v9 non-c4m journal listed under do-not-churn. New context: v9 rejected a journal that 'masqueraded as c4m while satisfying no chain semantics'; my J1 run shows a promise list can be a real chain (boundaries are verified accumulated-state IDs; it resolves, diffs and has an ID); and gc-requirements.md cannot be built against the two-field journal. Replace the journal with a holdings chain, or keep the journal and accept that a promise list would be a second record of the same fact?

State the rule 'only a held entry keeps bytes' out loud? It follows from three independent runs showing 'unaccounted is never removed' is false under dedup. Consequence: either c4git and imgbin register what they need, or each tool gets its own store and the shared ~/.c4/store advertised in the c4git README ends.

The default position: is 'nothing expires' still the product claim for agent undo (33 GB on your machine, about 2.9 GB/day measured for the loop), or does a default policy drop old entries? No design in this study decides it; the hybrid only makes either cheap.

Default entry name: the ID itself (invents nothing, keeps 'handles are IDs, never refs', one entry per ID with the newest claim time), the scan-start time, or a caller-supplied name (which is a ref namespace and reopens that rejection).

Does the promise list belong in the L0 standard, so a vendor can see and guarantee it, or is L0 only the bag plus three sentences with the promise held by the client? This determines what a vendor's durability guarantee is a guarantee of.

Ship in-place removal in v1.1 at all? Alternative: ship holdings plus logical drop plus the copy-out recipe now (no byte is ever unlinked by c4), and add reclaim later, after the writer/reclaimer protocol has been run under crash and at scale.

Destruction: is 'no longer servable from this store, and it may come back if the same bytes are snapshotted again' acceptable, or do you want a durable record of deliberate absence (a new concept)? Tied to this: must restore materialize what is held and declare the rest, which the hypothesis's last clause and the Design Philosophy both require and neither binary does today?

May a held entry name a description whose listings this store does not have (c4snap, a bounded mirror)? If yes, the keep-side fail-closed rule needs a stated exception or a second entry kind; if no, c4snap must hold every block.

The existing 33 GB store: about 950 objects (roughly 2.5 GiB) have no description anywhere. Is 'never removed unless you choose them by ID and size, largest first' acceptable, or is copy-out and retiring the directory the sanctioned path?

Two chain-grammar edges become load-bearing if holdings is a chain: 'restated-identical means removal' toggles a retried add (run), and an unterminated final line refuses the whole chain (run). Are these acceptable as rules on the writer, or do they need a grammar erratum across five implementations?
judges.is_the_hypothesis_right:
PARTLY RIGHT. The core is right and the framing around it is wrong.

RIGHT
- Retention is reachability from descriptions the store itself has promised to keep. Every surviving part of every position reduces to this, and every loss the adversaries produced came from roots the store could not see (pure bag a2/a7, witnessed A11) or from how a promise is withdrawn (journal X1), never from the reachability rule.
- The promise list is an ordinary c4m in the store. This is the strongest part, and stronger than the lead stated: J1 shows it can be a real patch chain on master today, which supplies compare-and-swap, history, the dry run, and a positive removal line with no new grammar.
- Destruction by ID is a separate act. All five positions and all five adversaries agree.

WRONG OR INCOMPLETE
1. 'One dial' is not fundamental and should be dropped as the headline. What is fundamental is the list; the dial is an L2 policy that edits it. 'Holding one description is ordinary filesystem behavior' is false in cost (a replace walks everything kept, measured at about 77k-108k entries/s with no sharing) and false in the minimum (Ash needs base + new + attic; c4snap needs a chain closure).
2. 'Dropping an entry is the only way space is reclaimed' conflates two acts. Dropping must free nothing; reclaiming is a second, explicit act computed from positive removal lines. A store with no entries (every 1.0.x store) needs a third state: never held, never removed.
3. It omits the sentence users must be able to repeat: only a held entry keeps bytes. 'Unaccounted bytes are safe' was claimed by three positions and falsified by run in each (x3, X3, A2).
4. It omits that entries must be written as a side effect of the act that prints the ID. A hand-curated list is the gc withdrawn on 2026-07-09.
5. 'Leaves descriptions as partial knowledge' is true for cat and diff and false for restore on both binaries (all-or-nothing on one absent leaf). A destroyed object also returns at the next snapshot of a tree that still contains it.
6. As stated it is, on the record, a rejected alternative. It is right to reopen it, but the reopening needs Joshua's ruling, not adoption by study.
judges.dissent:
I expect the other two judges (ordinary-user expectations, and implementation/vendor cost) to converge on a hybrid that keeps the v9 journal as built, adds a recoverable trash or attic store with a grace period, and possibly keeps a store-class word or a second configured store as the safety net. I dissent on four points.

1. THE JOURNAL SHOULD BE REPLACED, NOT PRESERVED. A journal beside a promise list is two records of one fact (time + root ID), in two grammars, with no order between them. That is the defect the journal proposer's own E3c demonstrated for journal + retain. 'Do not churn' protected a file that has shipped in no release, cannot carry root kind, and is silently not written when two stores are configured. Keeping it for continuity preserves the smell.

2. TRASH SHOULD BE A STATE, NOT A PLACE. Every position that made trash a directory or second store was broken through it: ingest dedups against it (x5, A1, E3a), rename preserves mtime so a '30-day trash' has zero grace (x9, A6), and the only irreversible step becomes an `rm -r` outside c4. 'Dropped, not yet reclaimed' in the chain gives the same recoverability with no directory, no clock and no extra store on the read path. The cost is real and I state it: once reclaim runs, the bytes are gone, where a trash store would still have them.

3. DO NOT SCORE 'UNACCOUNTED IS NEVER REMOVED' AS A GUARANTEE. If the expectations judge credits any position for protecting unregistered writers, that credit is unearned: three adversaries ran the dedup case and it failed each time. The honest rule is harsher and simpler.

4. THE C4-ONLY WITNESS RULE SHOULD NOT BE PROMOTED INTO THE CORE. It is the most attractive idea in the study and it answers 'may I drop this copy', not 'what does this store keep'. Promoting it adds verbs, flags and position-dependent store lists, and its own invariant fell to A13.

WHERE I MAY BE WRONG: my hybrid rests on one small experiment with a hand-built chain and unbuilt verbs. It leans on chain grammar whose edges (toggle removal, torn tail, O(sections x entries) fold) could turn into exactly the 'obscure edge cases' Joshua named. If those edges need errata in five implementations, the cost judge's preference for a flat rewritten listing or the existing journal may be the cheaper answer.

judges.lens:
Would real people trust it? Judged as an ordinary user, a studio data wrangler and an unattended agent harness, weighing surprising loss far above inconvenience.

I re-ran three load-bearing claims on the master build (d1d1b0a) under /tmp/retention-study/judge-expectations/v1, with HOME and C4_STORE isolated:
- **Repeat IDs.** Re-snapshotting an unchanged tree appends a second journal line with the identical ID, and `c4 log` shows only index, time and ID.
- **List-mode print barrier.** After moving closure(R1) minus closure(R2) (3 objects) to a trash directory T, I reverted the files and snapshotted with C4_STORE=M,T. The claim printed with exit 0 and no journal line was appended. From M alone, restore said 'Missing content for 2 entries; nothing restored' (exit 1).
- **Truncated closure.** `c4 cat -r` on that same snapshot from M alone exited 0.

I accepted every other adversary finding as reported; I did not re-run them. The hybrid below is a design and has not been run.

rankings.proposal: Holdings: one c4m listing in the store (one dial)
rankings.reason: This is the model people already have: a readable list of kept things with names and dates, removing a line lets it go, a trash, and a dry run that states the bytes. It is also the only proposal where a lost or overwritten root list releases nothing (x8). I accept both fatals as proposed, so it is capped at 3. In x3, thinning undo history sent c4git's only copy of an old version to trash while fsck reported 0 missing and `git checkout` exited 0 with a 90-byte file. In x1, 'a stale lock is resolved by rollback' with no definition of stale left held objects in trash with no lock. Three more findings would each produce an 'it deleted my work' report: a crashed release blocks every save and invites deleting the lock (x2); `hold proj.c4m` reads as additive and released three snapshots (x7); and the only irreversible step is an unguarded `rm -r` on a trash whose mtimes give no grace (x9). Default time-only names also let a 'keep 7 daily' policy thin a wrangler's one-off card snapshot. The removal rule is right; the write path, the verb and the trash are what failed.

It has the safest way of making promises: every printed ID is registered automatically, the default is keep, there is no mutable authority, and an empty journal yields an empty warrant. Nothing in the attack touched that half. I accept the fatals on the withdrawal half. In X1 the proposal's own time pipe released the current state of a project that had been undone or left idle, because a release names an ID and IDs repeat (I reproduced the repeat). In X2 the documented rescue printed success for a snapshot whose leaf was already gone. The trust problem is also plain: `c4 log` gives a person nothing to choose by except a time and a 90-character ID, so choosing is pushed onto scripts, and a script is where X1 happens. An agent harness would run that pipe unattended. `release` is also the wrong word in a project where a release is a published build.

'Undeclared store = archive, no verb removes by inference' is the one default that cannot surprise anyone, and `c4 has` with a three-valued answer is a real missing primitive. I accept the fatals. I reproduced A1: with the trash on the read path, a new kept snapshot's bytes exist only in the store that promises nothing. A12 shows a composition from the proposal's own table putting the only copy of new work in a cache. A2 shows 'unaccounted is never touched' failing for shared bytes. A4 shows a kept folded sequence's frames in the warrant, which hits the media users with the strictest loss expectations. Safety also depends on the order of an environment variable and on a file that rsync carries between stores (A9). 'Mirror' means a safe second copy to every studio engineer, yet here it is the word that opts a store into removal.

'I verified another copy before letting go' is how a data wrangler already works, and shed proper never removed a last copy at the moment it ran. I accept the fatals. In A2 the witness was an rsync backup of the store, the most likely second store an ordinary user has, and the next `rsync --delete` left zero copies. In A1 `shed --into trash` followed by deleting the trash removed four files of the current snapshot, because shed acts on what a description names and not on what only that description needs. A13 shed a listing object and A10 broke a chain of witnesses. A verified read proves possession at one instant; people will read it as a promise. A one-disk user gets either nothing or the withdrawn gc (A11). It answers 'may I drop this redundant copy', not the retention question.

rankings.proposal: Pure bag (roots are c4m files outside the store)
rankings.reason: The L0 contract (put/get/has/list/remove plus 'removes only when the owner asks for that ID') survived untouched and should be the standard. As a retention design it is the worst fit for this lens, and I accept all four fatals. In a2 a by-hand 'back up, then delete' snapshot was destroyed by a nightly policy while the dry run reported unaccounted=0 and `c4 log` still listed it. In a7 a keep file truncated at a line boundary parsed cleanly and quintupled the warrant. In a6 a writer printed a claim whose bytes had just been reclaimed. In a12 evict-by-evidence plus the other bag's reclaim left zero copies. The model also asks people to manage keep/ and drop/ folders and never leave a stale file in drop/, which is a standing deletion order. This is the casync position that Joshua withdrew on 2026-07-09 for the same reason.

judges.best_hybrid:
**Shape.** Promises are made automatically and append-only. They are withdrawn only through a listing a person can read. Withdrawn bytes go to a trash that c4 itself guards. None of this runs in a store that has not been opted in. The rule is reachability, but reads, writes and withdrawals are three separate paths.

**Phase A: subtraction only, before v1.1.0 freezes.** No deletion verb ships in this phase.
1. **L0 store contract.** put/get/has, optional list and remove(ID), plus three sentences: a store never removes bytes on its own initiative; served bytes hash to their ID; absence is an ordinary answer and never edits a description.
2. **Print barrier in list mode.** `-s` must put every object into the first store and journal there. Dedup against other stores in the list must be off for writes. I reproduced this: a printed claim absent from the first store, with no journal line.
3. **`c4 has`.** A fail-closed closure with three answers (held, missing these IDs, unknown below an absent listing), askable per store, with bare-ID output. `cat -r` must stop exiting 0 on a truncated tree.
4. **Restore on holes.** Materialize what is held and declare the rest (exit 2), instead of all-or-nothing.
5. **Help text.** Scope 'nothing a journal line reaches will ever be collectable' to stores with no holdings.
6. **c4git.** `c4git gc --force` must stop treating 'not referenced by this repo' as garbage. It is the one shipped path that already deletes another tool's snapshot.

**Phase B: reclamation, opt-in per store.**
1. **Default.** A store with no holdings file is an archive. No c4 verb removes anything from it except destroy by ID. Every existing store stays as it is.
2. **Making a promise.** Unchanged v9 journal: every printed ID appends `<time> <ID>`. Writers never touch the holdings file and are never blocked by a release. Their only lock is the existing append flock.
3. **The kept set.** kept = reach(holdings entries) ∪ reach(every journal line). Holdings is a one-level c4m listing with one entry per claim, never per ID, so a repeat ID stays kept while any entry or line names it. This is the fix for X1.
4. **Withdrawing.** The user-facing verb is subtractive and names entries: `c4 drop <entry>...`. It is never replace-the-whole-set (x7). It runs in three steps:
   - Fold the journal into holdings: take the append flock, rename the journal aside, release the flock, then add its lines as entries.
   - Compute released = reach(old) − reach(new ∪ live journal). Fail closed on the keep side.
   - Compare-and-swap the holdings.
   
   Dry run is the default. It prints the dropped entry lines, the exact bytes, and the largest released objects by path.
5. **Lock.** The drop lock carries an owner and is never broken by another process or by a rule of thumb. Only `c4 drop --resume` or `--abort` clears it. Saves do not wait on it.
6. **Trash.** `<store>/trash/` is a store. Each drop puts the old holdings listing there and journals it in the trash's own journal. That gives a real release time (x9 showed mtime does not) and makes undo findable: hold the old listing again. Any put or read of an ID in trash moves it back. Trash is never on a writer's dedup path.
7. **Emptying.** A c4 verb, `c4 trash --empty --older-than <D>`, long-form. It refuses while a drop lock exists and recomputes the kept set first. It is never a bare `rm -r`.
8. **Three classes.** Kept, released (in trash) and unaccounted (reported, never removed).
9. **Policies.** An automatic thinning policy may run only in a store owned by one product whose every writer journals (undo plugin, sync tool), and may drop only entries that product created. Claims a person made by hand are never dropped by a policy. This keeps a wrangler's card snapshot out of 'keep 7 daily' and keeps c4git's blobs out of undo thinning (x3, X3, A2).
10. **Shared stores.** The shared default store is not thinned. c4git either journals its blob IDs or gets its own store.
11. **Destroy.** `c4 destroy <ID>`, long-form, dry run by default. It lists every kept entry that will get a hole and refuses the empty-bytes ID (A10). It appends the ID to a plain deny list so the next snapshot does not put the secret back (A6, A9).
12. **Witness check.** A report only: `c4 has --verify` against another store answers 'is this copy redundant right now'. It never licenses an automatic removal (A2, A10).
13. **Legacy stores.** Copy out to a fresh store and retire the old directory, with `c4 has` as the pre-flight.

**What this does not close.** A non-journaling tool whose sole copy shares bytes with a dropped entry in a thinned store is still exposed after the trash window. Only rule 9 or rule 10 prevents it.
decisions_for_joshua: Whether to reopen the rejected writable in-store listing (the 2026-07-10 master c4m) as the withdrawal record, with the v9 journal kept unchanged as the automatic promise record. This needs your ruling that the new context is sufficient: gc-requirements cannot be built against the v9 journal, and release-by-ID is unsafe because IDs repeat.
Whether v1.1 ships with no reclamation at all (Phase A only) and reclamation follows separately. I recommend this; it puts the safe half ahead of the unresolved half.

The default for agent undo: 'nothing expires' (differentiator, disk grows about 2.9 GB/day at 1,000 snapshots) or a stated window that is on by default. Under this lens, a window is acceptable only in a store the plugin owns and only if the user was told the number.

Shared store or a store per purpose. Thinning is only safe where every sole-copy writer journals, so either c4git and imgbin learn to register, or anything that thins gets its own store and gives up cross-purpose dedup.
Whether claims carry a label or owner so a policy can be scoped to what it created. This reverses v9's 'no name, no origin'; the alternative is scoping by store.

Whether L0 is only the bag contract plus 'never removes on its own initiative', with holdings and trash as the reference store's L1 behavior, or whether a vendor store must also offer the mutable holdings cell.
Trash terms: the grace length, who may empty it, and whether an unattended harness is ever allowed to empty it.
Destruction: whether a deny list (a new record) is acceptable so destroyed bytes do not return on the next snapshot, and whether restore may complete with declared holes.
Legacy stores: whether 'never reclaimed in place; copy out and retire the directory' is an acceptable answer for the 33 GB default store, or whether an adoption verb is worth its cost.
Verb words. `hold` reads as additive, `release` means a published build in this project, and `mirror` means a safe copy. Each misreading produced a loss in the adversaries' runs.
judges.is_the_hypothesis_right:
**Partly right.** The core holds, but the hypothesis as worded would produce loss reports in six places.

**Right.**
- Retention as reachability from descriptions the store itself holds is what every trusted system converged on.
- It is the only rule under which a lost root list releases nothing.
- A readable in-store listing is how people choose.
- Destruction by ID is a separate act.

**Wrong or incomplete under this lens.**
1. **'One dial' is not how people hold files.** They hold three things: what I saved (kept until I say), automatic history (thinned by a policy I turned on), and a trash window. Every system users trust has a kept set plus a time-windowed net. A single dial with a filesystem position invites replace-on-save, which costs O(everything kept) and frees bytes other tools relied on.
2. **Promises must be made automatically.** A curated promise list is the withdrawn gc. The promise has to be a side effect of printing the ID.
3. **'Dropping an entry is the only way space is reclaimed' leaves out a third class.** Unaccounted bytes are never removed, and every existing store is 100% unaccounted.
4. **Reachability protects IDs, not the parties relying on them.** In a shared store, dropping an entry removed bytes that c4git alone was keeping (x3, X3, A2). The rule is only true in a store where every sole-copy writer promises.
5. **The withdrawal must be keyed per claim, not per ID.** Unchanged trees and undo repeat IDs (reproduced).
6. **The last clause is not true of the binary today.** Restore is all-or-nothing on one hole (reproduced), destroyed bytes return on the next snapshot, and nothing marks an absence as deliberate.
judges.dissent:
I expect the other judges to favor the smallest contract: the store as a bag, retention pushed to L2, and 'one dial' praised as the elegant statement. I expect at least one to promote the witness rule as the thing only c4 enables. I dissent on four points.

1. **A bag-only standard leaves nobody accountable for the promise.** Every 'it deleted my work' result in this study came from computing removal without a complete, automatically written, in-store promise record (a2, a7, A11, x3, X3). The promise record and a c4-guarded trash-emptying verb belong in the reference store, even though that costs a mutable file and a lock. The cost of concepts is paid once; a silent loss is paid by the user.

2. **Elegance of the rule is not safety of the path.** All five proposals have a tidy sentence, and all five lost data in their own documented workflow. The losses sat in the verb name, the lock, the trash, the list-mode dedup and the policy scope. A judge who scores the sentence will rank these too high.

3. **A verified read is not a promise.** Used as an automatic licence, it reaches zero copies through an ordinary rsync habit (A2) or a chain of sheds (A10). It should ship as a report, not as the retention rule.

4. **The default must be 'never', and v1.1 should ship no reclaim verb.** Disk growth is a nuisance with a workaround (copy out and retire the store). The first unattended thinning bug is the end of trust in a storage tool. I would rather the 33 GB store stay 33 GB for another release than ship any of these five as written.

judges.lens:
Cost to make true (judge-cost): concepts, formats, crash-safety obligations, conformance vectors, what is frozen forever, and migration from 1.0.18 and from the v1.1 journal. Judged as implementer of the ports and as a storage vendor.

Facts I checked myself (read-only on repos; runs under /tmp/retention-study/judge-cost/, HOME and C4_STORE isolated; oss/c4 status clean afterwards, nothing under ~/.c4 newer than my binary):
- "Five implementations" of a store is three today. Go, TypeScript and Python have a store; c4m-swift and libc4 have none (grep). Python's store has has/get/put only. TypeScript adds an optional remove. Only Go has enumeration (TreeStore.Walk) and only Go has the journal (c4m/journal.go, 231 lines). So anything put in the store contract beyond put/get/has is owed 2 to 4 times before it is true.
- Master's RETENTION help (oss/c4/cmd/c4/help.go:415-423) already says "stays restorable for as long as the store directory exists" and "Reclaiming space today means deleting a whole store yourself". A rule that reclaims by retiring a whole store leaves that text true and freezable. Every in-place design falsifies it.
- J1 (/tmp/retention-study/judge-cost/j1): store A with three journaled master snapshots plus one snapshot written by installed 1.0.18 (no journal line), 14 objects. My script gen.py walked reach(S3) fail-closed, hard-linked its 6 objects into new store B, and copied S3's journal line. B alone: `c4 log` lists the root, restore of S3 passes, restore of S1 says "is not in the store". With C4_STORE=B,A, S1 restores. A is untouched. The residue report split the 8 left-behind objects into 5 reached only by the two dropped journal roots and 3 unaccounted, and named the 1.0.18 root as an "unclaimed description" with its entry names.
- J1 hazard: with C4_STORE=B,A a new snapshot printed its ID with exit 0, left B hollow (restore from B alone fails on the reverted file) and wrote no journal line. Re-running with C4_STORE=B alone stored the object, journaled it, and restore passed. This confirms the dedupe-through-list and unjournaled-list-mode defects the attackers found (cmd/c4/id.go:550 and :611).
- J3 (/tmp/retention-study/judge-cost/j3): 50,421-object store, six snapshots, keep two. List 0.08 s; memoized reach 0.09 s (404 listings opened, 50,401 IDs); 50,401 hard links 18.4 s into a flat simulated layout; disk for both stores together 208,564 KB against 208,560 KB for the old one alone. Residue was exactly the 20 objects only the dropped roots reached. Restore dry run from the new store alone passed.
Limits: gen.py/gen2.py are my simulation of an unbuilt verb, local APFS only, names without spaces, no folds or chains, no crash injection.

rankings.reason: Capped by fatals I accept: a2 (a standalone snapshot whose root equals an interior node of a dropped root is removed with 'unaccounted=0') and a7 (a keep file truncated at a line boundary exits 0 and widens the warrant from 1 to 5). Its L2 rule is refuted. Under my lens its L0 is still the best thing in the set and no attack touched it: put/get/has/list/remove plus 'a bag removes only when its owner asks for that ID'. That costs a vendor nothing S3 lacks, admits 1.0.x, imgbin and rsync as writers, and freezes no file, lock or root format. What sinks it on cost is that the safety of the L2 rule needed the sniffed implicit-root predicate (two scanners already disagree, 13,851 vs 13,830, so five parsers would give five warrants) and a recheck that does not replace a lock (a6). The count '0 formats, 1 state, 1 verb' omitted the empty-listing exception, fold and chain rules, drop-file lifecycle and a writer protocol. I take its store contract whole and none of its reclaim rule.

Capped by two fatals I accept. x1: the lock has no owner or lease, so a slow hold and a 'stale lock' rollback leave 9 held objects in trash with no lock present; repairing it puts a lease protocol into the L0 contract for every port and vendor. x3: a c4git object shared with a dropped undo snapshot goes to trash and git checkout writes a 90-byte ID. Cost in its favor: no new parser, about 10-12 vectors, and it deletes the retain file, verdicts, aggregates and 38 vectors. Cost against: it is the only proposal that moves a mutable object, a CAS rule, a lock file and a trash directory into the standard, so the vendor contract grows from put/get/has to conditional create plus conditional replace plus move-to-trash plus lock recovery. It freezes a filename, a default-name rule and a resume ordering. It reverses the ratified v9 journal, so `c4 id -s` and `c4 log` change before the v1.1.0 freeze and four ports owe the write path. Save and delete share one lock (x2: a crashed release blocks every snapshot). Trash has no release time (x9). Each replace costs O(everything kept) under an exclusive lock (s2: 32.9 s and 349 MB of text for 2,000 small snapshots through cat -r). It removes more than it adds relative to gc-requirements.md, but it adds in the one place where additions are multiplied by vendors.

rankings.proposal: Store classes (retention is the store's contract)
rankings.reason: Capped by A1 (a kept root in a mirror reaches bytes that exist only in the cache, because ingest skips on has-in-any-store; I reproduced the same skip in J1) and A2 (an unlisted description sharing a file with a dropped root is hollowed). Cheap parts worth keeping: 'undeclared store = archive' costs one sentence and no code, and `c4 has` with a three-valued answer is a real missing primitive. Expensive parts: a new store-root file whose word is unenforced by the installed fleet (E4) and travels with rsync (A9); a mutable root cell that needs CAS, which on a local filesystem means the lock it claimed to remove (A5: 6 of 40 concurrent updates survive temp+rename); three frozen class words; and loss behavior that depends on the order of an environment variable (A12: cache,archive stores new work only in the cache with no journal line). The '12 vectors' estimate omitted folds (A4 under-marks five frames), escaped names, list-mode dedupe and root-cell contention. If mirror is really L1, L0 has two classes and that is the original tension restated as two words.

rankings.proposal: Journal + verdicts (steelman of the v1.1 design)
rankings.reason: Capped by X1 (a release names an ID, not a claim; restore and idle re-snapshots repeat IDs, so the proposal's own time pipe folded to live=0 and warrant 7 of 7) and X3 (three 1.0.18-written objects swept because a journaled root shared them). It has the cheapest starting point of the in-place designs, since the journal is built and roots are a side effect of printing the ID, and it correctly kills the second record file. But it then freezes the worst kind of thing: a positional grammar with verbs in it. Journal format 2 breaks the v1.1 reader ('want 2 fields, got 3'). The fold makes journals unmergeable and unshortenable forever (X10), which contradicts the head/tail shortening the master help documents. Repairing X1 changes the line grammar a third time. It needs the shared/exclusive lock that is designed, not built, and undefined on NFS, SMB and object stores. Four ports owe the journal, the fold, a byte-sniffing root classifier that flips on CRLF (X5), and the lock. A vendor gets nothing it can implement. About 15 vectors is an underestimate once claim identity and merge order are specified.

Capped by A1 (shed acts on what a description names, not what only it needs; `shed --into T S1` then deleting T removed 4 files of the current snapshot) and A13 (a listing aliased as a file leaf is shed, so home silently loses part of a description while cat -r exits 0). Its L0 is free and correct: the three sentences S1-S3, and 'has() is never evidence', which A4 and E2 show also has to be applied to ingest and restore pre-flight. Its runtime cost is the highest in the set: a full read and SHA-512 of every shed byte two or three times, which is paid egress on a vendor store, where the vendor's durability guarantee has no slot at all. Three verbs, three flags and a reserved in-store directory that TreeStore.Walk would list as objects. It gives a one-disk user no reclamation except the generation switch (E5), which it treats as a fallback. That fallback is the part I keep, as the primary rule.

judges.best_hybrid:
GENERATIONS: the store is a bag, the journal is the promise record, and space returns only by retiring a whole store.

Why this shape. Every fatal in the five attacks came from removing objects in place inside a live store: lock and lease (one-dial x1, x2), trash timing (x9, A6), the writer/collector dedupe race (pure-bag a6, classes A1), CAS on a root cell (A5), and claim identity under a fold (journal X1). Remove the in-place removal and those obligations disappear instead of being specified five times. The history agent flagged copy-out as the strongest untested lead; two attackers listed it under "survives"; I ran it as the primary rule (J1, J3).

L0, the standard. This is all a vendor or a port implements, and all that is frozen:
1. Store = put, get, has. Optional: list, remove(ID).
2. Three sentences. A store never removes an object on its own initiative. Bytes served under an ID hash to it; readers rehash and has() is not evidence. Absence is an ordinary answer and never edits a description.
3. reach(D), defined in the c4m grammar, not in the store. Every ID on an entry is reached. Descend only where the parent entry says directory, folded sequence (ID list) or chain base. An absent listing is an error. An absent leaf is not. The empty listing is special-cased. About 9 shared vectors: flat, nested, absent leaf, absent listing, fold, escaped-bracket literal, chain base, empty directory, symlink.
No roots, promises, classes, locks, trash or journal at L0. A vendor ships S3 as it exists; a generation on a vendor store is a bucket or prefix.

L1, the toolbox. Go first; a port needs only reach and has.
- `c4 has <ID|file.c4m>`: three answers (held / missing these IDs / unknown below an absent listing), asked per store, with a rehash option. `c4 cat -r` must fail on an absent listing and offer bare-ID output.
- `c4 fill <ID|file.c4m>...`: copy reach() into the write store from the read stores without the claim path. Hard link or clone on one device, server-side copy on object storage. Verify, then append one journal line per root.
- `c4 destroy <ID>...`: remove by ID from the named stores, long-form, with a dry run. It promises only "no longer servable here".
- The journal exactly as built (`@c4 journal 1`, `<time> <ID>`). It is L1 state of a directory store. No format change, no release lines, no retain file.

L2, the product. None of it is frozen.
- The dial is which journal roots are filled into the next generation. One root is filesystem behavior, all roots is full history, and never switching is today's v1.1.
- Procedure: make an empty store N. Fill the kept roots, chosen by time from `c4 log` or by a keep c4m with names. That keep file is the lead's promise list, used as an immutable argument; it can itself be claimed in N so the whole promise has one ID. Run `c4 has` on every journal root of N against N alone. Point C4_STORE at N. Keep the old store O readable as the trash for as long as wanted. Read the residue report. Retire O by deleting its directory or prefix.
- The residue report is list(O) minus list(N) in three groups: reached only by journal roots not kept (listed by time), unclaimed descriptions (a report-only sniff, showing entry names), and unaccounted bytes largest first. It also lists any O journal lines appended after the switch.
- Thinning policies (keep 7 daily, 30 days of undo) are programs that pick roots, off unless turned on.
- The only mutable binding is one that already exists: which directory C4_STORE names.
- The witness rule is the same check across machines: O may be retired when another store verifies the kept closure. This matches Ash ("the store exists only during a sync"), DIT card reuse, and imgbin's cache store.

Prerequisite fixes on master. All were found by runs, and all are needed under any design:
- Ingest must test and write store 1, not has-in-any-store (id.go:550, :611).
- Journal the claim in store 1 when several stores are configured.
- `cat -r` must fail closed.
- `-S` must store its ID list.
- A .c4m file inside a tree must be stored under its byte ID (attack-distributed A12).
- `id -s` must not print an ID when nothing was stored (A9).
- Restore should materialize what is held and declare the rest.

Cost count. Formats: 0 new. Store-root files: 0 new. Verbs: has, fill, destroy. Locks, leases, CAS, tombstones, trash timestamps: none. Vectors: about 9 reach, 4 has, 3 fill, 1 destroy, against 38. Migration from 1.0.18: none, those stores are simply never switched until someone claims the descriptions the report lists. Migration from v1.1: none; the journal and the RETENTION help text stay as written. gc-requirements.md and the retain file are withdrawn.

What it costs that the others do not.
- A switch is O(kept objects), not O(change). Measured: 50,401 links in 18.4 s, zero extra bytes. Extrapolated, not run: about 70 s at 194k objects and about an hour at 10M. So it is a batch act, not a per-save act.
- Across devices it is a full copy.
- Space returns only when O is deleted.
- Shared-content hazard: a writer that never journals (c4git, imgbin, 1.0.x) loses bytes at retirement if nobody filled them. The report shows them, but only "every writer claims" closes it. For c4git that is one Journal.Append per blob, or its own store.

Scripts and artifacts: /tmp/retention-study/judge-cost/gen.py, gen2.py, j1/, j3/.
decisions_for_joshua: Is 'no in-place deletion verb, ever; space returns only by retiring a whole store generation' acceptable as the rule? If yes, v1.1's journal and RETENTION help text freeze as written. If in-place reclamation is required, a lock or lease, CAS and trash timing enter the contract and must be specified per medium.

Does the L0 store contract contain no retention concept at all (put/get/has, optional list/remove, three sentences)? That moves 'the store names its own roots' from the standard to the Go toolbox and drops 'c4's tools are the only sanctioned writers'.

Reopen the 2026-07-09 ruling explicitly: once list-mode journaling is fixed, is the v1.1 journal a complete root catalog for stores written only by v1.1 and later? For legacy stores: adopt by claiming the descriptions a report lists, or never reclaim them?

The shared default store. Either ~/.c4/store stays shared by c4, c4git and imgbin and is archive-only forever, or stores become per-purpose, or c4git journals each blob it writes. No design in this study makes a shared store with unregistered writers safe to reclaim.
Default position of the dial for agent undo: 'nothing expires' (the built behavior and a stated differentiator) or an opt-in window of N days or N snapshots. Unchanged by any proposal and still open.
Names. May an L2 keep-list c4m carry meaningful names as inert labels, given 'handles are IDs, never refs' and the v9 nameless journal? Without names people can choose only by time.

Destruction record. Accept no tombstone at L0 (a deliberate hole and damage look the same; the next snapshot re-stores a secret still in the tree), or add one record somewhere and pay for it in every port.

Restore on holes. Change restore from all-or-nothing to 'materialize what is held, declare the rest' before the v1.1.0 machine contract freezes. Until then 'descriptions stay as partial knowledge' is false for the one verb undo depends on.
Formally withdraw gc-requirements.md and the <store>/retain architecture accepted 2026-07-10, amended in place. It cannot be built against the v9 journal in any case.

Scope of 'five implementations'. Swift and C have no store today, Python has no remove or list, and only Go has a journal. Decide which ports must ship a store, and whether reach and has are the conformance floor.
Which time a fill writes into the new generation's journal line: the original scan-start (my simulation carried the original line) or the time of the fill.
judges.is_the_hypothesis_right:
Partly right. The definition is right; the mechanism is the expensive part and should be dropped.

Right:
- The kept set is reach() from descriptions the store has promised. Every proposal and every attacker ended there, and the reachability sentence itself was never refuted.
- It is one dial, from one description to all of them. That holds at L2. L0 has no dial.
- Destruction by ID is a separate act that promises only "no longer servable here".

Wrong, on cost:
- "The promise list is itself an ordinary named c4m in the store." A mutable in-store list is the single most expensive object proposed. It needs compare-and-swap (proposer's own E4d; classes A5 lost 34 of 40 updates without it), a lock with a lease (one-dial x1), and its own history (x8: one lost file and the catalog is gone). It also puts all of that into the vendor contract. The built journal already records promises as a side effect of printing the ID, append-only, with no CAS. The c4m list is still useful, but as an immutable argument to a fill, not as store state.
- "Dropping an entry is the only way space is reclaimed." Removing in place on a list edit is where every fatal came from. The cheap true statement is that a list edit never removes bytes; retiring a store generation does.
- "Leaves descriptions as partial knowledge." True for cat and diff, false for restore on both binaries (run by five agents). It becomes true only after a restore fix that nobody has costed.

On the tension as Joshua stated it: neither horn is forced. A store that never removes anything is not "every version forever" once stores are cheap and plural. History is whichever generation you chose to fill, and the filesystem-like position is retiring the old generation. Nothing has to mimic block storage.
judges.dissent:
I expect the other judges to favor a repaired Holdings design: an in-store named c4m promise list with a trash state. It matches the snapshot-folder model people learn fastest and it reads as fundamental. From the cost side I think that is the wrong call, for three reasons.

1. The repairs are the design. After the attack it needs a lock lease, a release timestamp, verify-under-lock in every writer, a memoizing reach primitive, and a root-list history. Each lands in L0, multiplied by ports and vendors. Three of the ports have a store today and one has a journal.

2. "Unaccounted bytes are never touched" is being credited as protection for unregistered writers. It is not, in any design including mine. Content addressing means a c4git or imgbin object is in the warrant the moment a dropped root shares its ID (run three times by three attackers). Only "every writer claims" or "nothing is removed in place" closes it. A judge who scores Holdings or the journal design above 3 is implicitly accepting that hazard inside a live store, where it is silent. A generation switch at least confines it to one visible act with a report.

3. Replacing the ratified v9 journal with holdings.c4m churns the one piece of v1.1 that is built, crash-reasoned and listed under do-not-churn, to gain names that L2 can supply in a keep file at no cost to the standard.

Second dissent, against my own hybrid, so it is not oversold. Generations are O(kept) per reclaim and need a full copy across devices. They will feel worse than "delete a snapshot, see space return". A judge weighting user expectations may be right that people will not tolerate a batch step. If Joshua rules that in-place reclamation is required, the least-cost in-place form is the positive warrant moved to a second store, driven from the existing journal, in a store where every writer journals. It is not a new mutable list.

missing: STAKEHOLDER: c4d. Nobody opened oss/c4d (parked, last commit 9821074, 2026-03-11). It already contains the opposite rule to everything the study endorsed (source read, not run): a timer-driven negative mark-and-sweep (serve.go startGCLoop: every 60 s, faster under space pressure) from one mutable root plus in-memory refcounted holds (internal/c4db/db.go Hold, lost on restart); sweep unlinks immediately with no trash (gc.go sweep); a description that is absent or fails to parse is silently not traced (gc.go loadC4mFromStore returns nil -> restic #4612 class); plus TTL namespace expiry, max_store_bytes, and DELETE-by-ID over HTTP. Its store is ~/.c4d/store, separate from ~/.c4/store. Any L0 rule must say whether this code is withdrawn like `c4 gc` was; c4d is the piece that sits where a vendor would.

REQUIREMENT: durability, not only retention. Joshua's words were 'storage reliability'. Every position treats that as 'do not delete wrongly'. None covers silent corruption or media loss of a single-copy store: no scrub schedule, no repair-from-another-store rule, Has() is a stat (TreeStore.Has), restore pre-flight trusts existence. A store that never removes anything still fails ordinary expectations on one bad sector. Verify-and-heal across stores is the c4-only capability here and it has no verb in any hybrid.

FACT NOBODY RECORDED: whether the store holds the only copy. New measurement (read-only; /tmp/retention-study/critic/c4/redundant.py; sizes and IDs from the use-cases listing, Spotlight candidates confirmed by `c4-master id -q`): of the 200 largest objects in the default store (18.23 GiB, 55% of bytes), 121 objects / 8.27 GiB have a byte-identical ordinary file elsewhere on this Mac. That is a lower bound of 25% of the whole 32.9 GiB store being a second copy today. No design stores or can recompute 'ingested from a source that still exists', so 'how would we choose?' lacks its cheapest first answer: verified-redundant bytes go first. The witness proposal had this and was demoted to an L2 afterthought by all three judges.

DESIGN OPTION: ownership by creation instead of by reach. All three judges wrote that no mechanism fixes the shared-store dedup loss (x3, X3, A2). Untried: a dropped claim releases only objects that claim itself added to the store (ingest already knows this; cmd/c4/id.go skips on Has). In x3 and X3 as run, the unregistered writer wrote first, so the created-set of the later claim excludes its bytes (X3's own data: master 'added only a journal line', created-set empty, warrant would be 0 instead of 3). The reverse order stays open.

PRIOR ART NOT CITED: git freshens the mtime of an existing object when a writer re-writes it, which is what makes its prune grace protect a dedup hit. Run (/tmp/retention-study/critic/c2): master does not do this; re-snapshot left the mtime of all 3 pre-existing objects unchanged. Freshen-on-dedup-hit is the known answer to the writer/collector race (pure-bag a6) and to the reverse-order dedup case, at the price of a clock.

DESIGN OPTION: several promise lists, one per promiser (ZFS holds; the prior-art agent flagged it, no proposal used it). kept = union of lists; a policy may edit only its own list. This scopes thinning without 'one store per purpose' and without a ref namespace inside one list. Judge-expectations rule 9 reaches for it by store ownership instead.

DESIGN OPTION: shrink growth instead of choosing what to delete. attack-distributed A5 measured 735 KB of new listing objects per snapshot against 2.3 KB of leaves on a 10,000-file tree: in the snapshot loop, descriptions are the growth, caused by rewriting a whole one-level listing per change. Nobody tested snapshots written as patch sections against the previous snapshot (an existing primitive; c4snap already does it). If growth falls to KB per snapshot, 'nothing expires' may be affordable for undo and the retention question narrows to a few large leaves.

FAILURE MODE: the store itself gets backed up, synced or rolled back. A Time Machine or rsync restore of a store directory puts back an old journal/holdings against newer objects (entries naming reclaimed bytes) and resurrects destroyed bytes. A store on a snapshotting filesystem (APFS local snapshots, ZFS) returns no space on reclaim. No design has a rule for a restored store; only rsync-merge (X10, A9) was touched.

STAKEHOLDERS: (a) studio IT/legal: who is 'owner' on a shared NAS store (objects are 0600; anyone with write access can drop or destroy), contractual retain-until for camera originals, legal hold, erasure requests where filenames and IDs survive in descriptions. S3 Object Lock retain-until was listed as prior art and no proposal offers a time-bounded promise. (b) A real vendor: none was consulted or tested; a promise a customer can check ('do you promise this until X?') does not exist in any design, only has() now. (c) Windows/NTFS (beast2, planned Avalanche Windows app): every lock, rename, hard-link and mtime result is APFS-only. (d) Avalanche app users who never see a CLI or an ID.

FAILURE MODE: accidental ingest. 1.0.x writes to the store on a bare `c4 <path>`; the default store came from two bursts (March, April) and at least a quarter of it duplicates files still on disk. Some of the 'explosive growth' is bytes nobody meant to keep. No proposal asks whether v1.1 should store only when the caller states the store's role for that ingest.
unverified_claims: Judge-fundamental: 'compare-and-swap is already in the grammar; no lock with stale rules is needed'. Run (/tmp/retention-study/critic/c1, copy of the judge's store and chain): a second drop section computed against the stale base and appended makes `c4 id` and `c4 cat -r` refuse the whole file ('patch ID does not match prior content (line 7)') while `c4 log` and `c4 patch` exit 0 and apply both drops (resolved state: tree@3 only). So it is detect-after-write, the append-only file is then unreadable to strict readers until someone truncates it by hand, and two verbs disagree on the kept set.

Judge-fundamental: chain holdings cost. The O(sections x entries) fold was quoted from chain-resolution.md, not measured. Run (/tmp/retention-study/critic/c3/chain_scale.py): 10,000 entries + 200 drop sections resolves in 29.2 s against 0.08 s for the flat listing; 2,000 entries + 800 drops takes 17.8 s; same ID as the flat form in every case. About 146 ms per section at 10k entries. Unusable for per-prompt claims without compaction, and compaction is the rewritten mutable file the hybrid said it removed.

Judge-expectations: all of Phase B is unrun (stated). Two specifics fail on source read: (1) 'fold the journal by renaming it aside under the append flock': Journal.Append opens the path (c4m/journal.go:82) before it takes the lock (:88), so a writer that opened before the rename appends to the renamed-aside file after the fold has read it, and a printed claim is missing from the kept set. Not run as a race. (2) 'kept = reach(every journal line)' needs root kind, which the two-field journal does not carry, so the hybrid inherits byte sniffing on the keep side.

Judge-cost: generations were run only with `ln` into a flat simulated layout on one APFS volume. Not run: the real TreeStore layout and API, cross-device copy, S3 server-side copy (S3Store has no list, so no residue report), a writer active in the old store during the fill, Windows. The 70 s at 194k objects and one hour at 10M figures are extrapolations. Hard-linked generations share inodes, so the old store kept 'as trash' is not a second copy: corruption or an overwriting scrub hits both.

All three judges: 'no mechanism fixes dedup with unregistered writers'. Asserted from three attack runs; no one tried a fix (created-set release, freshen on dedup hit, per-promiser lists). Also unchecked: whether imgbin's Store.swift and c4git's clean filter call put unconditionally or test has() first, which decides whether a store could even observe their reliance.

Default-store characterisation rests on heuristics: 13,851 vs 13,830 'listing-like' objects, 96 or 114 root candidates, '~950 objects / 2.5 GiB with no description anywhere' (Spotlight-dependent), and 'sole copy cannot be determined'. My partial check found 8.27 GiB provably redundant among the top 200 objects, so the last statement is too strong.

Growth figures used to frame the default-dial decision were not re-measured: 2.9 GB/day at 1,000 snapshots (memory note), 86 h rehash and 12.46 TB for c4snap (its requirements doc), 0.79 GiB superseded in the Ash mirror (one push.log). 'Largest 1% holds 77% of bytes' is from a static 1.0.x store and A5 shows the snapshot loop has the opposite composition.

Vendor claims: 'nothing S3 lacks', conditional create and conditional replace for a root cell, server-side copy for fill, lifecycle interaction. No experiment touched any object store, though Go has an S3Store. NFS and SMB behaviour of flock, O_EXCL and rename: also never run.

Port claims: 'five implementations is three stores, one journal' is from grep. No port was executed. Whether c4py, c4ts, c4m-swift and libc4 agree with Go on the ID of a holdings-style listing (null sizes, reordered lines, escaped brackets, fold entries, the empty listing) is assumed by every hybrid's vector count.

Crash safety: no run killed a process or cut power. Every 'crash' was an injected exit in a shell simulation, and gc, hold, keep, shed, fill, release and destroy exist in no binary. 'Resumes correctly' and 'fails closed' are properties of the simulations.

imgbin 'put() clones on APFS' is from a source comment. My grep finds no clonefile, link or Chtimes call in oss/c4 store or cmd/c4 (only restore's chtimes), so Go-ingested objects are full copies; nobody measured logical bytes against space actually returned by deleting objects.

'Restore should materialize what is held and declare the rest' is a prerequisite in all three hybrids and was never prototyped. propose-distributed E4 showed the nulled-ID path exits 3 with 'verification failed', so the interaction with the as-built verification and the print barrier is unknown.

Prior-art root causes (Harbor #19308, distribution #4461, restic fix release, git-annex, Venti/Fossil recovery, Nix) come from issue text and search summaries; no tool was run. The c4d findings in my 'missing' list are likewise source reads, not runs.
next_experiments: Created-set release. Record store listing before and after each claim (shell is enough), then re-run attack x3, X3 and A2 in both writer orders with the rule 'a drop releases only what that claim added, minus reach(kept)'. Count which fatals close. Then add touch-on-dedup-hit and repeat the reverse order. Read imgbin Store.swift and c4git clean to see whether they put or has-then-skip. Settles the judges' shared 'no mechanism fixes it' and the shared-store-versus-store-per-purpose decision.

c4d as built. With HOME and store isolated, start c4d from the repo, put a nested description plus content, remove or corrupt one intermediate listing, wait one GC cycle, and check whether the children are deleted; restart the daemon while an ingest holds IDs. Settles whether c4d's sweep must be withdrawn before any L0 store contract is written.

Sole-copy census. Extend /tmp/retention-study/critic/c4/redundant.py from the top 200 to every object of 64 KB or more (about 23,000 objects, 91.6% of bytes) and add the /Volumes/External HDD backup as a second place to look. Output: bytes that are a verified second copy, bytes that are sole copies. Settles whether Joshua's own store is mainly a cache problem (witness rule first) or a history problem (promise list first).

Loop growth composition. Take 1,000 master snapshots of a real repo under agent-like edits; split new bytes into listings and leaves. Repeat with each snapshot stored as a patch section against the previous one. If growth drops to KB per snapshot, the default-dial decision for agent undo changes and 'nothing expires' may stand.

Promise record bake-off on one workload (30,000 adds, 1,000 drops per day, two concurrent writers): v9 journal, flat rewritten listing, patch chain. Measure per-claim latency, resolve time, behaviour after a torn tail and after a stale-base section. I measured the chain at 146 ms per section at 10k entries and a permanent strict-reader refusal after one stale section; the other two columns are missing. Settles judge-fundamental against judge-cost.

Writer versus reclaimer, combined, in a Go test harness on the real TreeStore layout (not shell, not flat): randomized interleavings with kill -9 at every step, invariant 'every printed ID restores from the first store alone'. Run it for in-place release, for move-to-second-store, and for a generation fill with a live writer on the old store. Settles whether any in-place form is shippable and whether generations really avoid the race.

Journal fold race. Go test: one goroutine loops Journal.Append, another renames the journal aside and reads it; count appended claims missing from both files' union as read by the folder. Settles judge-expectations rule 4.

Generations on real media. Fill 194k objects through the store API on the same volume (link, then APFS clone) and across volumes; record time and extra bytes; flip one byte in the old store and check the new one. Settles whether 'keep the old store as trash' is a copy or the same inodes, and the batch cost judge-cost extrapolated.

Object store reality check. Point the existing S3Store at MinIO or a scratch bucket: reach, has with rehash, fill by server-side copy, remove by ID, a conditionally written root object, list cost, egress for a verified read. Settles 'a vendor needs nothing S3 lacks' and whether a promise list can live at L0.

Port agreement. Feed the same holdings-style listings (null sizes, reordered lines, escaped bracket name, fold entry, empty directory, CRLF) to c4py, c4ts, c4m-swift and libc4; compare IDs and the reach() ID sets with Go. Settles the real conformance cost of reach() and whether kind-from-parent-entry is uniform.

Restore with holes. In a /tmp clone of oss/c4, prototype 'materialize what is held, exit 2 and list the rest'; re-run propose-distributed E4, attack-contract A10 and attack-distributed A9. Every hybrid and the hypothesis's last clause depend on it.

Blind user simulation (the crucible's cheap-model method). Give each hybrid's verbs and help text to simulated users with three tasks: free 10 GB, get back yesterday's file, purge a leaked .env. Count destructive misreadings (hold, release, mirror, trash emptying). Settles the trash-as-place versus trash-as-state dissent and the verb names.

Store rollback. Copy a store, drop and reclaim in the original, then restore the copy's journal or holdings over it (and the reverse: restore old objects under a new record). Record what each hybrid's reader does. Settles whether the promise record needs to be verifiable against the objects present.
